modulos.titulo: Módulo 1 — Money, blockchain and Bitcoin (≈17 min)

aulas.titulo: Aula 1.1 — What money actually is
aulas.gancho: A fifty-euro note is a piece of paper. So why do you agree to trade a day's work for it?

cenas.visual: Black screen. Text appears letter by letter: "Educational content. This is not financial advice. The risk of loss is real." Then Ruben in a medium shot, almost black background, gold details.
cenas.narracao: Hi, I'm Ruben Pereira, and this is the A Primeira Chave bootcamp. Before we start, there's a warning you must not skip. This bootcamp is educational. It is not financial advice. I won't tell you what to buy, or when. Crypto is a high-risk market: prices can fall a lot, and you can lose everything you put in. So the first rule of this house is this: never invest money you can't afford to lose. If you need it for next month's rent, that money is not for crypto. I've said it, and I'll say it again at the end of the module. If there's one thing from this bootcamp that stays with you, let it be this.

cenas.visual: Animation: a fisherman with a basket of horse mackerel at the door of a bakery. Two arrows cross between the two of them, and a question mark appears between the arrows.
cenas.narracao: Before money, people swapped things. Imagine you're a fisherman in Peniche. You take a basket of horse mackerel to the bakery, because you need bread. But what if the baker doesn't want fish that day? Or what if the fish spoils before he wants it? Economists call this the lack of a double coincidence of wants: the person who has what you want doesn't always want what you have. Direct swapping works, but it's slow and depends a lot on luck.

cenas.visual: Animated timeline, from left to right: shells, salt, metal coins, a paper note and, at the end, a balance flashing on a phone screen. At each step the object disappears and the same word stays in the centre: "trust".
cenas.narracao: That's why, throughout history, people chose objects that almost everyone accepted. There were shells, salt, livestock, metals. Then came coins, and after them paper notes. Today, most money isn't even paper. It's a number on your bank's screen. You pay for a coffee with your phone, you send money through a payment app, and none of it passes from hand to hand. It's still money, because you still trust the system that recorded it.

cenas.visual: A castle with three pillars, gold on charcoal. The pillars have captions: "the baker accepts", "the landlord accepts", "the State accepts". One of the pillars starts to tremble, subtly.
cenas.narracao: Notice what this means. If trust is the foundation of everything, whoever controls the system controls that trust. A central bank can create more units of currency. A government can change the tax rules. I'm not saying this is bad by definition. I'm saying it's a human choice, made by human institutions, and those choices reach everyone's wallet. As long as the three pillars are standing, the note is worth something. If one of them starts to tremble, the conversation changes.

cenas.visual: A fifty-euro note next to a bank card. Underneath, the sentence appears gradually: "Money is a promise."
cenas.narracao: The first big consequence of money being a promise is called inflation. You'll see it in the next lesson, with a coffee and a simple sum anyone can do in their head. For now, keep this idea: promises can be kept or broken, slowly and quietly.

cenas.visual: Ruben with an open notebook on the table. A two-minute timer appears in the corner of the screen.
cenas.narracao: Before we finish, a two-minute exercise. Take a note, or look at your bank balance. Ask yourself: what do I believe in, to accept this as value? Write the answer by hand. There's no right answer. The goal is for you to realise that you already trust many things without thinking about it.

aulas.titulo: Aula 1.2 — Inflation and the coffee
aulas.gancho: If you keep a thousand euros under the mattress for ten years, what can they buy at the end?

cenas.visual: A coffee in a cup, with a one-euro price tag. The tag starts to rise, cent by cent, like a counter ticking.
cenas.narracao: Let's do a sum. A coffee costs one euro today. It sounds like very little, and it is very little. Now imagine prices rise four percent a year. This is a round, hypothetical number, just so we can do the maths. It's an illustrative example, nothing more. After one year, the coffee costs one euro and four cents. After five years, it costs about one euro and twenty-two. After ten years, it reaches one euro and forty-eight. Nobody notices anything special. It's a cent here, another there, and suddenly the same coffee costs almost half as much again.

cenas.visual: Animated line chart: the price of the coffee rising year by year, with the 1, 5 and 10 year marks highlighted.
cenas.narracao: Now think about your money. If you have a thousand euros sitting in a drawer, ten years from now you still have a thousand euros on paper. But those thousand euros no longer buy what they used to. To keep being able to buy in ten years what a thousand euros buys today, you'd need about one thousand four hundred and eighty euros. Put the other way round: today's thousand euros are worth, in purchasing power, about six hundred and seventy-six euros.

cenas.visual: Two bars side by side. The first, full, labelled "1000 €". The second, shorter, labelled "≈676 € of purchasing power", with the difference slowly disappearing bit by bit.
cenas.narracao: Notice that this sum doesn't need a special year or a crisis. A small, steady inflation is enough. A rate of two percent, which is the European Central Bank's medium-term reference, already cuts money's purchasing power in half in about thirty-six years. Nobody feels that in a month. You feel it over a whole lifetime.

cenas.visual: Split screen: on the left, the formula "72 ÷ 4 = 18", on the right an hourglass emptying to the halfway mark.
cenas.narracao: There's a practical rule worth memorising. It's called the rule of 72. You divide 72 by the inflation rate, and you get, in years, how long it takes for money to lose half its purchasing power. At four percent, that's eighteen years. It's an approximation, but it gives you the order of magnitude. And the order of magnitude is what you need to decide well. When you hear someone say inflation isn't anything anymore, come back to this sum. A small number, repeated for years, is a huge force.

cenas.visual: Illustrative example: Inês, twenty-nine years old, a nurse in Coimbra, with a simple portrait and a drawn ID card, sitting at her desk with three thousand euros in a current account.
cenas.narracao: Let's be honest. Inflation isn't anyone's plan to harm you. It's a phenomenon that results from many decisions: demand, costs, monetary policy. But its effect always arrives the same way. Inês had three thousand euros in a current account earning practically nothing. She didn't want to risk everything, and she didn't want to watch her money shrink either. The first thing she did was understand the problem, not choose a product. That's the step I want you to take too. Before any decision, know how much money you have, how long you can leave it idle, and what the effect of inflation is in that specific case.

cenas.visual: Ruben with a calculator on screen. A list of four everyday prices appears: bread, petrol, a transport pass, part of the rent.
cenas.narracao: This matters for the rest of the bootcamp, because it's the first reason people look for alternatives. It's not because they want to get rich quickly. It's because they want their savings not to melt away in silence. So throughout this bootcamp, whenever we talk about returns, you'll ask one simple question: is it a gain above inflation, or just a nice-looking number on the screen? But be careful: looking for an alternative doesn't mean any alternative will do. Some assets rise a lot and fall even faster. In the next lessons, we'll see how to tell them apart.

aulas.titulo: Aula 1.3 — 2008: why Bitcoin was born
aulas.gancho: In October 2008, a short document appeared that changed the conversation about money. Let's look at the context.

cenas.visual: Stylised archive image, in greys and gold: a city skyline with the lights going out, one by one.
cenas.narracao: In 2008, the financial world was in crisis. Large banks had lent money to people who couldn't repay it, and the problem spread through the whole system. Governments and central banks rushed to rescue institutions. Many people lost their home, their job or their savings. It was in this context that many people started asking whether the traditional financial system was the only possible path.

cenas.visual: Screen with the title of a document being typed slowly: "Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System". Below it, the date: 31 October 2008.
cenas.narracao: On 31 October 2008, a document with that title appeared on the internet. It was signed by a person using the name Satoshi Nakamoto. To this day, nobody knows for sure who that person is, or whether it's a group. That's the first strange thing, and it's worth keeping in mind, because it forces us to judge the idea and not the person.

cenas.visual: A small diagram: two people exchanging a coin. Between them, a bank counter fades away, with a line crossing it out.
cenas.narracao: The central idea was simple to say and hard to do. Money that could be sent from one person to another without going through a bank, without an intermediary approving every transfer. Instead of relying on trust in an institution, it relied on a rule written in code, which the whole network checked. That's the difference to hold on to: trust in a person versus trust in a process.

cenas.visual: Timeline with two highlighted dates: "3 January 2009" and, underneath, a golden square block labelled "genesis block".
cenas.narracao: On 3 January 2009, the network created the first block, called the genesis block. Inside that block, the author left a message: a headline from a British newspaper about bank bailouts. You don't need to interpret it much. Whoever wrote it wanted to make clear the context in which the idea was born, and that tells you something about the distrust that animated it at the time. It isn't an absolute truth about anyone's intentions, but it's a historical fact that explains a lot of the discourse you hear today.

cenas.visual: Ruben sitting on a park bench, looking at the camera. Text in the corner: "Telling the story is not predicting the price."
cenas.narracao: Let's be clear about what I'm doing here. I'm telling a story. If you want context, think of it this way: back then, for most people, money meant a bank. Anyone who wanted to transfer value to the other side of the world depended on banks, on delays and on fees. The proposal was to cut out that middleman, and not much more than that.

cenas.visual: Three animated icons side by side: a payment arrow, a safe and a line chart. Each lights up in turn.
cenas.narracao: The problem the document tries to solve has a name: double spending. With a digital file, copying costs nothing. If you send a photo to someone, you still have it. With digital money, the question is different: how do you guarantee that the same unit isn't spent twice, without a bank confirming every operation? That question is older than Bitcoin, and it's the key to understanding everything else.

cenas.visual: An on-screen exercise, with a lined sheet of paper and a pen writing.
cenas.narracao: Reflection exercise: write on one line what you think an intermediary does when it approves a transfer. Then write what you lose if it doesn't exist. There's no right answer. The goal is for you to see what Bitcoin tries to replace, and what that replacement costs.

aulas.titulo: Aula 1.4 — The notebook nobody erases
aulas.gancho: Imagine a notebook that the whole village has, and that nobody can tear up without everyone noticing.

cenas.visual: A simply drawn village, with a square and several houses. In each house, an open notebook with the same handwriting.
cenas.narracao: Imagine a village where everyone has an account book. Every time someone owes money to another person, a line is written: who paid, who to, how much, and the date. Only here there's one rule. There isn't a single notebook kept by the head of the parish council. Everyone has a copy, and the copies are updated together. That is, in very simple terms, a blockchain: a chain of blocks, where each block is a page with several lines.

cenas.visual: Animated graphic `blockchain-caderno`: one line, one page, a chain of pages linked together. Each line of text appears inside a page.
cenas.narracao: Let's go step by step. First, the lines. A transaction says: this wallet sent so many units of this currency to that wallet. Second, the pages. A block bundles several transactions and closes when it's full, or when a certain amount of time has passed. Third, the link between pages. Each page has a kind of seal that results from the content of the page before it. Technically it's called a hash function, but think of it as a fingerprint of the content: if the content changes, the fingerprint changes. If someone alters an old line, the seal no longer matches, and all the following pages become invalid.

cenas.visual: Animation: someone tries to erase a line on an old page. The page turns red, and the following pages turn grey, one by one, like dominoes.
cenas.narracao: This is what makes the notebook hard to erase. It's not that changing anything is impossible. It's that changing it means redoing the whole path, and it has to be accepted by the majority of the network. And that majority has copies of the notebook. Anyone trying to tamper with an old page has to convince the whole village that the story is different. In practice, that doesn't happen.

cenas.visual: Two screens side by side. On the left, a computer solving a puzzle. On the right, a set of coins locked as collateral. Underneath, the labels "proof of work" and "proof of stake".
cenas.narracao: But then, who writes the new page? This is where many people find things confusing, and I'll simplify it. There are two main methods. The first is called proof of work, or mining. Computers compete to solve a difficult mathematical problem. Whoever solves it first writes the next page and receives a reward. It uses a lot of energy, and it's the method Bitcoin uses. The second is called proof of stake. Instead of competing with calculation, participants lock up coins as collateral, and the system chooses who writes the page. If that person tries to cheat, they lose the collateral. This is the method the Ethereum network adopted in September 2022, in a transition called The Merge.

cenas.visual: An animated scale: on one pan, "energy", on the other, "collateral". Both pans stay in balance, with an arrow saying "nobody writes without paying".
cenas.narracao: Notice what the two have in common. Nobody writes in the notebook without paying a cost, whether it's energy or collateral. And nobody decides on their own what is true. That's the big idea behind a blockchain: a shared record without a central authority having the last word.

cenas.visual: A highlighted warning, gold on charcoal, with a discreet exclamation mark: "Solid technology is not the same as a good project."
cenas.narracao: Now an important warning. A blockchain solves a specific problem: keeping a shared record without a central entity. That doesn't mean the project is safe, or that the currency is good, or that the price will rise. Solid technology can be attached to a badly designed product. We'll separate these things throughout the course, and from module 2 onwards you'll have tools to do that.

cenas.visual: Illustrative example: Inês explaining the four-page notebook to her husband, who works in logistics, with the pages linked by arrows.
cenas.narracao: Illustrative example, to close. Inês wanted to understand this with her husband, who works in logistics, and he asked her why nobody could erase the notebook. She answered with a simple three-step exercise: draw four pages, with two lines each, write on each seal a word that summed up the previous page, and then change one line on the first page to see what happened to the others. He got it in two minutes. You'll need a little more, and that's fine. You don't need to understand the maths to understand the logic. You just need to see why changing the past is so costly.

aulas.titulo: Aula 2.1 — Bitcoin: 21 million and the halving
aulas.gancho: There's a coin that will only ever exist in 21 million units. Sounds like good news. But there's a detail: how do those units come into existence?

cenas.visual: A golden digital safe on a charcoal background. A counter in the corner shows 0 and slowly climbs towards a limit marked in red: "21,000,000".
cenas.narracao: Bitcoin has a programmed limit: twenty-one million units, at most. That number wasn't chosen by chance, and it doesn't change by the decision of one person or one company. It is written into the protocol, and anyone who uses the network accepts that rule when they use it. It sounds simple, but it has an important consequence: the quantity of coins never grows without limit, and that is different from almost every currency you know.

cenas.visual: An animated clock with the caption "210,000 blocks ≈ 4 years". Each time the clock completes a turn, the reward is cut in half, with a small click.
cenas.narracao: This is the halving, which means cut in half. Every two hundred and ten thousand blocks, the reward is cut in half. Since blocks come out, on average, every ten minutes, this happens roughly every four years. It isn't exact, because the pace varies a little, but it's the right order of magnitude for you to see the pattern.

cenas.visual: Animated graphic `halving`: a descending staircase. Each step shows the date and the reward per block. The last step blinks.
cenas.narracao: Let's go through the sequence, which is what matters. Fifty units per block until 2012. Then twenty-five. In 2016, twelve point five. In 2020, six point two five. In 2024, three point one two five. Notice the pattern. Each cut slows the pace at which new units are created. The more time passes, the fewer new coins come in. That's why people who see Bitcoin as a store of value use this argument: it's a supply that shrinks over time, unlike currencies that central banks can issue with no technical limit.

cenas.visual: An animated scale: on one pan, "less new supply"; on the other, "demand, news, mood, regulation". The scale swings, without settling.
cenas.narracao: Now the counterpoint, because there has to be one. Less new supply doesn't guarantee a high price. The price depends on how many people want to buy, how many want to sell, news, mood, regulation, and everything else. Think of a limited edition of a book: the print run is fixed, but nobody guarantees that readers will show up. A cut in the reward is one factor among many. History shows that the effect on the price is neither automatic nor predictable, and anyone who sells you a certainty on this point is selling you a fantasy.

cenas.visual: A sum on screen, step by step: "50 + 25 + 12.5 + 6.25 + …" and, underneath, "× 210,000 = 21,000,000".
cenas.narracao: Let's do the sum, so you can see the number is real. If you add fifty, twenty-five, twelve point five, and so on, each period lasts two hundred and ten thousand blocks. If you multiply the sum of the rewards by that number of blocks, you get roughly twenty-one million. That's why the limit is what it is. It isn't a round number chosen to look nice; it's the result of a series that keeps shrinking. If you do the sum on your phone's calculator, you'll see the result approaches twenty-one million and never goes past it.

cenas.visual: Illustrative example: a cake with one hundred slices. Each person who helps bake receives ten slices, then five, then two and a half. The remaining slices are marked in grey.
cenas.narracao: Illustrative example, with round, invented numbers. Imagine a cake that only has one hundred slices. In the first days, each person who helps bake gets ten slices. Then they get five. Then two and a half. The cake never goes past one hundred slices, and new slices become rarer and rarer. But this says nothing about whether the cake is good, or whether it's worth eating. Scarcity is a property, not an investment thesis.

cenas.visual: Illustrative example: Tiago, twenty-eight years old, a programmer in Braga, making notes in a notebook beside his laptop.
cenas.narracao: Illustrative example: Tiago, twenty-eight years old, a programmer in Braga, understood this argument and found it reasonable. But he didn't stop there. He asked himself who was buying, why, and what would happen if those people stopped buying. That's the question I want you to keep in mind throughout this module. Scarcity explains one part of the story. Demand explains the other.

aulas.titulo: Aula 2.2 — Ethereum: the village with rules that enforce themselves
aulas.gancho: Bitcoin is a notebook of accounts. Ethereum tries to be a whole village, with rules that enforce themselves.

cenas.visual: Two notebooks side by side. The first has a single column, "who has what". The second has columns, functions and small blocks of code.
cenas.narracao: Bitcoin was designed, above all, to record who has what. Ethereum launched in 2015 with a different ambition: to let anyone write rules into the notebook, and to have those rules run by themselves, without an intermediary. It isn't just a record of balances. It's a kind of shared computer, where many people run programmes at the same time, and everyone confirms the result.

cenas.visual: An animated vending machine. A coin goes in, the selection lights up, the product drops. Above it, the caption: "if this, then that".
cenas.narracao: These rules are called smart contracts. The name is a bit misleading. They aren't contracts in the legal sense, and they aren't smart in the sense of thinking. They are programmes that run on the network. A helpful analogy is the vending machine. You insert a coin, choose an option, and the machine hands over the product. You don't need an employee to confirm it. The rule is inside, and it applies the same way to everyone. A smart contract works like this: if this happens, then that happens. When the condition is met, the action executes. Each of these programmes has the same skeleton: a rule, a condition and an automatic execution. The difference lies in what gets executed, and in who is responsible if something goes wrong.

cenas.visual: Four small icons: a loan, an exchange market, a game, a digital collection. Each has a question mark underneath.
cenas.narracao: This opens many doors. You can have automatic loans, exchange markets between people, games, digital collections. I won't tell you which of these will work. Not all of them do, and some should never have existed. Just because something is technically possible doesn't mean it's a good idea to use it, or that it has any real use for you.

cenas.visual: A contract written on a screen, with a red line and a flashing warning: "error in code".
cenas.narracao: And here comes the warning that is worth its weight in gold: code can fail too. A contract written in a hurry can contain a mistake, and mistakes on a blockchain are hard to correct, because the notebook can't be torn out. In 2016, a project called The DAO lost an enormous amount of ether because of a flaw in its code, and that led to a split of the network itself. I don't want to scare you with numbers. I want you to understand one thing: code is not a guarantee of anything on its own.

cenas.visual: A timeline: 2015 labelled "launch", September 2022 labelled "The Merge", and between the two an arrow changing colour from red to gold.
cenas.narracao: Now let's talk about the big change in 2022. Until September of that year, Ethereum used proof of work, like Bitcoin. Then it moved to proof of stake. That transition is called The Merge. The network stopped depending on computers competing through calculation, and started depending on participants who lock up coins as collateral. The change altered how the network uses energy and how new coins are issued. But it didn't remove the need to understand what you're buying. A better technology doesn't fix a badly designed project.

cenas.visual: A wallet screen with a fee field flashing in yellow. Beside it, a label: "twenty euros sent, similar fee".
cenas.narracao: It's also worth understanding how Ethereum charges for operations. Every action on the network has a cost, called a fee, and that fee varies with demand. At busy moments, it can become expensive. If you ever send a small amount and are surprised by the cost, now you know why. Illustrative example: Inês wanted to send twenty euros from one wallet to another, and the fee ended up almost as high as the transfer itself. It wasn't a tragedy. It was a lesson. Also think about this: when the network is very full, each operation competes with the others for space, and whoever pays more goes first. So the same transfer can cost little on a calm morning and a lot in a busy afternoon. Before any operation, always check how much it's going to cost you.

cenas.visual: Two columns on a board: "Bitcoin" and "Ethereum". Ruben writing, by hand, a question at the bottom: "do I need a notebook or a programme?"
cenas.narracao: Think of these as two different tools. A simple notebook is good for recording who owes what. A programme running on the network is good for executing complicated rules without an intermediary. Both are useful, and both have their own risks. The common mistake is to assume that complexity means quality. Often it's just more surface area for things to go wrong.

aulas.titulo: Aula 2.3 — Stablecoins: the digital dollar and the risk of whoever issues it
aulas.gancho: There's a crypto that is supposed to always be worth one dollar. It looks like a safe vault. Ask yourself: who holds the key to the vault?

cenas.visual: A digital coin with the dollar symbol, sliding along a line that should be perfectly straight. The line trembles slightly.
cenas.narracao: A stablecoin is a digital coin that tries to hold a fixed value, normally one dollar. The best-known examples are USDC and USDT. It sounds like the ideal scenario: a digital dollar that moves across the network in seconds. But notice the word tries. A stablecoin has no magic guarantee. On the contrary, its value depends on a concrete promise, and that promise has to be kept by someone.

cenas.visual: An illustration of a casino chip: a value written on its face, and behind it a small hand holding the promise.
cenas.narracao: What a stablecoin promises is something specific: that, for each unit issued, there is an equivalent reserve, in cash or in low-risk assets, and that the issuer redeems it at the exact value. Think of a casino chip, or a supermarket voucher. The chip is worth what is printed on it because the casino honours it. If the casino stops honouring it, the chip loses value. A stablecoin works in the same way: its value depends on who issues it. An everyday example: a company meal card is only worth what the restaurant accepts, and the restaurant only accepts it while the system keeps paying it. Trust runs down in layers, and one weak layer drags the others down with it.

cenas.visual: A diagram with three linked boxes: "reserves", "issuer", "redemption". A panic arrow, coming from many people, points to "redemption".
cenas.narracao: That's why there's a term you should know: issuer risk. Whoever issues the coin has to hold verifiable reserves, has to follow rules, and has to be able to redeem coins when people ask. If there are doubts about the reserves, or if many people try to redeem at the same time, the value can drift away from the dollar. That isn't a theoretical possibility. It's exactly the scenario that gets tested when the market panics.

cenas.visual: A line chart that rises to the right and, on one day, drops sharply. The caption says "loss of peg".
cenas.narracao: This has already happened. In 2022, an algorithmic stablecoin, from an ecosystem that at one point became enormous, lost its peg to the dollar and dragged a lot of value down with it. It was not a coin backed by dollar reserves. It was a balancing mechanism between two digital coins. When that balance broke, the value collapsed. This story is the best argument for not trusting the word stable.

cenas.visual: A generic regulatory seal logo, with the abbreviation "MiCA" (Markets in Crypto-Assets) and a date: 30 December 2024.
cenas.narracao: In the European Union, there is now a legal framework called MiCA, which has applied to crypto-asset service providers since thirty December 2024. It brings more rules, more transparency and more supervision. It's a real step forward. But rules are not price guarantees, and it's important not to confuse the two. A stablecoin can comply with regulation and still carry risks that depend on its reserves, its liquidity and the trust of the people who use it. Notice a practical difference: a regulation obliges companies to meet their duties. It doesn't oblige the coin to hold a fixed price. They are different things, and one doesn't replace the other.

cenas.visual: Illustrative example: one hundred units of a stablecoin, with the value dropping from one dollar to ninety cents.
cenas.narracao: Let's look at an illustrative example, with round, invented numbers. Imagine you hold one hundred units of a stablecoin that is worth one dollar. If the coin loses its peg and drops to ninety cents, your balance is now worth ninety dollars. Nothing dramatic at first glance. But if you were using it as a safe haven, you've lost ten percent at the exact moment you were looking for security. That's what makes the example uncomfortable.

cenas.visual: Illustrative example: Rui, forty-one years old, a teacher in Leiria, at his desk with a notepad and three questions written on it.
cenas.narracao: Why do people use stablecoins? To get out of volatile positions quickly, to send value between countries, to hold a digital dollar for a period of time. These are legitimate uses. But none of them removes the risk. Illustrative example: Rui, forty-one years old, a teacher in Leiria, had put part of his savings into a stablecoin, convinced it was idle money with no risk. When he asked where the reserves were and who audited them, he realised he had assumed something without checking it. He didn't lose everything, but he learned to ask questions. If you have doubts about how a value behaves, the first question is always the same: who is obliged to redeem it, and under what conditions?

aulas.titulo: Aula 2.4 — Altcoins, memecoins and the seven questions
aulas.gancho: There are thousands of coins, and most of them will disappear. How do you tell a serious project from a joke with a logo?

cenas.visual: A screen full of coin logos appearing and disappearing, like leaves in the wind.
cenas.narracao: We call altcoins all the cryptocurrencies that are not Bitcoin. There are many, with very different goals. Some try to be better payment systems, others want to connect data chains, others want to be platforms for applications. And then there are memecoins, which deserve a section of their own. A reminder: this is educational content, and not financial advice. The risk of loss is real, and in crypto it is often total.

cenas.visual: A coin drawn with a smiling face and the caption "born from a joke". Underneath, an attention bar that rises and falls quickly.
cenas.narracao: A memecoin is often born from a joke, an image or a social media trend. As a rule, it doesn't solve a concrete problem. Its value depends almost entirely on the attention it receives. When the attention changes, the price changes. This can happen in hours, sometimes in minutes. Think of a soap bubble at a birthday party: it's pretty, everyone points at it, and it bursts without warning. And notice a word that keeps coming up: attention. If the value comes from attention, whoever sells early wins, and whoever buys late loses.

cenas.visual: Split screen: on the left, an advert with stars and the phrase "guaranteed profit". On the right, the same phrase crossed out in red.
cenas.narracao: I'm not saying all of them are fraud. I'm saying the risk is extremely high and that, often, the marketing is the only product. When someone sells you a coin with a guaranteed profit, the right response is to be suspicious. No honest project can guarantee a return, and anyone who says it can is trying to stop you asking questions.

cenas.visual: A panel with seven numbers, from one to seven, in a row. Each number lights up when Ruben talks about it.
cenas.narracao: So that you don't rely on instinct, I'm going to give you a tool: seven questions. They aren't a formula, they're a filter. If you can't answer one of them, you're not ready to buy. First: what problem does this project solve? If the answer is just it's going to go up, that's a bad sign. Second: who is behind it, and is that public? An anonymous team isn't necessarily fraud, but it raises the risk, and you need to know that before deciding. A project with identified people who publicly stand behind what they do carries a different kind of risk. Neither of them is free of risk.

cenas.visual: A pie chart: one very large slice in dark grey, labelled "one wallet", and small slices for the rest.
cenas.narracao: Third: what is the total supply, and who holds it? If a small number of wallets hold most of the coins, the price can be manipulated easily. Fourth: is there real utility, or only speculation? Ask who uses the project for anything other than buying and selling. Fifth: who controls the code, and can they change it? If one person can change the rules without warning, you need to know that before you get in. A supplementary question worth asking: who decides on updates, and how are those decisions communicated?

cenas.visual: An exit door labelled "liquidity". The door is narrow, and in front of it many people are pushing at the same time.
cenas.narracao: Sixth: where is it traded, and is there enough liquidity to sell? An asset without buyers is an asset you can't sell at the price you see on the screen. Seventh, and perhaps the most useful: what happens if the project disappears tomorrow? If the answer is nothing, I lose everything, you already know how much you can risk. If you have no way of selling, the chart on the screen is just an opinion. These seven questions won't give you certainties. They'll give you better questions than the ones the advertising asks you.

cenas.visual: Illustrative example: a card with four lines marked in red and a final stamp: "don't enter".
cenas.narracao: Illustrative example, with invented numbers. Imagine a coin that promises high yield, has a founder with no face, holds ninety percent of its supply in a single wallet, and has no use outside the coin itself. You've answered badly to almost all of them. You don't need anything more to decide not to enter. And if, on the other hand, the answers were good, they still wouldn't oblige you to buy. A good answer only tells you it's worth studying more, never that the price will go up. Also watch out for requests: if someone asks you to send crypto to unlock a sum of money, or pressures you to decide today, that isn't analysis. It's pressure. We'll talk about scams in more detail in module 5. Notice that I haven't asked you to get it right. I've asked you not to be carried away by haste, and to understand what you don't know yet.

modulos.titulo: Módulo 3 — Buying for the first time (≈17 min)

aulas.titulo: Aula 3.1 — Authorized platform and KYC
aulas.gancho: Your first crypto purchase might ask for your ID card, a selfie and your tax number. Strange? It isn't. It's there for a reason.

cenas.visual: A phone screen with a gold button that says "buy". Above it, a red warning: "Confirm before you continue."
cenas.narracao: Before you buy anything, you need a platform. It's called an exchange, or trading platform. It's where you swap euros for cryptocurrencies and back again. And at this stage, the choice is the most important decision you'll make in the whole bootcamp. More important than the price, the coin or the timing. Why do I say that? Because most of the serious losses people suffer don't start with the market. They start with the platform.

cenas.visual: An illustration of a bank vault with a half-open door and a small warning sign beside it.
cenas.narracao: A platform that isn't authorized can run off with your money, freeze your account or lie about where the funds are. It doesn't have to be a sophisticated fraud. It just has to have nobody supervising what it does. Think of it this way: a restaurant with a license from the city council and one without a license can serve the same food. Only one of them has someone answerable to the law if something goes wrong. So the first test is simple: is the platform authorized, and does an official body supervise it? If the answer is no, the conversation ends here.

cenas.visual: A regulation document with the acronym "MiCA" highlighted, and beside it an official seal with the word "register".
cenas.narracao: In the European Union there is the MiCA regulation, which we've already talked about. Platforms that provide crypto-asset services need authorization and are supervised. In Portugal, the body that supervises the securities markets is the CMVM, the Portuguese securities market regulator. Go to the official website of that body, or of the authority in the country where the platform says it's based, and check whether the platform appears on the register of authorized providers. If it isn't there, it doesn't matter how nice the website looks.

cenas.visual: Three sources of information side by side: an advert with stars, an influencer video, an official register page. The first two are blurred; the third is sharp.
cenas.narracao: Don't rely only on a logo, an advert or an influencer who gets paid to talk about a platform. Trust the official register. Write down the platform's exact name, search for it in the register, and compare the name and the website domain with what's listed there. It sounds like extra work, and it's exactly the work that scammers hope you won't do. One minute of checking is worth more than any promotion that reaches you by message.

cenas.visual: A form screen with fields to fill in: name, date of birth, tax number, and a button to upload a photo of your document.
cenas.narracao: Now, KYC. The letters stand for know your customer, and it's the identity verification process. You'll need to provide an identity document, often a selfie holding that document, and your tax number. It might feel intrusive. But it's exactly what the law requires to fight money laundering and fraud. It's also the difference between a serious platform and one that just wants your money with no questions asked. Anyone who asks you for documents is doing their duty. Anyone who asks for nothing deserves a second look. Notice that this isn't distrust of you. Banks do exactly the same when you open an account, and nobody finds that strange. In crypto, a lot of people still think anonymity is a feature. Almost always, it's a risk signal.

cenas.visual: A phone receiving a message with a link. Below it, an alarm icon and the sentence: "Deposit now to unlock your account."
cenas.narracao: It's worth spotting a warning sign. If a platform lets you deposit without verifying your identity, be wary. If it asks you for money off the books, or to unlock an account, or to pay a fee you've never seen before, set it aside. KYC isn't an obstacle. It's a sign that someone is doing their homework. And a message rushing you to deposit is almost always a message from someone who wants your money before you've had time to think.

cenas.visual: Illustrative case: Gonçalo, thirty-two, a maintenance technician in Setúbal, looking at a laptop with the official register open.
cenas.narracao: Illustrative case: Gonçalo, thirty-two, a maintenance technician in Setúbal, was about to deposit money into a platform that had reached him through a message. It looked well made, and it even had a support contact with a name. Before going ahead, he checked the official register and couldn't find the platform. He didn't buy anything. He learned that the message was a trap. It sounds like a small thing, but it was the most valuable decision he made that month.

aulas.titulo: Aula 3.2 — The real cost of buying
aulas.gancho: You buy a hundred euros of a crypto and, a minute later, it's worth less than a hundred euros. The price hasn't even moved. So what happened?

cenas.visual: An animated purchase receipt. Each line appears in turn: "amount", "fee", "spread", "total". The total is underlined.
cenas.narracao: When you buy crypto, you pay more than the price you see on the screen. That's not a trick. These are costs, and it's worth knowing them before you buy, not after. Imagine you're buying an item of clothing in a shop, and at the till an extra amount appears that wasn't on the price tag. You don't feel cheated if you already knew that amount existed. You feel cheated when nobody warned you. There are three costs that almost everyone runs into. The first is the platform fee. It's a percentage of the value of the transaction, and it can vary depending on the payment method and the type of account. Always read the full fee table, not just the summary on the front page.

cenas.visual: A bar with two prices: on the left, "buy price", a little higher; on the right, "sell price", a little lower. A gap between the two bars, marked in gold.
cenas.narracao: The second cost is the spread. It's the difference between the price at which you buy and the price at which you sell, at the same moment. If the buy price is a bit higher than the sell price, that difference is the spread, and it stays with the platform or with whoever is making the market. It sounds like a detail, but you feel it on every trade, even when you don't notice it.

cenas.visual: A wallet icon receiving an arrow, labelled "network fee". The arrow changes size depending on demand.
cenas.narracao: The third cost, if you transfer to your own wallet, is the network fee. Every transfer on the blockchain has a cost, and it changes with how busy the network is. We've already seen this with Ethereum. It isn't the platform that charges it, it's the network itself. And anyone who doesn't know this is surprised when the amount that arrives is smaller than the amount they sent.

cenas.visual: Illustrative example: a paper receipt with round numbers. "€100 purchase", "− €1 fee", "− €0.50 spread", "= €98.50 real value".
cenas.narracao: Let's do the sums with round, hypothetical numbers. Illustrative example. You buy one hundred euros. The platform charges a one percent fee. The spread, at that moment, is half a percent. You're paying around one and a half euros in costs. About ninety-eight euros and fifty cents is left, in market terms. That seems small. But look at it from the other side. A cost of one and a half euros on a hundred-euro purchase looks like rounding. Only, the cost doesn't sit still: it works against you from the first second.

cenas.visual: An arrow pointing down two percent from the 98.50 euro position. The balance drops to 96.53, and a second arrow, pointing up, tries to get back to the starting point.
cenas.narracao: If the price falls two percent straight after, your balance drops to around ninety-six euros and fifty cents. You need the price to rise by more than two percent just to get back to where you started. The costs push you backwards before the market gives you any gain. And the more often you buy and sell, the more the costs eat into the result. Every trade carries a small, invisible tax, and it adds up. This isn't a rule made up by sellers. It's arithmetic. Someone who gets in and out often has to earn more just to stay where they were. This example isn't special in any way: it's the same for anyone buying the same amount, with the same fees.

cenas.visual: Ruben holding a calculator in his hand, turning the camera to show the screen.
cenas.narracao: This is the part a lot of people skip. Think about the total cost of getting in and getting out. If you buy and sell, you pay twice. If you just hold, you pay once, but waiting also costs something, in risk and in opportunity. I'm not saying buying is bad. I'm saying the cost has to be on the sheet before the first click. If you only think about the price, you're seeing half the bill. And there's one detail that's worth its weight in gold: the cost of buying with a card is often different from the cost of transferring from a bank. Always ask which method is cheapest for your case, and compare against the official fee table, not against your memory.

cenas.visual: Illustrative case: Inês comparing an app with a notebook, a pencil crossing out a line.
cenas.narracao: Illustrative case: Inês made a small purchase and noticed the app showed a slightly lower value than what she had paid. She thought the app was wrong. It wasn't. It was the fees and the spread. After working it out with pen and paper, she understood everything, and from then on she looked at the cost before every trade. It was the best way for her to learn, because the mistake cost her very little.

aulas.titulo: Aula 3.3 — Market order or limit order
aulas.gancho: You press the buy button, and the price on the screen isn't the price you pay. Let's understand why.

cenas.visual: Two buttons side by side: "market" and "limit". Under each, a short text explaining the difference.
cenas.narracao: When you place an order on a platform, you have to choose an order type. The two most common are the market order and the limit order. They sound like technical jargon, but they decide what happens to your money. Let's take them one at a time, calmly, because this is one of the points where people most often slip up on their very first purchase.

cenas.visual: An animation of an arrow shooting up fast, with a market order executed a little above the price shown on the screen.
cenas.narracao: A market order tells the platform: buy now, at whatever price is available. It's fast, and it guarantees the purchase goes through. The risk is that the price can move between the moment you press the button and the moment the order is executed. In fast markets, that's called slippage, and it can be significant. You're certain to buy, but you're not certain of the price. Think of a market stall: you pay the price written on the sign. On a busy platform, the price can change between when you press the button and when the order arrives. It's the same idea, just at a different speed.

cenas.visual: A horizontal line marked "€100". A limit order sits below it, labelled "I only buy up to here". The price arrow comes down, touches the line, and the order executes.
cenas.narracao: A limit order says: only buy if the price is equal to or lower than this value that I choose. You control the maximum price you'll pay. The risk is that the order never gets filled, if the price never reaches your level. You're left without a purchase, and nothing happens. It seems weak, but it's a form of protection. In practice, a limit order won't buy for you at the worst moment. It can also be only partly filled if there isn't enough liquidity at that price. Read the platform's terms on this point, because they vary from place to place.

cenas.visual: Illustrative example: an asset at €100. Two scenarios in parallel: one rises to €102, the other stays put, waiting.
cenas.narracao: Let's go with an illustrative example and invented numbers. Imagine an asset that's trading at one hundred euros, and you want to buy one hundred euros' worth of exposure. With a market order, you buy straight away, and the price may rise to one hundred and two in the second it takes to execute. With a limit order at ninety-eight, you only buy if the price falls to that level. If it doesn't fall, you don't buy. Neither one is the universal answer. Each one chooses a different risk.

cenas.visual: A set of scales with two pans: one says "certainty of execution", the other "certainty of price". The scales wobble, and the needle settles in the middle.
cenas.narracao: Notice what this means. A market order trades certainty of price for certainty of execution. A limit order trades certainty of execution for certainty of price. There isn't one that's better in every situation. Anyone who says one order type is always superior to the other is oversimplifying, and in markets, oversimplifying tends to be expensive. There's one that suits what you're doing, the time you have and how much price movement bothers you. Think about time too: if an order stays open for days, the market can change completely, and the order you wrote yesterday may no longer reflect what you want today.

cenas.visual: A table with two columns: "I use market when" and "I use limit when". Ruben pointing at the columns.
cenas.narracao: For someone just starting out, the practical rule is this. Use a limit order when you're not in a hurry and want to control the price. Use a market order when you need to get in now and you accept the price movement. But never use a market order in a moment of panic, because that's when the price moves the most. If the screen is red and you feel the urge to get in right now, that urge is your signal to stop and read your notes. And watch out for a common mistake: setting a limit too close to the current price, thinking it's a bargain, and then staring at an order that never fills. A limit has to be a decision, not a guess.

cenas.visual: Illustrative case: Gonçalo, the technician from Setúbal, looking at a trade history with a market order highlighted.
cenas.narracao: Illustrative case: Gonçalo placed a market order on a day of fast-moving news, and paid more than he had expected. It wasn't a disaster, but he learned that an order is a decision, not an automatic click. Since then, he always writes down the maximum price he's willing to pay before pressing any button.

aulas.titulo: Aula 3.4 — Your first euro
aulas.gancho: Your first purchase should be the smallest of all. It isn't timidity. It's method.

cenas.visual: Ruben writing a number on a sheet of paper, then underlining it twice. A caption appears: "loss limit".
cenas.narracao: We've reached the moment of buying. Before that, I want you to set a limit. Not a profit target, a loss limit. An amount that, if it disappears, won't change your life. Choose it calmly, without rushing. Ask yourself: how much money can I lose without hurting my income, my food, the household bills, my emergency fund? That amount, or a small fraction of it, is your first euro. If you can't find an amount like that, don't buy. There's no hurry, and no coin will vanish because you waited a week. A loss limit isn't a forecast. It's a rule you write for yourself, before the market starts talking.

cenas.visual: An animated list of steps, each with a tick appearing: "2FA", "address verified", "small test", "decision made", "record kept".
cenas.narracao: Let's go through the practical steps, so you don't improvise. One: turn on two-factor authentication on the platform. It's the code that goes to your phone when you log in. Without it, anyone who finds out your password can get into your account. Two: confirm the address of everything you're going to use. The site, the app, the platform's name. Type the address by hand or save it in your bookmarks, and never click on links that reach you by message.

cenas.visual: A small deposit animation, with a symbolic amount going into the account and a tick appearing beside it.
cenas.narracao: Three: do a test run first. A small deposit, a small purchase and, if relevant, a small transfer to check the route works. Only then do you increase. The first operation is there to learn the process, not to make money. If something doesn't add up, you'll find out with little at stake. And a golden rule: don't test with the amount you intend to use for the big purchase. The test is for learning the route, not for testing your luck.

cenas.visual: A market screen flashing green, and below it a buy button with a small padlock showing it isn't loaded yet.
cenas.narracao: Four: buy only after you've made the decision, not during a price move. When the screen is flashing green, the temptation is to jump in now. That urge is the first sign to stop. Decisions made under the pressure of a chart are rarely the best, because the chart knows nothing about your life. A useful trick: write the decision down in a note before you open the app, with the amount and the reason. If the urge to buy passes, the note is still there, and you decide with a cool head.

cenas.visual: An open notebook with a table drawn in it: "date", "amount", "price", "fee", "order type", "reason".
cenas.narracao: Five: record everything. Date, amount, price, fee, order type, reason. It sounds like paperwork, but that's where you learn. In three months' time, you'll look back at this record and understand better than you do today what worked and what didn't. People who don't keep records tend to remember only what went well, and that fools anyone. If, when you review the record, you notice you buy whenever the price goes up and make mistakes when it goes down, you already have precious information about yourself. That's worth more than any technical analysis.

cenas.visual: Illustrative case: Inês with the printed checklist on a café table, each line ticked off in pen.
cenas.narracao: Illustrative case: Inês did exactly this. She chose an amount she didn't need, turned on authentication, tested with a small deposit and wrote each step in a notebook. She didn't get rich or poor in the first month, and that wasn't the goal anyway. She ended up with a process, and that's what we want you to have. The process is what protects you when emotions get in the way. And if one day the checklist tells you no, that isn't a failure. It's the process working.

cenas.visual: Ruben standing, medium shot, closing the notebook. On-screen text: "Educational content, not financial advice. The risk of loss is real."
cenas.narracao: Exercise: create a five-line checklist with the steps I've just gone through, and tick each one off as you do it. Don't move on to buying until you have all five. If you think one line doesn't apply, write down why, and talk to someone you trust before you cross it off. Let me repeat the essentials of this module: educational content, not financial advice, and the risk of loss is real. If the amount you've chosen doesn't let you sleep soundly, it's because it's too high.

modulos.titulo: Módulo 4 — Your key: wallets and the seed phrase (≈17 min)

aulas.titulo: Aula 4.1 — Hot and cold wallets
aulas.gancho: A wallet doesn't store coins. It never has. It stores keys. And whoever holds the key holds the money.

cenas.visual: An animation of an open wallet, with a golden key coming out of it. Behind it, the blockchain appears as a grid of pages, and the key points to one of them.
cenas.narracao: Let's correct something right away, because it's the most common confusion. A crypto wallet isn't a safe with coins inside. The coins live on the blockchain, the shared ledger we talked about in module 1. The wallet holds the keys that let you sign transactions, and those keys are what give you access to the value. Once you understand this, the way you think about security changes, because you stop looking for where the coins are and start looking for where the keys are. Think of an everyday analogy: your bank card number doesn't give you money, but anyone who has it and knows the code can spend. With crypto, the key plays that role, only there's no counter and no complaints department.

cenas.visual: A golden key in the foreground against a charcoal background. The sentence appears slowly: "In crypto, whoever holds the key holds the money."
cenas.narracao: That's why the key is the metaphor for this bootcamp. In crypto, whoever holds the key holds the money. There's no manager you can ask for a replacement, and no counter where you can explain that you lost your card. If the key is lost, access is lost. If the key is stolen, the value goes with it. That may sound harsh, but it's exactly what gives meaning to the phrase being the owner of your money. Being the owner also means being responsible.

cenas.visual: A phone screen with an app open, and a small padlock blinking in the corner. Label: "hot wallet".
cenas.narracao: There are two main types of wallet. The first is the hot wallet. It's an app or a program connected to the internet. It's convenient, quick, and good for everyday operations. The risk is that, because it's connected, it's more exposed: to an infected phone, a fake website, a copied app that looks identical to the original. Convenience and exposure always go together. A well-built app isn't insecure for that reason, but you need to check every time where you downloaded it from.

cenas.visual: A small physical device being plugged into a computer with a cable. Beside it, a screen on the device itself asks for confirmation. Label: "cold wallet".
cenas.narracao: The second is the cold wallet. It's a physical device, often the size of a USB stick, that keeps your keys offline. To sign a transaction, you plug it in and confirm on the device itself. A well-known commercial example is Ledger, which is sold in the MTM shop. The advantage is that the key never leaves the device. The downside is that it's less convenient, and if you lose it without a backup, the problem remains. We'll get to that.

cenas.visual: An animated bar chart `tipos-carteira`: two columns compared in bars. "Convenience", "exposure", "daily use", "long-term storage". Each bar grows into its place.
cenas.narracao: Here's a simple comparison. A hot wallet is like having cash in your pocket: it's within reach, and it's good for buying a coffee. A cold wallet is like a safe at home, with a key that only you use, for your savings. Neither one is the universal answer. It depends on how much you have, how often you move it, and how much risk you're willing to take. The chart shows the trade-off: the more convenience, the more exposure. It isn't a quality ranking. A cold wallet isn't better in every situation; it's better for certain situations.

cenas.visual: Ruben pointing at a rule written on a board: "small amount, frequent use → hot. Amount parked → cold."
cenas.narracao: There's a practical rule worth keeping. Small amounts you use often can live in a hot wallet. Amounts you won't touch for months deserve a cold one. And no wallet protects you from your own mistakes, like sending to the wrong address, or signing something you didn't understand. Technical security doesn't replace attention. Before you confirm any transaction, read what you're confirming. Also note that a cold wallet won't save you from scams. If someone convinces you to sign a malicious transaction on the device itself, the technology is there, but you're the one deciding.

cenas.visual: Illustrative case: Tiago, a programmer from Braga, looking at his phone with a "wallet recovered" message on the screen.
cenas.narracao: Be careful: the wallet address is public, like an account number. You can share it to receive funds. But the private key and the recovery phrase never. Illustrative case: Tiago had almost everything in a phone app. One day he lost the device. He managed to recover the account because he had the recovery phrase stored, but he spent a whole weekend sorting it out. He learned that convenience has a price, and that the price is paid in time, stress and attention.

aulas.titulo: Aula 4.2 — The seed phrase: the words that are worth everything
aulas.gancho: Twelve or twenty-four words, in a precise order. Whoever has them has the money. Nobody else needs you for anything.

cenas.visual: A grid of twelve numbered boxes, filling in word by word, with the label "seed phrase".
cenas.narracao: When you create a wallet, the app or the device generates a recovery phrase. It's called a seed phrase, or secret recovery phrase. It usually has twelve or twenty-four words, in a specific order. In practice, that phrase is the master key to your wallet. It isn't a password you can change whenever you like. It's the origin of the keys themselves, and whoever has it can recreate the wallet anywhere. Think of it as the combination of a safe, not the door: whoever knows it can open the safe from anywhere, at any time, and leave no trail that anyone can follow in time. Also note that the phrase is generated once, when you create the wallet. That's why it's the moment you need to be most alert.

cenas.visual: A lost phone on a table, and beside it a sheet of paper with the words handwritten. An arrow shows the wallet reappearing on a new computer.
cenas.narracao: Why does it matter so much? Because if you lose your phone, if the app fails, if the device breaks, you can recreate the wallet somewhere else with just those words. Without them, there is no recovery. And with them, whoever holds them can do everything you do. They don't need your password, your code or you. This is the difference that most people don't understand.

cenas.visual: A screen with four numbered rules appearing one by one, each with a "not allowed" icon beside it.
cenas.narracao: That's why there are rules that always apply. There are no exceptions. First rule: never enter your seed phrase on a website. Not to verify, not to recover, not to unlock. No serious platform, no legitimate support team, no official app will ever ask you for those words. Second rule: never send it to anyone, by message, email, call or photo. If someone introduces themselves as support and asks for the phrase, it's a scam. Full stop.

cenas.visual: A phone screen with an incoming call and a generic name: "Support". Below it, the line: "Confirm your words to validate your account."
cenas.narracao: Third rule: never photograph it, and never store it on your phone, your computer, your email, a notes app or in the cloud. Any digital copy is a copy that can be stolen, often without you noticing. Fourth rule: write it by hand, on paper, with a pen. And never keep it in the same place as your bank card or your passwords.

cenas.visual: Illustrative example: Inês on the phone, with a notes sheet on the table and a question mark growing on the screen.
cenas.narracao: Does this sound like overkill? Think about it. Most people who lose crypto don't lose it because of the market. They lose it because they gave the words to someone who phoned them saying they were from support. Illustrative example: Inês received a call from a number that claimed to belong to a platform. The person on the other end was friendly, had a professional tone, and asked her for the words to confirm her identity. She hung up. Only later did she realize she had come within a step of losing everything, and that the pressure was part of the scheme.

cenas.visual: Three keywords highlighted one at a time: "urgency", "authority", "request for words". Below them, the caption: "always the same script".
cenas.narracao: Notice the pattern. Urgency, authority, a request for words. It's always the same script, and only the platform's name and the tone of voice change. When you feel the pressure rising, stop. No legitimate person needs you in that much of a hurry. No message, no video and no call that starts with urgency is a good reason to unlock anything. Urgency is the favorite tool of anyone who wants your money before you've had time to think. And if the call pushes you to decide now, the answer is to hang up and call the official number yourself. We'll look at all the scam patterns in module 5.

cenas.visual: Ruben at a clean sheet of paper, writing the words one by one, with the number beside each, then checking them with his finger.
cenas.narracao: Let's go through the correct way to store it. Take a clean sheet of paper, write the words one by one, with the number beside each, and check them twice. Then keep the sheet somewhere dry and secure. Don't fold it too often, because paper and damp don't get along. If you ever write a word down wrong, don't try to guess the correction on anyone's screen. Start the sheet again, calmly, at home, with nobody rushing you. And don't show it or photograph it, not even to remind yourself of a word. If you ever need to recover, use only the official app, downloaded from the official stores, and never a link someone sent you.

aulas.titulo: Aula 4.3 — Not your keys, not your coins
aulas.gancho: Leaving crypto on a platform is a bit like leaving money in a bank. It's convenient. But who holds the key?

cenas.visual: A sentence highlighted in gold on charcoal: "not your keys, not your coins". Below it, the plain meaning: "if you don't hold the keys, you don't hold the coins".
cenas.narracao: There's a phrase that veterans repeat: not your keys, not your coins. In plain terms, it means: if you don't hold the keys, you don't hold the coins. Let's understand what that means, without dramatizing it, because the phrase doesn't mean that leaving crypto on a platform is automatically a mistake. It means you need to know what you're accepting when you do it.

cenas.visual: An illustration of a platform as a big safe with many drawers. Each drawer has a username. One of them is marked: "your balance".
cenas.narracao: When you buy crypto on a platform and leave it there, the platform keeps the keys for you. This is called third-party custody. It's the most convenient option. You recover your password if you forget it, you see your balance on the screen, and you can sell with one click. For many people, this convenience is exactly what they're looking for, and there's nothing wrong with that, as long as the choice is made knowingly.

cenas.visual: A line between two boxes: "platform" and "you". The line grows thin and flickers, with a warning icon.
cenas.narracao: The price of that convenience is that you start depending on the platform. If the platform has a technical problem, if it's attacked, if it's badly run, or if it stops operating, your access can be blocked. In some cases, the money may not come back. It isn't the most common scenario, but it's exactly what the word custody means: someone looks after what belongs to you, and you have to trust that they do. Think of a traditional bank: the money is in your name, but the bank has the systems, and you trust it to keep them secure. With crypto it's similar, only the regulation and the recovery rights vary a great deal from case to case.

cenas.visual: A split screen: on the left, a personal wallet with a key in the hand of the person using it. On the right, a platform vault with a padlock that isn't yours.
cenas.narracao: And there's the opposite too. A personal wallet, with no custody, gives you full control. But if you lose the key, you lose everything, and there's nobody to ask for help. The risk moves from whoever holds it for you to yourself. Notice that the word recover can mean two things: recovering your account, when you've forgotten your password, and recovering your money, when something goes wrong. The first is normal. The second depends on who holds it and on the rules you accepted when you signed up. There's no abstract right choice. There's the right choice for your situation, for your amount, for the way you handle technology.

cenas.visual: A simple chart: a large bar labeled "trading", sitting above a small bar labeled "savings parked". An arrow marks the split.
cenas.narracao: Many people use a hybrid approach. They leave on the platform the amount they use for trading, and move to a cold wallet the amount they want to keep for months. It isn't the only way to do it, but it's a sensible way to separate what moves from what rests. And separating is often the best protection there is. Remember the essentials: separating isn't running away. Someone who separates has a plan for each part, and that's what sets management apart from improvisation.

cenas.visual: A rule written on a board: "the more value and the less use → more self-custody. The less value and the more use → regulated platform, with support."
cenas.narracao: Here's a practical rule. The more value you have, the less waiting time you accept, and the greater the need for self-custody. The less value and the more you use it, the more sense it makes to be on a regulated platform, with support and account recovery. Nobody is forcing you to pick one extreme. You can sit somewhere in the middle, as long as you know where you stand. Before you leave value anywhere, read the custody terms, find out who is responsible and how an account is recovered. If you can't find that information, it's one more question to ask before you go ahead.

cenas.visual: Illustrative case: Rui, a teacher from Leiria, looking at a notebook where he has written a list of steps, with a tick beside each one.
cenas.narracao: Illustrative case: Rui, a teacher from Leiria, had everything on one platform and had never thought about it. When he understood the difference, he didn't change everything overnight. It isn't about being better or worse. It's about knowing where your responsibilities lie. He started by moving the part he wasn't using into a cold wallet, and left the rest where it was for trading. He made the change calmly, and wrote down each step. It took a few weeks, and he says it was the best use of his time in crypto so far.

aulas.titulo: Aula 4.4 — The storage plan: copies that survive
aulas.gancho: A wet piece of paper can't be read. A stolen photo protects nothing. How do you keep a key safe for twenty years?

cenas.visual: Three animated icons in a row: a flame, a drop of water, a clock labelled "years". Each one passes over the backup without destroying it.
cenas.narracao: We've reached the last lesson of the module, and the plan you're going to put together. The central idea is this: your backup has to survive three things. Fire, water, and your own forgetfulness. It may sound like an exaggerated list, but it's the list of problems most people report when they lose access. A good plan thinks about these three risks from the start, not when it's already too late.

cenas.visual: A metal plate slowly rotating, with the words engraved on it. Label: "Cryptotag Zeus, sold in the MTM shop".
cenas.narracao: Paper is cheap and good for getting started. But paper degrades with damp, with time, with a spilled coffee. That's why many people use metal plates, with the words engraved or stamped into them. One product sold in the MTM shop is the Cryptotag Zeus, a metal plate for recording your seed. It isn't the only method, and it isn't mandatory. It's a way to have a copy that doesn't wear out easily, and that already counts for a lot.

cenas.visual: A four-step plan appearing on a board: "1. how many copies", "2. where", "3. who knows", "4. test".
cenas.narracao: Let's build the plan in four steps. First, decide how many copies you want. Two is the reasonable minimum. One copy means that if it's lost, you lose everything. And if the paper copy and the metal copy are in the same place, you aren't making two copies. You're making one, twice. More than three complicates management and increases exposure. For most people, two well-kept copies are the right balance between security and simplicity.

cenas.visual: A simple map of a house and an outside location, with two copies marked in different spots. A dotted arrow links the two places.
cenas.narracao: Second, choose different locations. If both copies are in the same drawer, a fire or a burglary takes both. Think about home, and a trusted place outside it, with safe and discreet access. The goal isn't to hide them, it's to spread the risk. A copy that survives a problem at home is a copy that saves you.

cenas.visual: Two people on a screen with a padlock between them. The one on the left has a sealed envelope. The one on the right has nothing in their hand.
cenas.narracao: Third, decide who knows what. Nobody needs to know the phrase. It's enough for someone you trust to know that a plan exists, and where the copies are, in case something happens to you. That person doesn't need to have the words. If they do, they become one more point of failure, and one more place where the phrase can be copied without you knowing.

cenas.visual: A test screen: an empty wallet, a phrase being entered, and a green tick appearing when the wallet recovers successfully.
cenas.narracao: Fourth, test the recovery. This is the part almost nobody does, and it's the most important. With a zero or negligible amount, in an official app, try to recreate the wallet using only the written phrase. If you manage it, the copy works. If you don't, you've discovered the problem now, and not when you really need it. A failed test today is a cheap lesson. A test that reveals a failure ten years from now is a loss. Repeat the test whenever you change wallet or app, and at least once a year, because apps change and memory does too.

cenas.visual: Illustrative case: Inês with a metal plate in one hand and a folded sheet of paper in the other, on a wooden table.
cenas.narracao: Illustrative case: Inês engraved the phrase on a metal plate, kept a second paper copy in a relative's safe, and did the recovery test with a symbolic amount in a test wallet. It took an afternoon. For her, it was the most useful afternoon of the year as far as crypto goes. Not because she gained anything, but because she stopped depending on luck. Notice that the plan doesn't require anything technical. It requires method and discipline. Inês didn't have to become an expert. She had to have a plan and stick to it.

cenas.visual: Ruben closing a notebook, with the phrase "the key has to work before you use it for real" appearing in the corner.
cenas.narracao: The idea I want you to take from here is that the four steps have one common goal: for your key to keep existing when you're no longer paying attention to it. A key that only works in your head isn't a key. It's a hope. And hope isn't a security plan. Think of it as insurance: you don't like paying for it, but you never see it as wasted on the day you need it.

aulas.titulo: Aula 5.1 — Fake support and requests for your key
aulas.gancho: Imagine you get a message from a platform's support team saying your account has been blocked and you have to act right now. If that makes you nervous, this lesson is for you.

cenas.visual: A phone screen with a private message notification. The logo looks almost identical to the original, but the lettering is slightly different. A clock in the corner is counting down.
cenas.narracao: Let's start with the most common scam, and also the easiest one to stop. Someone messages you on social media or in a group chat and presents themselves as a platform's support team. They say your account has been blocked, that there's an urgent verification, and that they need to confirm something. The message looks real. It has the right logo, the right language and even a reference number. But it's a lie, and the urgency is the first clue. Whoever is trying to catch you needs you to make a quick mistake, without thinking twice. That's why the countdown clock isn't a detail. It's their main weapon.

cenas.visual: Three padlocks animated as they close, labelled: password, two-factor code, seed phrase.
cenas.narracao: Here's the rule that is never broken. No legitimate support team will ask you for your seed phrase. They won't ask for your password, or for the code that arrives by SMS or in the app. And they won't write to you first to say you have a problem. The seed phrase, those twelve or twenty-four words you keep to recover your wallet, is the key to everything you hold there. Whoever has it has the money. There are no exceptions, not for support, not for a technician who calls you, not for anyone who says they work with the platform. If a message asks you to confirm something you never even looked for, the answer is no.

cenas.visual: Illustrative case. A café in Coimbra, Inês sitting by the window with her phone in her hand. Small caption: "illustrative case".
cenas.narracao: Let me tell you an illustrative case. Inês, twenty-nine, a nurse in Coimbra, received a message like this one on an afternoon off, while she was having a coffee. The support name looked official, and they asked her to validate her account through a website. She was suspicious for a simple reason: the message arrived without her having asked anyone for help. Instead of clicking, she closed the conversation, opened the app she already had installed and looked for herself. There was no block at all. There was a trap waiting for one tap.

cenas.visual: A split screen. On the left, a long, strange link. On the right, the official app, with the address typed by hand into the browser.
cenas.narracao: That's exactly what Inês did, and it's what you should do too. If you think there's a problem with an account, don't use the link you received. Open the official app, or type the website address by hand into your browser. Look for the information there. If the problem is real, you'll find it in the right place, in the security area or in the notifications. If nothing shows up, the message was fake, and you stopped it without losing anything. This habit seems small, but it's what separates people who lose money from people who don't. Also save the official address in your bookmarks, so you can use it next time without relying on anyone.

cenas.visual: Large text on screen: "If someone asks for your key, it's a scam." The word "support" is crossed out in red.
cenas.narracao: Keep this sentence: if someone asks for your key, it's a scam, even if they look like support. Don't reply out of politeness, don't send a test message and don't click to sort it out quickly. Block the contact, report it on the platform where it appeared, and warn anyone who might be in the same situation, especially older family members, who are a favorite target for these messages. Scammers buy lists of accounts and phone numbers at random, and send thousands of identical messages. It isn't a personal attack, it's a volume business, which is why the best response is to give them nothing at all. If by any chance you've already given away your seed phrase, consider the wallet compromised. Create a new wallet on a clean device, and move what you can as quickly as possible. Then contact the platform. Every minute counts, because the person who scammed you is in a hurry too.

cenas.visual: The clock from scene 1 stops at zero. An arrow points to lesson 5.2.
cenas.narracao: To sum up: nobody legitimate asks for your key, urgency is always a clue, and the link in a message is never the right way in. In the next lesson we'll look at the promise to double your money. It seems very different, but it's the same story in different clothes, and the maths behind it is even more revealing.

aulas.titulo: Aula 5.2 — Doubling, pyramids and promises
aulas.gancho: If someone guarantees that your money will double in a few days, the first thing you should feel is distrust, not excitement.

cenas.visual: An on-screen advert: "Send 500 and receive 1,000 in 7 days". Below it, a label: "guaranteed doubling".
cenas.narracao: This is the oldest promise in the world in new clothes. You send crypto to an address, or you join a group, and they tell you you'll get double back in a short time.
