Sometimes it's presented as a prize draw, sometimes as a sign-up bonus, sometimes as a rewards programme that levels up. The format changes, but the structure is almost always the same. Before anything else, ask yourself one very simple question: where does the money for that doubling come from? If there's no answer, the conversation ends there.

cenas.visual: An animated diagram: people joining from the bottom, money rising to those at the top, and more and more small circles coming together.
cenas.narracao: In a pyramid scheme, the money paid to the first participants doesn't come from any real product or activity. It comes from the people who join later. To pay those who joined early, more and more people have to keep joining. And here's the arithmetic that's usually hidden. Imagine that each person has to bring in two new people to move up a level. By the tenth level, that step alone needs one thousand and twenty-four new people. By the twentieth, it's more than a million. No market can sustain that sum for long, and whoever joins late is the one left paying.

cenas.visual: An animated list with four signs, one at a time: "fixed high return", "today only", "bring friends to level up", "fees to withdraw".
cenas.narracao: There are signs that keep repeating. They promise a fixed, high return, with no risk explained. They create time pressure, with phrases like today only or last place. They pay bonuses for bringing in friends, rather than for using a product or a service. And when you ask to take money out, fees, deadlines or new requirements appear, as if you had to pay to get out. If you see two or more of these signs at the same time, it's not the moment to study the offer calmly. It's the moment to leave.

cenas.visual: Illustrative case. A small office in Leiria, Tiago, thirty-four, a refrigeration technician, looking at his phone. Caption: "illustrative case".
cenas.narracao: Let me tell you an illustrative case. Tiago, thirty-four, a refrigeration technician in Leiria, joined a group because a friend told him he had got double his money back. At first, everything seemed to work, and they even paid him a small amount to build his trust. Then they asked him for another two hundred euros to level up. When he tried to withdraw what he had, the request was under review for weeks. He realized too late that the payments he was receiving came from the money of the people who joined after him. As this is an illustrative case, the numbers belong to nobody, but the pattern repeats in many stories.

cenas.visual: A blank screen with one large question: "Who pays your profit?"
cenas.narracao: The question you should always ask is this: who pays the profit? In a real investment, the return comes from something real, such as an activity, a company or a market with genuine supply and demand. It can go up or down, and you can lose everything, but there's a visible source. If the answer is the people who join next, you're looking at a pyramid, however well packaged it is. And pay attention to the pressure to invite other people, because that's how the scheme grows. When your success depends on bringing in people, the product is the entry itself.

cenas.visual: A split screen. On the left, a chart that always goes up. On the right, the same chart with a warning line saying "withdrawal blocked".
cenas.narracao: Notice a detail that fools a lot of people. The first payments are usually real. They're there precisely to give you confidence. The problem shows up when you want to withdraw a large amount, and that's when the door slowly closes. So never judge an offer by what you've already received. Judge it by how easily you're allowed to get out. If you can't get out easily, it isn't an investment, it's a trap with a nice-looking receipt. So what do you do when someone promises you double? You don't join, you don't send anything to test it, and you don't ask the contact who wrote to you for more details. Search for the project's name together with the word scam and read what other people have said. And before any money decision, apply the 24-hour rule, which we'll look at more closely in the checklist. An honest offer can handle that wait without any problem.

aulas.titulo: Aula 5.3 — Phishing, airdrops and approvals
aulas.gancho: Sometimes a single swapped letter in a website address is enough to make you lose your entire wallet. Let's see how that happens.

cenas.visual: Two almost identical addresses side by side. One letter in the second address is highlighted in red.
cenas.narracao: Let's talk about phishing. It's a copy. Scammers build a site that looks identical to the original, with the same logo, the same colors and the same buttons. Often only one letter in the address changes, or they use a lookalike domain with one extra little dash. When you get there, you type in your password or connect your wallet, and whoever set up the site keeps whatever you gave them. The site looks right, but the address is different. And the difference is in the address, which is what saves you. These sites are built in minutes and tend to last only briefly, because they're reported quickly. So don't trust the appearance, or how fast the page loads.

cenas.visual: A search engine screen with the first result marked "Ad".
cenas.narracao: There's an extra caution here. Sponsored ads at the top of search engines can also lead to fake sites. Don't trust a result just because it appears first. Look for the official site, check the address and, if you can, save it in your browser bookmarks. Notice that the genuine site rarely asks you for anything urgent on its homepage. If a page pressures you to enter details, be suspicious of the page itself.

cenas.visual: A message on screen: "You've received 5,000 free tokens! Connect your wallet to claim them". A red counter counting down.
cenas.narracao: Airdrops are free distributions of tokens. They do exist, but they're rare, and they almost never arrive by private message from a stranger. When someone offers you free tokens and asks you to connect your wallet to a site, you're giving a permission. And that permission can allow someone to move your funds. The red counter is the same old pressure, dressed up as a game. If something is free and asks you to connect your wallet, be suspicious first and research afterwards. If someone asks you to share your screen while you claim the prize, it's even more serious, because they can see everything you do.

cenas.visual: A simulated approval window on screen. The word "unlimited" is highlighted, with an arrow pointing to the "Approve" button.
cenas.narracao: Here's the technical detail most people never read. When you use some decentralized applications, the wallet asks for an approval. It's an authorization for a contract to move certain tokens you hold. Often, the approval comes with an unlimited amount already selected by default. If you approve a malicious contract with unlimited permission, it can withdraw those tokens whenever it likes, without asking you again. So always read what you're authorizing. And revoke the approvals you no longer use, with the official permission-revocation tools.

cenas.visual: Illustrative case. A student bedroom in Braga, Gonçalo, twenty-six, watching the countdown of an airdrop on his laptop. Caption: "illustrative case".
cenas.narracao: Let me tell you an illustrative case. Gonçalo, twenty-six, a student in Braga, received a link to claim an airdrop. The page was attractive, it had a countdown, and even a list of winners that kept updating. He connected his wallet, approved something he didn't understand and went to bed. Days later, he noticed tokens were missing. Nobody had asked him for his seed phrase, but he had given permission to whoever wanted it. The mistake wasn't technical. It was haste, and haste is exactly what these sites are designed to provoke.

cenas.visual: A screen with three questions in a row: "Who's asking? Why now? What am I authorizing?"
cenas.narracao: Before any connection or approval, ask yourself three questions. Who is asking? If you don't have a clear answer, that's a warning sign. Why is this happening now? If the justification is urgency, or a prize that expires today, be suspicious. And what am I authorizing, exactly? If you can't answer that precisely, don't sign. Every signature is a decision, not a courtesy click. You can hold on to a simple rule, and it's worth repeating: if you don't understand it, don't sign it. No prize is worth losing your wallet. And if you've already signed something suspicious, revoke that permission as soon as you can and check your balances. That doesn't mean everything is lost, but it does mean you need to act now, not tomorrow. In the last lesson of this module we'll look at the hardest part of all: the scam that is simply a friendly conversation.

aulas.titulo: Aula 5.4 — Romance, pressure and the 10-point checklist
aulas.gancho: The scam that's hardest to stop doesn't start with a website. It starts with a friendly conversation that gets closer and closer.

cenas.visual: A dating app screen with a smiling photo and the line: "I met you by chance, you seemed so nice".
cenas.narracao: There's a scam that begins slowly. Someone meets you on a dating app, or in a group chat, and the relationship grows closer over several weeks. You share routines, photos, jokes and confidences. When the subject of money comes up, the person talks about a crypto investment that's going really well for them, and offers to let you in too. They show you screenshots of profits and a platform with a beautiful dashboard. The closer the relationship gets, the harder it is to be suspicious. It comes disguised as friendship, and that's what makes it so dangerous. Look at the dashboard. Those numbers are designed to look real, and whoever shows them to you controls everything you see. It proves nothing. A platform that only exists inside a screen someone else shows you doesn't prove a profit, it only proves that somebody knows how to draw a chart. If you can't withdraw the money without paying more fees, or without waiting weeks for a new verification, the problem is there, not in your bad luck.

cenas.visual: An animated checklist, with the points appearing one by one, each with a tick.
cenas.narracao: So let's go through the ten-point checklist, which you can print and keep. One: nobody asks you for your seed phrase, your password or a code, ever. Two: you type the address by hand or use a verified bookmark, and you never click a link that reached you by message. Three: the platform is authorized under MiCA, the European regulation for crypto-asset service providers, and you can confirm that on the register of the authority in the country where it operates. Four: you turn on two-factor authentication with an app, not with SMS. Five: you use a unique password, stored in a password manager. Six: you're suspicious of any guaranteed return or any doubling. Seven: time pressure is an alarm, not an incentive.

cenas.visual: The checklist continues, with points eight to ten appearing on screen.
cenas.narracao: Eight: you never approve a contract you don't understand. Nine: you never install remote-access software at the request of a stranger, because whoever controls your screen controls everything you do. Ten: before you move any money, you wait twenty-four hours and talk to someone you trust. That last rule protects more people than any software does. Haste is the fuel of every scam, and waiting is the cheapest antidote there is.

cenas.visual: An animation of five concentric rings, each with a short label. Chart ID: camadas-seguranca.
cenas.narracao: No single defense is enough, so think in layers. The first layer is your email account, with a strong, unique password. The second is app-based authentication on the platforms you use. The third is a verified address, always the same one, saved in your bookmarks. The fourth is withdrawal limits and the allowed-address list, when the platform offers that option. And the fifth, the most important one for large amounts, is keeping most of it in a cold wallet, away from any screen connected to the internet. If one layer fails, the next one still protects you.

cenas.visual: A screen with a large clock and the line: "Is the person not letting you think? You already have the answer."
cenas.narracao: When someone pressures you to decide today, you're not talking to a friend who wants to help you. You're talking to someone who needs you not to think. A serious investment can withstand a week of reflection, and an honest project doesn't get angry when you ask for time. If the person gets irritated, disappears or makes you feel guilty for hesitating, you already have your answer. Your calm is the best defense you have, and it costs nothing.

cenas.visual: A screen with the title "Module mission" and a box to tick.
cenas.narracao: The module's mission is simple and concrete. This week, print the ten-point checklist and place it next to your computer. Check whether your platforms have app-based authentication. Review the active approvals in the wallets you use, and revoke any you don't recognize. And write your seed phrase on paper, by hand, in a safe place, without photographing it or sending it to anyone. When you've done all of this, tick the word done. This is the first key to your shield, and it's the one that matters most.

modulos.titulo: Módulo 6 — DCA, cycles and halving (≈17 min)

aulas.titulo: Aula 6.1 — DCA, the boring method that takes the guesswork out
aulas.gancho: There is a way of investing that almost nobody wants to hear about, because it is boring. That is exactly why it takes the guesswork out of the equation.

cenas.visual: Animated calendar with one marked day in each month and a coin falling onto every marked day.
cenas.narracao: DCA stands for regular buying, or dollar cost averaging. The idea is simple. Instead of investing everything at once, you buy a fixed amount at regular intervals. It can be one hundred euros a month, or twenty euros a week. You buy when the price is high and you buy when it is low, without trying to pick the right moment. The goal is not to hit the top or the bottom of the market. It is to stay disciplined for a long time, without relying on a hunch that makes you stop or speed up. This is the part that sounds unexciting, and it is also the part most people give up on. Think of it as the monthly savings you put aside, except that instead of leaving it sitting still, you put it into an asset.

cenas.visual: Animated table with the illustrative example: three purchases of one hundred euros, at prices of fifty, twenty-five and fifty. Caption: “illustrative example, made-up figures”.
cenas.narracao: Let's look at an illustrative example, with made-up, round prices, just to understand the mechanics. Imagine you buy one hundred euros a month, for three months, in a hypothetical asset. In the first month it costs fifty euros, so you buy two units. In the second month the price drops to twenty-five, and with the same one hundred euros you buy four units. In the third month it goes back up to fifty, and you buy two more. In total you have eight units and you have spent three hundred euros. Your average price per unit is thirty-seven euros and fifty cents. Notice that this figure is below the simple average of the three prices, because you bought more when it was cheap.

cenas.visual: Split screen. On the left, the lump sum: three hundred euros at fifty, six units. On the right, DCA: eight units. The totals change across three milestones.
cenas.narracao: Now the comparison. If you had invested the full three hundred euros in the first month, at fifty euros, you would have six units. At the end of the example, with the price back at fifty, the eight DCA units are worth four hundred euros, and the six lump-sum units are worth three hundred. But look at the middle of the path. After the second month, with the price at twenty-five, DCA has six units, worth one hundred and fifty euros on two hundred invested. The lump sum also has six units and is worth one hundred and fifty, but on three hundred invested. In percentage terms, the lump sum is down fifty percent and DCA is down twenty-five percent.

cenas.visual: Red alert on screen: “Not a guarantee of profit”. Below it, a chart of a price that rises right at the start and never comes back down.
cenas.narracao: Now notice what this example does not say. It does not say that DCA is always better. If the price had risen in the first month and never come back down, the lump sum would have earned much more. DCA trades part of that opportunity for less stress and less risk of buying everything at the top. It is not a guarantee of profit, and an asset can fall for years without recovering. So the amount you use in each purchase has to be an amount you can afford to lose, without it affecting your income, your bills or your sleep.

cenas.visual: Calendar with a tick mark in each month, and beside it a sheet with the rules written down.
cenas.narracao: DCA works like a habit. The biggest enemy is not the market. It is your hand pressing the button when the price falls and fear kicks in, or when it rises and greed kicks in. So write the rules down before you start. How much you buy, on which day, on which platform, and what you do if one month you are short of money. Then stick to them. A rule written on a sheet of paper is worth more than ten decisions made in a hurry, in the middle of the night, with your phone in your hand. Once the rule is written, the emotion of the day no longer runs the show.

cenas.visual: Arrow pointing to lesson 6.2. Text beside it: “What actually changes?”.
cenas.narracao: In the next lesson we will look at one of the most talked-about topics in the crypto world, the halving, and why so many people get so excited about it. You will understand what actually changes on the network, and what is just noise around the date. Keep the central idea of this lesson: DCA does not predict anything. It organises your purchases and lets the market do whatever it wants. Work through the sum yourself, with other made-up prices, and you will understand the logic in ten minutes.

aulas.titulo: Aula 6.2 — Halving: the supply clock
aulas.gancho: Roughly every four years, the creation of new bitcoins is cut in half. Do you know why, and do you know what that really means?

cenas.visual: Animation of a reward bar shrinking in five steps, with the dates underneath: fifty, twenty-five, twelve point five, six point two five, three point one two five. Chart ID: halving.
cenas.narracao: New bitcoins are created by miners, as a reward for validating blocks of transactions. That reward is not fixed. It is set in the protocol itself: every 210,000 blocks, which takes about four years on average, the reward per block is cut in half. This is called the halving. When the network started, in 2009, the reward was fifty bitcoins per block. In 2012 it dropped to twenty-five. In 2016 it went to twelve point five, in 2020 to six point two five, and in 2024 to three point one two five. Each step cuts the new supply in half. Notice that the rule does not depend on any one person: it is written in the code and applies in the same way to everyone.

cenas.visual: Screen with the phrase “21 million” and a bar filling up, almost to the top.
cenas.narracao: With this rule, the total supply converges towards the limit of twenty-one million bitcoins. Most of it has already been issued, and what remains comes out in smaller and smaller slices, almost unnoticed. This is a fact about new supply, and that is what makes the topic interesting. Fewer new bitcoins per day means, in theory, less supply entering the market. Miners also pay for energy and equipment, so the drop in reward has a big effect on their accounts. But theory and price are different things, and this is where many people get it wrong. Supply is one piece of the puzzle. Demand, context and the mood of all the participants are the other pieces.

cenas.visual: Line chart with the price and vertical markers at the halving years. Above it, a box saying “what happened before”.
cenas.narracao: It is tempting to look at past halvings and conclude that the price always rises after each one. That conclusion is dangerous. There are too few cases to draw a rule from, the context changed a lot from one cycle to the next, and the market may have anticipated the event months earlier. Each halving is a fact about supply, not a date marked for a price rise. Use it as information to understand the market, never as a certainty about what will happen.

cenas.visual: Illustrative case. A bedroom in Aveiro, Marta, 38, a teacher, with her laptop open at night. Caption: “illustrative case”.
cenas.narracao: I want to tell you an illustrative case. Marta, 38, a teacher in Aveiro, watched a video about the halving and became convinced that a rise was certain. She bought everything at once, in one night, with money she had set aside for the car. In the following weeks the price fell, and she was left staring at the screen, not knowing what to do. She did not sell in a panic, but she did not have a plan either. The mistake was not the halving, which is a real fact. The mistake was treating a date as a guarantee, and using money that should not have been used. If the purchase had been made in instalments, with a written plan, she would have had time to review her decisions at every step.

cenas.visual: Split screen: on the left, the logo of a proof-of-work network; on the right, that of a proof-of-stake network. Text: “Not every network has a halving”.
cenas.narracao: A technical note, because it is easy to get confused. Not every network works this way. Bitcoin uses proof of work, with miners competing with energy and equipment. Ethereum moved to proof of stake in September 2022, in the event known as The Merge, and it no longer has mining or halvings. Each network has its own issuance rule. Before you say that something will rise because it has a halving, first ask yourself whether that network has a halving at all, and what kind.

cenas.visual: Screen with a big question: “Fact, news or promise?”. Three boxes underneath.
cenas.narracao: So what does the halving teach you that is useful? It teaches you to think in long cycles and in supply, not in the news of the day. It also teaches you to be wary of anyone who sells the halving as a money machine. There is a lot of content that turns a date into a show, with countdown clocks and dramatic music. You do not need any of that. You need to understand the rule, keep the fact in mind, and decide what to do with your money based on a plan, not on a countdown. That brings us to the topic of the next lesson: how to read the market without guessing.

aulas.titulo: Aula 6.3 — Cycles, volatility and dominance: reading without guessing
aulas.gancho: The crypto market goes up and down with a force that frightens anyone who is not prepared. The question is not how to get it right. It is how to read it without guessing.

cenas.visual: Chart with a volatility line and the caption: “drops of more than 70% in different years”.
cenas.narracao: Let's start with volatility, which is the size of price movements. In crypto it is very high. Bitcoin has fallen more than seventy percent from its peak, on more than one occasion, and many other coins have fallen even further. Before you buy, ask yourself an honest question: if my balance fell by half, could I carry on without selling in a panic? If the answer is no, your exposure is too big, whatever the videos say. This question is worth more than any forecast.

cenas.visual: Cycle curve drawn on screen, with four phases marked: accumulation, uptrend, euphoria, downtrend.
cenas.narracao: Many people talk about cycles: a phase of accumulation, a strong rise, a euphoria in which everyone seems rich, then a long decline and a period of exhaustion. Cycles are a useful way of reading the past, because they help you recognise patterns of human behaviour. But they are not a calendar. In the euphoria it seems the whole world has got rich, and in the decline it seems it will never recover. Nobody knows exactly when the phase changes. There is a dangerous phrase you hear in every cycle: this time is different. Sometimes there are real changes, but the wish for it to be different is always the same old emotion. Anyone who swears they know is almost always trying to sell you something. You do not need to memorise any of this.

cenas.visual: Pie chart with the bitcoin slice standing out, and an arrow going up and down.
cenas.narracao: Another indicator is bitcoin dominance, which is the percentage of the total market value that belongs to bitcoin. When dominance rises, money tends to concentrate in bitcoin, which is seen as the most established asset. When it falls, there can be more appetite for altcoins, which are riskier and more volatile coins. It is not a magic rule, and it can mislead you if you read it on its own. But it is a way of seeing where the money is going, and that is already useful information for your plan. Notice that dominance also rises when the market falls back, because smaller coins usually drop harder.

cenas.visual: Screen with three headlines in a row: “It's going to explode!”, “It's all over!”, “Official news: new rule published”. The last one is highlighted.
cenas.narracao: Learn to separate news from noise. News is a verifiable fact: a law passed, a confirmed technical failure, a concrete change in supply or regulation. Noise is an opinion repeated a thousand times, the alarmist headline, and the video with epic music and red arrows. Before you react, ask: has this changed anything in the project, or has it only changed people's mood? If it is only mood, you usually do not need to act today. A good habit is to save the news in a list and review that list a week later. If nobody is talking about it any more, it was probably noise.

cenas.visual: Screen with a weekly calendar and the phrase “Plan before the guess”. A clock with its hand stopped.
cenas.narracao: Reading the market without guessing means accepting that you do not know what comes tomorrow, and organising yourself for that. Define your plan before things happen. Write down what would make you change your mind, and trust that piece of paper more than the noise of the moment. Check your balance once a week, not every minute, because watching nonstop increases emotion and reduces clarity. Someone without a plan ends up reacting to everything, and reacting to everything is usually expensive, because decisions get made out of fear or euphoria. The market owes you nothing, and that is not a problem. The problem is being left without a plan.

cenas.visual: Final screen with the phrase: “Reading without guessing = written plan + verified information”.
cenas.narracao: To sum up this lesson: volatility shows you how much you could suffer, cycles show you patterns that are not a calendar, dominance shows you where the money is going, and verifiable news is separated from noise. None of these pieces gives you the right answer for tomorrow. Together, they give you something better, which is a criterion for deciding calmly. If any of these ideas seem complicated, that is fine. Just start with one of them and write down what you observed. In the last lesson of this module we will turn all of this into a concrete buying plan.

aulas.titulo: Aula 6.4 — Module mission: your DCA plan
aulas.gancho: Moving from theory to practice is the step most people skip. Today we are not going to skip it. We are going to do it with paper and pen.

cenas.visual: Sheet with five fields to fill in: monthly amount, fixed day, platform, exception rule, review date.
cenas.narracao: We are going to build a DCA plan, step by step. First, choose a monthly amount that you could lose without it ruining your life. It is not whatever happens to be left at the end of the month by chance. It is what remains after your fixed bills, an emergency fund and the taxes you already have to pay. Second, choose a fixed day, for example the day after payday. Third, choose the regulated platform where you will buy, and confirm that verification and authentication are in order. Fourth, write the exception rule: what you do in a month when it is not possible. Fifth, mark when you will review the plan, for example every three months. Remember: the plan is not a contract with the market. It is a contract with yourself.

cenas.visual: Large warning on screen: “Never money for rent, your transport pass or water”.
cenas.narracao: One rule that is not negotiable: never use money you need for rent, your transport pass, water, electricity or the IRS, the Portuguese income tax. If a month goes wrong, you do not want to be forced to sell in order to pay for your home, and that is exactly when decisions turn bad. Start small. Ten or twenty euros a week is enough to learn the process, understand the fees and see how you feel when the price falls. That feeling is the most valuable part of the training. If you have doubts about the platform, ask before you buy, never after.

cenas.visual: Screen with the MTM logo and the text “Salas DCA com MTM”, with a group room made of small squares.
cenas.narracao: If you want to practise with support, there are the Salas DCA com MTM, the DCA group rooms, where this method is worked on as a group, with examples and live questions. I am not going to promise you results or returns, because I do not control them and I cannot guarantee them to anyone. What I can say is that learning from other people, discussing plans, mistakes and doubts, helps you avoid deciding alone and in a hurry. And there is the MoreThanMoney community, where you can ask simple questions without feeling embarrassed. If you decide to join, remember that the group is there to help you learn, not to tell you what to buy. If it makes sense for you, take a look, with no rush and no pressure. The decision is yours.

cenas.visual: Checklist with boxes to tick: written plan, date, verified platform, active authentication, 24-hour wait.
cenas.narracao: Once you have written the plan, sign it with the date and keep it somewhere safe, separate from your seed phrase. Before the first purchase, confirm that the platform is verified, that two-factor authentication is active, and that you have the addresses saved in your bookmarks. And let 24 hours pass before you make the first purchase. That wait is the final test: if, the next day, you still want to, the plan is yours. If you no longer want to, good thing you waited. Do not rush just because the market seems to be in a good mood that day. Also write down what you will do if the price falls by half, so the rule is clear before the scare, not during it.

cenas.visual: Screen titled “Module mission” with a box to tick. Underneath, the warning phrase in small letters.
cenas.narracao: The module mission is this: write your DCA plan on paper, with the five points we covered, and sign it. Do not buy anything yet if you do not have the platform verified and two-factor authentication active. And always remember: this is educational content, not financial advice, and the risk of loss is real. You can lose what you put in. So the plan is your protection, and haste is the enemy. Keep this paper and reread it before every review.

cenas.visual: Closing screen with the number 7 and the phrase: “Next module: your DCA with the MTM tools”.
cenas.narracao: With this lesson you close Module 6. You now know what DCA is, you can read the halving without falling for the show, and you can separate volatility, cycles, dominance and noise. In the next module we take this plan and put it to work with the MTM tools: the DCA Inteligente MTM, the MTM System app, the Portefólios and two scanners that help you choose the size of each top-up. Until then, write your plan and stick to it. Thank you for getting this far, I really mean it.

modulos.titulo: Módulo 7 — Your DCA with the MTM tools (≈16 min)

aulas.titulo: Aula 7.1 — DCA that is not dumb
aulas.gancho: DCA has a reputation: it is the method for people who don't think. You always buy the same amount, on the same day, whatever happens. And what if I told you that you can think a little, without spoiling what is good about DCA?

cenas.visual: Ruben in a medium shot, almost black background, details in gold. Text on screen: “Educational content. The risk of loss is real.”
cenas.narracao: In the previous module you wrote your plan: an amount, a fixed day, a platform. That plan is the most important thing in this bootcamp, and we are not going to touch it. What we will do in this lesson is give it a small steering wheel. Classic DCA always buys the same amount. Smart DCA always buys too, but it lets you adjust the size of each purchase depending on whether the market is more expensive or cheaper than usual. Notice the word “always”. Smart DCA never stops buying because of an opinion. It only changes the size.

cenas.visual: Animation: a price line with small gold circles on every Friday. At first they are all the same size; then, on the days when the price drops, the circles get bigger; on the days of euphoria, they get smaller.
cenas.narracao: The idea is old and it is common sense. When the price has dropped a lot in one day, your money buys more units. When the price has shot up, it buys fewer. If you top up a little more on the days of decline and a little less on the days of euphoria, your average price tends to become more balanced. Tends to. I don't guarantee anything, and nobody can guarantee anything to you. But it is a line of reasoning you can understand and check with pencil and paper.

cenas.visual: Screen of the MTM System app, Portefólios tab, “Análise DCA” panel. Slow zoom onto the labels: Forte Compra, Compra, Aguardar, Não Reforçar.
cenas.narracao: At MoreThanMoney this has a name: DCA Inteligente. Every day the system looks at the assets in the portfolios, crypto and ETFs, compares today's price with recent behaviour, and gives each one one of four labels. Forte Compra, which means strong buy, when there has been a sharp drop. Compra, which means buy, when there has been a relevant drop. Aguardar, which means wait, when everything is calm. And Não Reforçar, which means do not top up, when the price has risen a lot in a single day and it is best not to chase it.

cenas.visual: Animated table, gold on charcoal: “Forte Compra → up to 2× the base · Compra → 1.5× · Aguardar → half · Não Reforçar → zero on that asset”.
cenas.narracao: Each label comes with a suggested size, always relative to your base amount. In crypto, for example, a daily drop of eight percent or more gives Forte Compra and suggests up to double the base. A drop of four percent or more gives Compra, and suggests one and a half times the base. For ETFs the thresholds are lower, because they move less. Remember: these are suggestions from a system, for education. The decision is yours.

cenas.visual: Ruben is back, with a notebook. On screen the phrase appears: “The ceiling matters more than the label.”
cenas.narracao: And now the rule that makes this safe. Your monthly ceiling does not change. If your plan is one hundred euros a month, it is one hundred euros a month, whether there is a Forte Compra or not. How does that work? With a reserve pot. In the weeks when the label says Aguardar or Não Reforçar, the part you don't spend goes into the pot. In the weeks of Forte Compra, the extra top-up comes out of the pot. If the pot is empty, you buy the base and that's it. You never go and get money from outside the plan.

cenas.visual: Exercise sheet with four Fridays, one column “label”, another “purchase” and another “pot”.
cenas.narracao: Two-minute exercise. Imagine a base of twenty-five euros a week. On the first Friday the label is Aguardar: you buy twelve euros and fifty cents, and the twelve euros and fifty cents go into the pot. On the second, Não Reforçar: zero on that asset, twenty-five into the pot. On the third, Forte Compra: you buy fifty, twenty-five from the base and twenty-five from the pot. On the fourth, Compra. Do the sum yourself. An illustrative example, of course.

aulas.titulo: Aula 7.2 — The MTM System app in your pocket
aulas.gancho: If you have to remember to go and check the market, you will forget. The trick is for the market to come to you, at the right time, and only with what matters.

cenas.visual: Phone screen recording: opening the MTM System app, logging in with the account, main menu.
cenas.narracao: Let's go to the app. Everything you see in this lesson is in the MTM System app, on your phone or on your computer. I won't show you balances, because they don't matter here. I'll show you three places: where the daily analysis appears, where the portfolios are, and where you turn on the alerts.

cenas.visual: Screen of the DCA analysis channel in the app chat: the daily post with the summary and the opportunities by label.
cenas.narracao: First place: the Análise DCA Inteligente channel. Every day the system posts a summary there, split into crypto and ETFs and stocks, with the assets that are in Forte Compra or Compra and a short reading of the day. You don't need to read this every day. You need to read it on your DCA day. If your day is Friday, you open Friday's post.

cenas.visual: Portefólios → Análise DCA screen, with the list of assets, the price, the change and the label for each one.
cenas.narracao: Second place: inside Portefólios, the Análise DCA panel. Here you see asset by asset: the price, the change, the label and a one-line explanation. This is the screen where you make your choice for the week. Look only at the assets that are in your plan. The others can be in Forte Compra all they like. They are not in your plan, so they are not your concern.

cenas.visual: Settings screen with the DCA alerts switch being turned on. A notification drops onto the lock screen.
cenas.narracao: Third place: the alerts. Turn on the DCA alerts in the app settings. That way, when an asset enters a top-up zone, you get a notice. Careful, this is not an order to buy outside your day. It is information. The discipline of the fixed day still applies. The alert is there so that you reach Friday already knowing what is waiting for you.

cenas.visual: Ruben, close-up, speaking directly to the camera.
cenas.narracao: An honest note. The app is a tool for following the market and for education. It does not buy for you, it does not keep your money, and it does not know what will happen tomorrow. You make the purchase yourself, on your authorised platform, as you learned in module three. The app helps you decide calmly and with information, which is already a lot.

cenas.visual: Checklist on screen with three boxes: “DCA channel open”, “Análise DCA panel viewed”, “alerts on”.
cenas.narracao: Mission for this lesson: open the app, find the three places and tick each one. It takes five minutes. In the next lesson we will look at the portfolios, which is the best way I know to learn how to do DCA by watching someone else do it.

aulas.titulo: Aula 7.3 — The Portefólios: learning by watching someone else
aulas.gancho: The best way to learn to cook is not to read recipes. It is to stand in the kitchen next to someone. With DCA it is the same.

cenas.visual: Portefólios screen with the two house portfolios side by side: “Crypto” and “ETF”, with the evolution curve.
cenas.narracao: In the app there are two house portfolios: one crypto and one ETF. They are topped up every Friday, with fixed amounts per asset, and they are recorded in the app, purchase by purchase. You can see what was bought, when and at what price. It is an open DCA diary.

cenas.visual: Zoom into the portfolio's list of movements: Friday dates, asset, amount, reason “weekly DCA”.
cenas.narracao: Notice the dates. Friday, Friday, Friday. Weeks of good markets, weeks of bad markets, and the purchase is there. This is what I want you to see: the hard part of DCA is not the maths. It is carrying on buying when everyone around you says it is nonsense, and not buying too much when everyone says it is now or never.

cenas.visual: Animation: the portfolio split into coloured slices, with captions “one larger asset, some medium, some small”.
cenas.narracao: Also look at how the portfolio is divided. There is a larger weight on a few assets and smaller weights on others. I am not telling you to copy these assets. I am telling you to copy the idea: a portfolio has a structure, written down beforehand, and that structure does not change every week because of a headline.

cenas.visual: Ruben showing the notebook with a table: “asset · weight · amount per week”.
cenas.narracao: Now do yours. Write down the assets in your plan, the weight of each one and the amount per week. If you are starting out, less is more. One or two assets are perfectly enough. Remember the seven questions from module two before you put any name on this list.

cenas.visual: Screen split in two: on the left the house portfolio, on the right the student's table.
cenas.narracao: Use the house portfolios as a mirror, not as a template. When you have doubts, for example “should I buy this week, with the market falling like this?”, go and see what happened in the house portfolios in similar weeks. You will see that the answer, almost always, was to buy the base and move on.

cenas.visual: Final text on screen with the warning: “Demo and educational portfolios. Past results do not guarantee future results.”
cenas.narracao: The house portfolios exist for learning. What they did in the past says nothing about what they will do in the future, nor about what yours will do. In the next lesson we will go up a step and look at the chart, with a tool you already know by name: Momentum.

aulas.titulo: Aula 7.4 — Momentum on the big chart: choosing the size, not the day
aulas.gancho: Momentum is a trading scanner. So what is it doing in a DCA module? It is acting as a traffic light.

cenas.visual: Screen recording of TradingView: daily Bitcoin chart with the Momentum scanner. Cloud, exponential average, volume panel and RSI.
cenas.narracao: You have already heard of Momentum, the MTM scanner that works with colours. Green for buy, red for sell. Traders use it on fifteen-minute or one-hour charts. We are going to use it differently: on the daily and weekly charts, the big charts, which show the underlying direction and not the noise of the day.

cenas.visual: Animation with five squares lighting up one by one: cloud, position of the cloud, exponential average, volume, RSI.
cenas.narracao: Momentum has five confirmations, and each one is worth one point. Is the cloud present and the right colour? Is the cloud on the correct side of the candles? Does the exponential average agree? Does the volume have the colour of the direction? And is the RSI crossing in the right zone? Five out of five is the most complete signal. Four out of five is still good. With fewer, Momentum is telling you it does not have a strong opinion.

cenas.visual: Three daily charts side by side, with captions: “green and in favour”, “strong red”, “lilac boxes”.
cenas.narracao: Now, how does this fit into DCA? With three simple readings, on your top-up day. First: a green daily chart, with four or five buy confirmations. The underlying trend is in your favour. You make the top-up that DCA Inteligente suggests. Second: a strong red daily chart, five out of five sell. The decline is under way. You buy the base, but you don't empty the pot yet. You wait for the selling pressure to ease. Third: lilac boxes on top of the candles, a sideways market. For a trader, this is where you don't enter. For someone doing DCA, it is an ordinary day. You buy the base.

cenas.visual: Weekly chart of the same asset, with a slow zoom out.
cenas.narracao: And the weekly chart? Use it once a month, to see the whole picture. If the weekly chart has turned to buy after a long decline, it is a good moment to review your plan and confirm that the pot is ready for the Forte Compra weeks. If the weekly chart is in strong sell, you change nothing. DCA was designed for exactly those phases.

cenas.visual: Ruben, close-up, with the phrase on screen: “The traffic light does not switch off the car.”
cenas.narracao: The golden rule: Momentum does not stop your DCA. Never. It helps you decide whether you use the pot or not, and how much. If you ever catch yourself saying “I'm not buying this week because it's red”, come back to this lesson. Red on the daily chart, for someone doing DCA, means base, not zero.

cenas.visual: Exercise sheet with three charts and three boxes to fill in: “reading”, “points”, “what I do”.
cenas.narracao: Exercise: open the daily chart of an asset in your plan with Momentum. Count the confirmations. Write down the reading, the points, and what you would do next Friday: base, base plus pot, or base without the pot. Do this for three Fridays in a row, without buying anything extra, just recording. You will learn more from this than from any video.

aulas.titulo: Aula 7.5 — DEFY: when the price stretches too far
aulas.gancho: There are days when the price falls so much that it looks like an elastic band stretched to its limit. DEFY was built to show you those days.

cenas.visual: Daily chart with DEFY: inner, middle and outer exhaustion bands around a smooth average, with the dashed projection.
cenas.narracao: DEFY is another MTM scanner. It draws exhaustion bands around a smooth average: an inner one, a middle one and an outer one. When the price stretches out to the outer band and turns with a strong candle, DEFY marks an idea. For a trader, it is a possible entry point. For us, who do DCA, it is something else: it is a sign that the price is stretched to the downside, far from its normal level.

cenas.visual: Zoom into a DEFY buy idea, with the stars above the candle.
cenas.narracao: DEFY also adds up confirmations. Is the price at a level where it has reacted before? Is the trend cloud on the same side? Is there a volume break? With three confirmations, one star appears. With more, two or three. And when everything lines up, the candle turns gold. The stars measure how many confirmations there are. They do not measure the certainty of the result, because that does not exist.

cenas.visual: Animated table: “DCA Inteligente on Forte Compra + DEFY with a buy idea on the daily → use the pot”.
cenas.narracao: How is it used in DCA? As a second opinion. If on your top-up day DCA Inteligente says Forte Compra, and DEFY has a buy idea on the daily chart, with stars, the two readings agree: the price is stretched and there has been a sharp drop. That is the kind of week where it makes sense to use the reserve pot. If only one of them agrees, you buy the base and a little more from the pot, if you want. If neither agrees, base only.

cenas.visual: Ruben drawing a small three-line decision table in the notebook.
cenas.narracao: Let's put this into a simple table, to stick next to the screen. Two readings in favour: base plus pot. One reading in favour: base plus half the pot, at most. None: base only. And above all of it, the monthly ceiling, which is not broken. Choose one tool, Momentum or DEFY. Using both at the same time, at the start, is too much noise.

cenas.visual: Warning on screen, large letters: “DEFY signals are for trading. In DCA, they only affect the size.”
cenas.narracao: Be careful of a temptation. DEFY draws entry, stop and targets, because it was built for trading. Using DEFY does not give your DCA a stop and targets. Your DCA is long term, and it stays that way. If one day you want to trade with DEFY, that is a different course, a different account and a different risk.

cenas.visual: Summary screen with the complete decision table.
cenas.narracao: Lesson summary: DEFY shows you when the price has stretched too far. In DCA, it only helps you decide whether to use the pot. In the next lesson we bring everything together into a Friday ritual that fits in fifteen minutes.

aulas.titulo: Aula 7.6 — The Friday ritual in 15 minutes
aulas.gancho: Fifteen minutes a week. That is all your DCA needs from you. The rest of the week is for living.

cenas.visual: Animated clock with fifteen minutes split into five slices, each with an icon.
cenas.narracao: Let's bring everything together. The ritual has five steps and fits into fifteen minutes. Always do it on the same day and at the same time. I suggest Friday afternoon or the end of the day, but choose whatever works for you.

cenas.visual: Step 1 on screen: “Plan in front of you (1 min)”. Ruben opens the notebook at the page with the plan.
cenas.narracao: Step one, one minute: open your written plan. Base amount, assets, monthly ceiling and how much you have in the pot. Without this in front of you, nothing else gets done.

cenas.visual: Step 2: “DCA Inteligente (3 min)”. Portefólios → Análise DCA screen.
cenas.narracao: Step two, three minutes: open the Análise DCA panel in the app and write down the label of each asset in your plan. Forte Compra, Compra, Aguardar or Não Reforçar.

cenas.visual: Step 3: “Daily chart (4 min)”. TradingView with Momentum or DEFY.
cenas.narracao: Step three, four minutes: open the daily chart of each asset with your tool, Momentum or DEFY. Write down the reading: in favour, against or neutral.

cenas.visual: Steps 4 and 5: “Decide and buy (5 min)” and “Record (2 min)”. Record sheet with columns: date, asset, label, reading, purchase, pot.
cenas.narracao: Step four, five minutes: apply the decision table. Base, base plus half the pot, or base plus the pot, always within the ceiling. Make the purchase on your authorised platform. Step five, two minutes: record everything in one line of the sheet. Date, asset, label, reading, how much you bought and how much stayed in the pot. This sheet will serve you for taxes, which you will see in the next module, and for learning from yourself.

cenas.visual: Ruben closing the notebook. Final text: “Module 7 mission: three Fridays in a row, full ritual, recorded.” Underneath, the educational warning.
cenas.narracao: Module mission: do the ritual on three Fridays in a row and record the three lines. If you are not buying yet, do the ritual anyway and record what you would have done. That is how you train. And keep this: the MTM tools help you decide with more calm and more information. They do not decide for you, they do not guarantee anything, and the risk of loss is always yours. Educational content, not financial advice. See you in the last module.

aulas.titulo: Aula 8.1 — Core and satellites
aulas.gancho: Imagine a house. You have a structure you never touch, and some rooms you decorate over the years. A crypto portfolio works in much the same way.

cenas.visual: Ruben in a medium shot, almost black background, details in gold. Text on screen: “Educational content. The risk of loss is real.”
cenas.narracao: Before you set up anything, I want you to understand one thing. In a portfolio, the most important question is not which coin I buy. It is how much of my money goes into each piece, and why. This module is about that question. We are going to build the portfolio in layers, from the most stable to the riskiest, and each layer has its own role. If you have got this far, you already know what DCA is and you already have your plan, with a base amount, a fixed day and a ceiling. What is missing is giving shape to what you buy. And notice: we are talking about organisation and education. No portfolio gives you guarantees. The risk of loss is real, and it can be total.

cenas.visual: Animation: a large gold circle in the centre, with smaller circles around it. Labels: “core” in the centre, “satellites” around it.
cenas.narracao: The model we are going to use is called core and satellites. The core is the big part, the one you intend to hold for years. It is usually made up of the best-known assets with the longest history, and that is where your DCA spends most of its time. The satellites are the smaller part: smaller, more volatile assets, each with its own thesis, which you must be able to explain in two sentences. The core weathers the storms. The satellites are where you can regret things fastest. So the core is the foundation, and the satellites are an extra, with a cap.

cenas.visual: Stacked bar chart: core at the bottom, satellites on top, with a dashed line marking the satellite cap. Caption: “illustrative example”.
cenas.narracao: Let us put numbers on it, so you can see the order of magnitude. Illustrative example: a plan of one hundred euros a month. Ninety euros go to the core and ten to the satellites. Then, within the satellites, no single asset gets more than a small slice, say a third of the satellite pie. These numbers are not a recommendation. They are a way of making visible a decision that, without paper, stays hidden in a Thursday-night impulse. Once the decision is written down, it is much harder to take it badly on impulse. Notice that the sum is always the same: first the total, then the split, and only at the end the name of each asset.

cenas.visual: Ruben with an open notebook, a page divided into two columns: “core” and “satellites”, with a space underneath for the thesis of each asset.
cenas.narracao: Every satellite needs a written thesis. Ask yourself: why is it here? What problem does it solve, or what bet am I making? If the answer is “because it went up a lot last week”, that is not a thesis, it is a headline. Write the thesis before you buy, and review it once a month. If you can no longer explain why it is there, take it out of the satellites. Careful: DCA does not stop because of that. It is the plan that changes, in the notebook, calmly, and never in the middle of a drop. The new money then goes somewhere else in the plan.

cenas.visual: Split screen: on the left, a wallet with ten tiny slices; on the right, one with three well-defined slices. Text: “fewer assets, more thesis”.
cenas.narracao: A very common trap is holding twelve assets with one-euro slices. It looks like diversification, but in practice it is a collection of decisions you do not understand. Anyone starting should have a core of one or two assets and, at most, two or three satellites. If you are thinking about more, wait. You can always add later, once you have the habit of writing the thesis and recording every purchase. Fewer assets, more thesis, and a DCA you actually follow, rather than a DCA lost on a screen full of coins.

cenas.visual: Exercise sheet with three lines: “core”, “satellite 1”, “satellite 2”. Ruben writing by hand.
cenas.narracao: Three-minute exercise. Take your plan and write three lines in the notebook. On the first, the core, with the asset and its percentage of the plan. On the second and third, the satellites, if you want to have them, with the thesis in two sentences each. If you have no satellites, write “no satellites” and move on. It is a valid decision, and often the most sensible one. Next lesson we will see how much to put into each piece and how stablecoins fit into this sum. There is no exact percentage that suits everyone. Anyone who tells you there is, is selling you something.

aulas.titulo: Aula 8.2 — How much in BTC, ETH and stablecoins
aulas.gancho: Everyone asks how much to put into each coin. The honest answer starts with a different question: what is each one for?

cenas.visual: Three cards on screen, one per coin: BTC, ETH and stablecoins, each with a short line about its role.
cenas.narracao: Let us look at the three most common pieces of a crypto portfolio. Bitcoin is the oldest and best-known coin, which is why many people use it as the base of the core. Ethereum is a platform on which applications run, and its role is different: it is a bet on how that platform is used, with more variables along the way. Stablecoins are tokens, generally tied to a currency such as the dollar. They try to keep a stable value, but they are not money in your bank account, and they carry risks of their own. Each one answers a different question. Do not throw them all in the same bag.

cenas.visual: Animation: a bar at one hundred per cent, split into three parts, labelled “BTC”, “ETH” and “stablecoins”. Corner of the screen: “illustrative example”.
cenas.narracao: Let us do some sums with an illustrative example. Imagine a plan of one hundred euros a month and a rule you wrote yourself: the core is Bitcoin, the satellites are Ethereum, and a small part stays in stablecoins. One possible design, just so you can see the sum, would be seventy, twenty, ten. Seventy euros in Bitcoin, twenty in Ethereum, ten in stablecoins. Notice that this is not a recommendation. It is an example, to show how a percentage turns into euros, and to make clear that your design has to fit your plan, not what you saw in someone else's video.

cenas.visual: Animated table: “plan of €100 · illustrative example”, with the rows BTC €70, ETH €20 and stablecoins €10. Underneath, one line: “if ETH falls 20%, its share is worth less”.
cenas.narracao: Now, what happens when the market moves. Imagine, illustrative example, that the Ethereum part falls twenty per cent. The twenty euros you put in there are now worth sixteen. That is not a tragedy, it is arithmetic. What matters is that the split of your plan does not change because of it. The following month is still one hundred euros, and the split is still seventy, twenty and ten. If you change the split in the middle of a drop, you are deciding out of fear. If you still need to change it, record the change in the notebook and write down why, with the date.

cenas.visual: Ruben with a three-column table drawn in the notebook: “role”, “when it makes sense”, “what can go wrong”.
cenas.narracao: Let us go through the role of each piece, which is what should guide your choice. Bitcoin has the role of base, with a long history, a lot of liquidity and a lot of discussion around it. Ethereum has the role of a bet on the platform, with more complexity and more factors that can change. Stablecoins have the role of parking and liquidity, never of growth, and they bring issuer risk, risk linked to the reference currency, and regulatory risk. Notice that what can go wrong is written next to each one. Anyone who only writes the good side has not yet done the work.

cenas.visual: Screen with a table titled “cap per coin”. Note in the corner: “illustrative example, not a recommendation”.
cenas.narracao: A practical rule: set a cap per coin before you start. Illustrative example: no satellite goes above ten per cent of the plan, and stablecoins do not go above twenty per cent, even if they seem safe. These numbers are only there so you can do your own sums. What matters is that the cap exists, that it is written down and that you keep it. If your plan is small, do the sums with five or ten euros and see whether the design still makes sense. Often it does not, and it is much better to find that out on paper than with the money already on the platform.

cenas.visual: Exercise sheet with a blank table. Ruben crosses out a line and writes another one above it.
cenas.narracao: Exercise: write your monthly plan, say one hundred and fifty euros, and split it into three lines: BTC, ETH and stablecoins. Use a design that seems reasonable to you. Then do the sum for one month in which the smallest part falls twenty per cent, illustrative example, and for another in which it rises. It is not about getting it right. It is about seeing whether you could keep the plan without touching it. If the answer is “no”, the design is too big for your wallet or for your stomach. Adjust it until you can stick to it.

aulas.titulo: Aula 8.3 — Rebalancing and the reserve pot
aulas.gancho: A portfolio moves on its own. One coin rises, another falls, and the split you wrote three months ago no longer exists. What do you do about it?

cenas.visual: Two bar charts side by side. Left: 70, 20 and 10. Right: 80, 12 and 8. Caption: “illustrative example”.
cenas.narracao: It is called drift. Illustrative example: you started with seventy per cent in Bitcoin, twenty in Ethereum and ten in stablecoins. A year later, Bitcoin has risen a lot and you have eighty per cent. Ethereum and the stablecoins have fallen to twelve and eight. Nobody gave you a signal. The portfolio simply changed shape. Rebalancing is the act of going back to the split you wrote down, using a rule you defined beforehand, and not the mood of the day. It is not a guess about what is going to happen. It is keeping the risk you chose.

cenas.visual: Ruben with a calendar in his hand and a board with two rules written: “calendar: once a quarter” and “band: I act if it drifts five points”.
cenas.narracao: There are two simple ways to rebalance. The first is by calendar: once a quarter, you review the split and correct whatever has drifted. The second is by band: you only act when a part drifts further than a certain number of points from its target. Illustrative example: a five-point band. If the core is written as seventy, you act only if it leaves sixty-five or seventy-five. Each method has its advantages. The calendar is simpler to follow. The band only reacts when the drift is real. Choose one, write it in the notebook and keep to it, with no exceptions invented on the spot.

cenas.visual: Animation: a clay pot with gold coins, label “reserve pot”, arrows coming in from the left and going out to the right.
cenas.narracao: Now the reserve pot, which you already know from module seven. It is the part of the plan's money that was not spent in a given week. It does not disappear and it is not lost: it is kept aside, and it has one use only. Topping up in weeks when the MTM Smart DCA label is Strong Buy, within the monthly ceiling. The ceiling comes first. The pot is not a second account to spend freely. That is why it has to be in the notebook, with a balance and an exit rule, so that it is never an improvised decision.

cenas.visual: Notebook sheet with four fields: “pot: balance”, “in”, “out”, “rule”.
cenas.narracao: The exit rule is the most important part, and you write it down before you need it. For example: the pot is only used in Strong Buy weeks, and never for more than half of its balance at once. Illustrative example, of course. And there is another rule that is never broken: the pot is never used to buy what has risen sharply. If the market is euphoric, the pot stays still. When you use the pot, record the week, the asset and the reason on the same Friday ritual sheet, so that the saved money always has a history you can account for.

cenas.visual: Ruben, close-up, talking to camera. Line on screen: “Rebalancing is not guessing.”
cenas.narracao: A common confusion: rebalancing is not an attempt to guess the top or the bottom. When you sell a little of what has risen to get back to the split, you are not saying the price is going to fall. You are keeping the risk you chose. And when you buy what has fallen to restore the split, you are not saying it will rise. You are respecting the plan. Rebalancing also has costs: platform fees, possible taxes, which we will look at at the end of the programme, and the work of recording everything. So do not rebalance every week, and always confirm the conditions on your authorised platform.

cenas.visual: Exercise sheet with the line “date · split before · split after · reason”. Ruben writes the rule and a starting balance.
cenas.narracao: Five-minute exercise. Write your rebalancing rule in the notebook: calendar or band, and the value. Then create your pot: one line with the starting balance, which can perfectly well be zero. Write the exit rule in one sentence, and keep the notebook. You do not have to rebalance today. You have to know, before you need to, what you would do. That is what separates a plan from a wish. If you do not know which to choose, start with the calendar, because it is the easiest to keep in a busy week. Notice that you are not choosing the best rule in the world. You are choosing one you are going to respect.

aulas.titulo: Aula 8.4 — Reading the house Portfolios without copying them
aulas.gancho: Copying is the shortest route to learning nothing. Looking carefully is slower, and gives you much more.

cenas.visual: Screen of the MTM System app, Portfolios tab, with the two house portfolios. Text on screen: “demonstration and education portfolios”.
cenas.narracao: You already know the two house portfolios: one crypto and one ETF, topped up every Friday and recorded purchase by purchase. Today we are going to learn how to read them. Not to copy them, but to see a recorded structure working over time. A demonstration portfolio does not tell you what to do. It tells you what was done, with rules that, ideally, are written down, and it lets you ask why. That question is what is worth taking from this lesson. You do not need to memorise them. You need to open them with a clear goal, which is to learn the method and not to copy the result.

cenas.visual: Zoom into three areas of the screen, each with a caption: “structure”, “dates”, “consistency”.
cenas.narracao: Look at three things. First, the structure: how many assets there are and which one carries the most weight. Second, discipline: the dates of the moves, all on a Friday. Third, consistency: compare each top-up with what the MTM Smart DCA indicated that day. If the portfolio follows its own rule, you can see it in the dates and in the labels. If it does not, ask why. A careful reader is not looking for the right answer. They look for the rule behind each move, and notice when it does not appear. Do this reading with the notebook open, not from memory, because memory tends to keep only what we like to see.

cenas.visual: Ruben showing the notebook, with two columns: “what I copy” and “what I learn”.
cenas.narracao: There is one distinction I want you to always make. What to copy: no assets, no percentages, no moments. What to learn: the order of things. First you write the structure. Then you define the rhythm. Only then do you top up. Another person's assets, or the house's, are the context of that portfolio, and your context is different: a different base amount, a different time horizon, a different tolerance for falls. Copying someone else's context is the fastest way to buy at the wrong bottom without understanding why. Once the distinction is clear, the house portfolio stops being a mirror of ambition and becomes a mirror of method.

cenas.visual: Animation: three questions appear one by one over a chart: “Why is it here?”, “How much does it weigh, and has that changed?”, “Which rule explains the change?”.
cenas.narracao: When you look at a portfolio, ask it three questions. Why is this asset here? How much does it weigh, and has that changed over time? Which rule explains a change? If you find no answer, that is not a fault of yours. Often the answer is simply not written down. In that case, the portfolio is not an example for you, it is just a record. And that is fine: a record also teaches, as long as you know you are not looking at a manual. Write the answers with the date beside them, because in a few months you will want to compare your reading today with the one you make when you have more experience.

cenas.visual: Split screen: the house portfolio on the left, the student's table on the right. Text on screen: “mirror, not mould”.
cenas.narracao: Use the house portfolio as a mirror. When you have your own table, put the two side by side. Ask: does my split follow the same logic? Does it have a core, capped satellites, a pot and a rule? If yours has something the house does not have, for example a different satellite, write down why. The difference is not an error. It is your decision, and that is what we want to see in the notebook. And remember: past results do not guarantee future results, neither those of the house nor yours. If any difference bothers you, do not erase it straight away. Write it down and leave it there for a week before you decide what to do.

cenas.visual: Ruben with the notebook closed in front of him. A warning in large letters on screen: “Demonstration and education portfolios. Past results do not guarantee future results.”
cenas.narracao: Mission for this module: write your target portfolio in the notebook. One page. It has the core, with the asset and its weight. It has the satellites, if you have them, each with its thesis. It has the split in euros for your monthly plan, your cap per coin, the rebalancing method and the pot, with its exit rule. And it has a final line: what you would do if the core fell twenty per cent in one month. You do not need to buy anything to complete the mission. The mission is to write. See you in module nine, where we read the market more calmly.

modulos.titulo: Módulo 9 — Reading the market as an investor (≈14 min)

aulas.titulo: Aula 9.1 — Weekly Momentum
aulas.gancho: A daily chart shows the week that has passed. The weekly chart shows the year. If you only look at one of them, you are seeing half the film.

cenas.visual: Ruben in a medium shot, almost black background, details in gold. TradingView screen recording: the weekly Bitcoin chart with Momentum. Text on screen: “Educational content. The risk of loss is real.”
cenas.narracao: Today we are going to read Momentum on the weekly chart. You already know the five confirmations: the cloud present and in the right colour, the cloud on the right side of the candles, the exponential moving average in agreement, the volume in the colour of the direction, and the RSI crossing in the right zone. On the weekly chart, each candle is a whole week. That changes the rhythm of the reading. A weekly reading does not change from Friday to Monday. So it is a background frame, not a button. Anyone who reads the weekly chart every morning is looking for noise under a magnifying glass. And the risk of loss is real, on any chart, and it always stays with you.

cenas.visual: Animation: five squares on a weekly chart light up one by one. Below, three bands: “five out of five”, “four out of five”, “three or fewer”.
cenas.narracao: Read the confirmations the way you read them on the daily chart, but with more patience. Five out of five, in green: the long-term trend is in favour. Four out of five is still a useful reading. Three or fewer: the weekly chart does not have a strong opinion, and that is also information. The question you ask is simple: does the weekly chart confirm what the daily chart is saying? If the daily is green and the weekly is red, that is not a contradiction to resolve in a hurry. It is a sign that the fall may not be over, and that the pot should be used with more calm, not more haste.

cenas.visual: Three weekly charts side by side, with captions: “turned to buy after a long fall”, “prolonged strong red”, “sideways with lilac boxes”.
cenas.narracao: Let us go through three typical scenarios. First: the weekly chart has turned green after a long fall. It is a good moment to confirm that the pot is ready, because Strong Buy weeks may come next. Second: strong red for several weeks. Here the rule is the same as in module seven: base always, and the pot kept still until the weekly chart starts to ease. Third: lilac boxes on the weekly chart, a sideways market. For the DCA, it is a period to accumulate with patience, with no hurry to use the pot. In none of these three cases does the weekly chart stop the DCA. It only helps you decide the size.

cenas.visual: Ruben showing a calendar with two markings: “weekly: once a month” and “daily: every Friday”.
cenas.narracao: Now the rhythm, which is the part most people get wrong. You read the weekly chart once a month, on a quiet weekend, to see the whole picture and review your plan. You read the daily chart every Friday, within your ritual. The weekly reading does not replace the daily one: the weekly sets the context, and the daily decides the day. If you ever catch yourself opening the weekly chart every morning, stop, breathe and go back to the notebook. That is anxiety dressed up as analysis, and it costs a lot in hasty decisions.

cenas.visual: Ruben, close-up, talking to camera. Line on screen: “The weekly gives you the map, not the timetable.”
cenas.narracao: A common mistake is looking on the weekly chart for the exact day to buy. That day does not exist. The weekly chart gives you the map: the direction of the background and the weight of the trend. It does not tell you whether tomorrow is the best day for anything. And there is another trap: changing your plan just because the weekly chart changed colour once. Wait for the change to be confirmed over another one or two candles. If your plan is long term, the weekly chart serves to adjust the size of the pot, and never to stop the DCA. Never.

cenas.visual: Exercise sheet with four columns: “month”, “weekly”, “confirmations”, “did the plan change?”.
cenas.narracao: Three-minute exercise. Open the weekly chart of an asset in your plan, count the five confirmations and write the result in the notebook, with the date. Then write, in one sentence, whether the plan changes or not. If it does not change, write “no change”. It may look like a formality, but it is discipline. Six months from now, you will have a history of readings, not a memory of when you happened to remember. And memory, as you know, tends to side with the story that suits us. If the weekly chart is unreadable to you, that is fine. Write “cannot read it” and ask yourself why. Very often it is a lack of habit, and habit comes with repetition.

aulas.titulo: Aula 9.2 — DEFY as a second opinion
aulas.gancho: A second opinion is only worth something if it is not a copy of the first. So let us see what DEFY asks that Momentum does not.

cenas.visual: Daily chart with DEFY: exhaustion bands, inner, middle and outer, around a smooth average, with the dashed projection.
cenas.narracao: You already know DEFY from the earlier lessons. It draws exhaustion bands around a smooth average: an inner one, a middle one and an outer one. The question DEFY asks is a different one. While Momentum asks whether the direction is in favour, DEFY asks whether the move has already gone too far. These are different questions, which is why they can disagree. When they disagree, nothing is broken. There is information. And that information is worth more than a forced agreement. We are not going to repeat everything you saw in module seven. We are going to look at DEFY as an extra reading, which comes after Momentum, not before it.

cenas.visual: Close-up of a candle that touches the outer band and turns with a strong candle. Above it, the stars of the idea.
cenas.narracao: When the price reaches the outer band and turns with a strong candle, DEFY may mark an idea. The stars count the confirmations: has the level already reacted before? Is the trend cloud on the same side? Is there a volume break? Three confirmations give one star, more give two or three, and when everything lines up the candle turns gold. The stars measure how many confirmations there are. They do not measure the certainty of the result, because that does not exist. A gold candle is not a guarantee of a rise. It is a stretched price with many pieces fitting together, and that is all it is.

cenas.visual: Animated table with four rows: “Momentum green with 4 or 5 · DEFY with stars”, “Momentum green · DEFY without stars”, “Momentum red or lilac · DEFY with stars”, “Momentum red or lilac · DEFY without stars”.
cenas.narracao: Let us go through the combinations. Momentum green and DEFY with stars: both readings in favour. If the MTM Smart DCA label also helps, it is a week to use the pot with judgement. Momentum green and DEFY without stars: one reading in favour. Momentum red or lilac with stars on DEFY: also one reading in favour, because a buy idea exists, but the trend does not yet agree. And Momentum red or lilac without stars: no reading in favour, and the base is enough. Notice that there is no row that says “buy everything”. That row does not exist, and if you find it in some group or other, be suspicious of it.

cenas.visual: Ruben drawing a three-line decision table in the notebook: “two in favour: base + pot”, “one in favour: base + at most half the pot”, “none: base”.
cenas.narracao: Let us put this into a simple frame, to stick next to the screen. Two readings in favour: base plus pot, within the ceiling. One reading in favour: base plus, at most, half the pot. None: only the base. Above everything sits the monthly ceiling, which is never breached, and the MTM Smart DCA label, which gives the starting point. DEFY is a second opinion. It is not the first criterion, and it has no power to cancel the label. It helps you choose how much of the pot to use, and that is all. Print it or copy it by hand, and always keep it in front of you on Friday, so that the decision does not depend on who is most tired that day.

cenas.visual: Warning on screen, in large letters: “DEFY signals are for trading. In DCA, they only affect the size.”
cenas.narracao: Repeat after me: DEFY signals were designed for trading. They carry an entry, a stop and targets, because that is what a trader needs. In DCA you do not use those levels. You do not buy at the “entry price”, you do not place a stop and you do not take profit at targets. Your DCA is long term, and DEFY only affects the size of the top-up. If one day you want to trade with rules, that is a different path, with different training, a different account and a different risk. It is not this one. And having DEFY on the screen does not give your DCA a stop.

cenas.visual: Exercise sheet with three charts and three boxes to fill in: “stars”, “Momentum”, “decision”.
cenas.narracao: Exercise: open the daily chart of an asset in your plan with DEFY. Count the stars, if there are any. Then look at the Momentum on the same chart. Write down the two readings and the decision: base, base plus half the pot, or base plus the pot, always within the ceiling. Do this for a week, without buying anything extra. You will see that the two tools disagree more often than you imagined, and that the disagreement teaches more than agreement does. If there are no stars in any week, that is also a valid reading. Record that there was no idea and follow the plan, without looking for a star that is not there.

aulas.titulo: Aula 9.3 — Sentiment, fear and euphoria, and BTC dominance
aulas.gancho: You have heard someone say “there is fear in the market” or “this is euphoric”. It sounds like information. But what actually changes in your plan? Let us find out.

cenas.visual: Screen with a sentiment gauge, a scale from zero to one hundred in gold tones. Text on screen: “public sentiment indices · context, not a signal”.
cenas.narracao: Sentiment is the collective mood. There are public indices that try to measure whether people are frightened or greedy. They usually combine several signals, for example volatility and public attention to the topic, and present the result on a scale from zero to one hundred. Zero is extreme fear; one hundred is extreme euphoria. Notice the words: these indices are constructions. They are not the market. They are a snapshot of how people feel about the market. Before you use any of them, read on its own page how it is built. Useful for context, but never a command.

cenas.visual: Animation: a scale with three zones, “extreme fear”, “neutral” and “euphoria”, and an arrow pointing to the plan: “the number does not change the top-up”.
