cenas.narracao: Why do fear and euphoria matter? Because people's behaviour tends to get worse at the extremes: they buy more at the top and sell more at the bottom. DCA was designed precisely to escape that trap. So sentiment does not tell you how much to buy for the base. It tells you where you stand in the collective emotion. Extreme fear is a good moment to remember the written plan. Extreme euphoria is a good moment to remember the ceiling. In neither case does the DCA stop, and in neither case does the index number by itself change the top-up.

cenas.visual: Line chart of Bitcoin dominance, with the caption: “BTC dominance = Bitcoin's share of the total crypto market value”.
cenas.narracao: Now Bitcoin dominance. It is the share Bitcoin occupies in the total value of the crypto market. Illustrative example: if the whole market were worth one hundred, and Bitcoin were worth fifty, dominance would be fifty per cent. When dominance rises, it usually means that money is concentrating in Bitcoin and that the smaller coins suffer more. When it falls, the opposite can happen, with the smaller coins gaining ground. These are patterns that are observed, not laws. You never know how long they last, and you never know whether they repeat in the same form.

cenas.visual: Split screen: on the left, the plan's split written in the notebook; on the right, the same split with the satellites worth less. Caption: “illustrative example”.
cenas.narracao: Let us see how this falls on your plan. Illustrative example: dominance goes from fifty to fifty-six per cent. If your satellites are small coins, it is quite possible they have fallen more than the core. This is context for your notebook, and the question is a different one: has my split changed? If it has, it is time to look at the rebalancing rule you wrote in module eight. Do not buy more satellite just because dominance has risen. First confirm that the satellite has a written thesis and that the core still fits the plan.

cenas.visual: Ruben, close-up, with the line on screen: “Sentiment is context. The label is the starting point.”
cenas.narracao: The golden rule of this lesson: sentiment and dominance are context. They do not replace the MTM Smart DCA label, they do not replace Momentum or DEFY, and they do not change your ceiling. They can go into a line of the notebook, something like “context for the week: high fear, dominance rising”. That is useful for you to look back at in three months. But they do not change the amount of the purchase. If you catch yourself saying “with this euphoria, I am not buying”, come back to this lesson. Euphoria is a reason to look at the pot calmly. It is not a reason to stop the plan.

cenas.visual: Exercise sheet with four columns: “date”, “sentiment”, “dominance”, “did the plan change?”.
cenas.narracao: Two-minute exercise: write in the notebook the current value of the sentiment index you use and Bitcoin's dominance, with the date. Then answer one question: did my plan change because of this? In most weeks, the answer is no, and that is fine. This line is not there for you to change your purchase. It is there so that, over time, you can see the moments when the market's mood pushed you to decide badly. Once that pattern is written down, it has less power over you. If you use more than one index, write them all down, and note whether they point the same way. When they do not, that is useful information too.

aulas.titulo: Aula 9.4 — Putting it together to choose the size of the top-up
aulas.gancho: You already have several tools in your head. But Friday's question is only one: how much do I buy? Let us answer that question in order.

cenas.visual: Chalkboard drawing with four numbered steps. Text on screen: “1 label · 2 readings · 3 context · 4 ceiling and record”.
cenas.narracao: Let us put everything together into one method, with four steps, always in this order. First, the MTM Smart DCA label, which gives the starting point. Second, the daily readings: Momentum and DEFY, counting how many are in favour. Third, the context: sentiment and dominance, which are written down but do not change the number. Fourth, the monthly ceiling and the record. The order matters. If you start with the context, you begin building your story before you have looked at the chart, and that is exactly where decisions become emotional.

cenas.visual: Animated table with the four labels: “Strong Buy”, “Buy”, “Wait”, “Do Not Add”. Beside them, the starting point for each.
cenas.narracao: The label gives the maximum for the day. Strong Buy can go up to twice the base. Buy, one and a half times. Wait, half the base, and the rest stays in the pot. Do Not Add, zero for that asset that week, and the whole base goes into the pot. Do Not Add never uses the pot. Then the readings decide how much of the pot comes in. Two or more in favour: base plus pot, within what the label allows. One: base plus, at most, half the pot. None: only the base. In no row is the monthly ceiling exceeded.

cenas.visual: Screen with an example over four weeks, with columns: “week”, “label”, “readings”, “purchase”, “pot”. Caption at the top: “illustrative example”.
cenas.narracao: Let us look at an illustrative example, with a base of twenty-five euros a week and a pot that starts with forty euros. Week one: Strong Buy, two readings in favour. You buy fifty: twenty-five from the base and twenty-five from the pot, and the pot falls to fifteen. Week two: Buy, one reading in favour. You buy twenty-five from the base and, at most, half the pot, seven euros and fifty cents. The pot stays at seven euros and fifty cents. Week three: Do Not Add. Zero for the asset, and the twenty-five from the base go into the pot, which rises to thirty-two euros and fifty cents. Week four: no reading in favour, so only the base is bought. The new money for the month was one hundred euros. What came out of the pot was money that was already saved.

cenas.visual: Ruben, close-up. Line on screen: “The DCA does not stop. It only changes size.”
cenas.narracao: This sentence is the most important one in the programme so far. In the example we have just seen, there was not a single week in which the plan stopped. There were weeks with a bigger purchase, one week with only the base, and one week in which the asset received no purchase, but the money went into the pot and remains part of the plan. There is one thing you never do: stop the plan because the chart looks ugly, or because everyone is euphoric. If your DCA stops, it is no longer a DCA. It has become a guess with a calendar.

cenas.visual: Friday ritual sheet with the columns: “date”, “asset”, “label”, “readings”, “sentiment and dominance”, “purchase”, “pot”.
cenas.narracao: Where is everything recorded? On the Friday ritual sheet you have used since module seven. Date, asset, label, Momentum and DEFY readings, one line of context with sentiment and dominance, how much you bought, how much went into the pot and how much came out of it. Without this record, the decision stays in memory, and memory tends to embellish what we did. With it, months from now you can see your own pattern: whether you buy more when you are euphoric, whether the pot always stays still, whether the label gives you more signals than the readings do. That is real learning.

cenas.visual: Ruben with a calendar showing four marked Fridays. Final text on screen: “Module 9 mission: four Friday readings, recorded.” Underneath, the educational warning.
cenas.narracao: Module mission: do the four Friday readings and record each one. On each Friday, follow the four steps: label, readings, context, ceiling and record. If you do not have money to buy, do the reading anyway and record what you would have done. The mission is the record, not the purchase. Four consecutive Fridays give you the first history of your own method. At the end, set aside five minutes and compare the first reading with the last. And remember: none of this guarantees results. It is education. The risk of loss is real, and it always stays with you. See you in module ten.

modulos.titulo: Módulo 10 — Taking profit and protecting (≈14 min)

aulas.titulo: Aula 10.1 — Taking profit with written rules
aulas.gancho: Almost everyone knows how to buy. Very few know when to sell, and even fewer know why they sold. Today we write that down before we need it.

cenas.visual: Ruben in a medium shot, almost black background, details in gold. Text on screen: “Educational content. The risk of loss is real.”
cenas.narracao: First, the warning that will appear whenever we touch money: educational content. The risk of loss is real, and in crypto it can be total. With that said, let us go to a question that almost nobody answers seriously: when do you take profit? Many people only think about it once the price has already risen or already fallen, and then the decision is emotional. Greed on one side, fear on the other. The idea of this lesson is simple: the decision to sell has to be taken on a calm day, on paper, with rules you wrote beforehand. When the market accelerates, it is not the time to think. It is the time to carry out what you have already decided.

cenas.visual: Animation: a price line rising in steps. At each step, a small gold slice is taken out and set aside. Text: “profit-taking ladder”.
cenas.narracao: We call this a profit-taking ladder. Each rung is a level of gain, measured against your average purchase price. On each rung you sell a fixed part of the position, and the rest stays with you. Notice what this does: the part you sell is converted into euros, and the part you keep continues to take part if the market keeps rising. It is not a magic formula, and it does not tell you when the top arrives. It only tells you what you will do on each rung, before the rung is reached. That is what takes the drama out of the decision.

cenas.visual: Table drawn in Ruben's notebook, with the title “Illustrative example”. Columns: rung · gain against average price · part to sell · what is left.
cenas.narracao: I will give you an illustrative example, just so you can see the mechanics. Imagine a position with an average price of one hundred. On the first rung, at plus fifty per cent, you sell a fifth of the position. On the second rung, at plus one hundred per cent, you sell another fifth. On the third, at plus two hundred per cent, you sell one more fifth. What is left stays with you, under its own rule. The numbers are mine, chosen for the example. They are not a forecast, not a target and not a recommendation. You choose your own rungs and your own percentages, according to your plan and your tolerance for risk. What matters is that they are written down.

cenas.visual: Notebook page with three rules written by hand, next to a stopped stopwatch. Text: “rung · part · date”.
cenas.narracao: Each rung has three pieces of information, and all three have to be written down. First: the rung, as a percentage against your average price. Second: the part, as a fraction of your position and not in euros, so the rule still makes sense when the position changes. Third: the date or the condition for review. For example, I review the ladder on the first Friday of every month. If there is neither a date nor a condition, the rule does not exist, it is just a wish. And there is one thing the ladder does not replace: the DCA. Purchases still happen on your day, as in module seven. Selling a part is a separate decision, with its own role.

cenas.visual: Ruben talking to camera, with the line on screen: “What is not written down does not exist.”
cenas.narracao: There are three mistakes I see often, and the ladder prevents them. The first is changing the rule halfway, because the price is running and you want to see more. The second is selling everything at once out of fear, on a day of panic, and then watching the rise without your part. The third is selling nothing and calling that patience, when in fact it is a lack of plan. With the ladder written down, any of these mistakes has to go through paper first. That alone gives you a pause. And in fast markets, a pause is worth more than it seems.

cenas.visual: Exercise sheet with four blank lines and the title “My ladder”. Ruben with the pen in the air.
cenas.narracao: Five-minute exercise, to do today. Take your notebook and write your ladder for one position in your plan. Three rungs are enough. For each one, write the rung, the part and the review date. You do not have to get it right. You have to write it down, and do it calmly, without the screen open beside you. Then keep the sheet next to the plan from module seven, so the two can be read together. Next lesson we talk about what to do when the market does not rise, but falls in a brutal way, and why that plan also has to be written down before it is needed.

aulas.titulo: Aula 10.2 — What to do in a crash: the plan written beforehand
aulas.gancho: A day of heavy falls does not look like a crisis. It looks like a notification, a friend calling and a finger that wants to press sell. That is why the plan has to be written beforehand.

cenas.visual: Daily crypto chart in a steep fall, red candles, no legible numbers. Text on screen: “Plan written beforehand.”
cenas.narracao: Large falls happen in crypto. I am not going to tell you when or how big, because I do not know, and nobody knows. What I do know is that they happen often enough to deserve a plan. And the moment when decisions are most often made badly is precisely the moment of the fall, when the screen is red, the conversations are in panic and the brain wants to do something, anything, right now. The solution is not to have more courage in the moment. It is to have fewer decisions to make in that moment. That is why we write the plan today, when we are calm, and not tomorrow, when it is already on fire.

cenas.visual: Ruben sitting at a table, with the notebook open to three sections: “before”, “during”, “after”. Text: “three parts, one page”.
cenas.narracao: The plan for a crash has three parts. Before: what you already have set up. Your base amount, your monthly ceiling, your reserve pot and the alerts switched on in the app. During: what you do in each band of decline, written with the same logic as the MTM Smart DCA, in which the Strong Buy label changes the size of the top-up and does not tell you to stop. After: when and how you review the strategy. One page is enough. If it does not fit on one page, it is still being thought out too much, and on the day of the fall nobody reads twenty.

cenas.visual: Animation: a price line falling in steps. In each step, a box with the phrase “written action”.
cenas.narracao: Now the during, which is the heart of the plan. For each band of decline, you write the action. For example, illustrative example: if the asset falls more than thirty per cent against your average price, the DCA continues on the base. If the pot has money, you use part of it, within the ceiling, as module seven teaches. You do not sell anything in that band. Notice this carefully: the DCA never stops, it only changes size. A fall does not give you permission to stop buying, and it does not oblige you to buy more than the ceiling allows. If your strategy has a position you genuinely want to sell in a fall, that is a separate written rule, with its own condition.

cenas.visual: Phone screen with a fall notification, and a thumb hovering over the word “sell”. Text: “24-hour pause”.
cenas.narracao: There is one rule that should be in every crash plan: the pause. When something makes you want to sell outside the plan, you wait twenty-four hours. It is not a punishment, it is a filter. A great deal of panic decisions disappear within twenty-four hours. If after the pause you still think the sale makes sense, write down why, with the condition that justifies it, and check whether it matches the rule you wrote for the crash. If it does not match, keep to the plan. And switch off price notifications during the day of the fall. Looking at the chart every five minutes does not help you think. It only gives you the feeling that you are doing something.

cenas.visual: Ruben talking to camera, with the line on screen: “Nobody will remind you of the plan for you.”
cenas.narracao: I will tell you this plainly: in a fall, the people around you will say things. Some will tell you to sell everything, others to buy everything, and others will show charts that look like certainties. None of them has your table. That is why the plan stays written and signed by you, kept where you can see it. If you only have it in your head, in a fall your head will tell you whatever it likes. Also write down the contact of one trusted person who can remind you of the plan. Not to decide for you. To remind you of what you decided when you were calm.

cenas.visual: Crash sheet with the three sections filled in with an example. Ruben points at the “after” section.
cenas.narracao: Mission for this lesson, ten minutes: write your crash plan on half a page. Before, during and after. Include at least three bands of decline, with the action for each one, the twenty-four-hour pause rule and the name of the trusted person. At the end, sign and date it. Keep the sheet next to the profit-taking ladder from the previous lesson. Next lesson we talk about the part nobody takes seriously until it is too late: the safety of your seed, and why a digital copy is the worst place for it to be.

aulas.titulo: Aula 10.3 — Advanced security: copies, metal and places
aulas.gancho: Your seed is your entire account. And the worst thing you can do to it is not to lose it on an unlucky day. It is to leave it where someone can look at it at their leisure.

cenas.visual: Ruben with a paper card with the words covered, empty table around him. Text on screen: “Never digital.”
cenas.narracao: In lesson four we talked about your seed, the words that give access to your coins. Now we go one level up, because when the value grows, the risk changes shape. There are two threats that weigh the same: losing the seed, and someone else getting hold of it. Any security plan has to deal with both. The rule that is not negotiable is this: the seed never exists in digital form. Not a photo, not a note on your phone, not an email to yourself, not a file in the cloud, not a password manager. Any of these can be copied, synced or stolen, and all of that can happen without you noticing anything.

cenas.visual: Animation: a metal plate with engraved letters, being placed in a safe. Text on screen: “paper burns · metal endures”.
cenas.narracao: If it is not digital, is it paper? It can be, but paper is fragile. It burns, it gets wet, it breaks down over time, and a house move can throw away a folded sheet in a drawer. That is why the most solid option is metal: a plate or a holder where the words are engraved or punched, resistant to fire and water. Using paper as the first copy is not a mistake, as long as the metal copy follows. The goal is for the information to survive a fire, a flood or a day when your home is turned upside down.

cenas.visual: Simple map with two addresses marked with crosses. Text on screen: “two copies · two places”.
cenas.narracao: Now the rule about copies. Two copies, in two different places. Not the same drawer, not the same safe, not the same house. If a fire or a burglary takes one, the other is still there. One option is a safe at home, well hidden and fixed to the structure. The other can be a safe in a trusted place, outside the home. There is no perfect place. There are places where the risk of loss is low and the risk of improper access is also low. Choose with that balance in mind, and write in the plan where each copy is.

cenas.visual: Ruben holding a warning card with an alert symbol. Text on screen: “No legitimate support asks for the seed.”
cenas.narracao: A rule that sounds obvious and that many people break: nobody asks you for the seed. No legitimate support service, no authorised platform, no person saying they are from support asks for the words. If anyone asks, even if the request comes with a beautiful logo, an urgent message or a friendly phone call, the answer is no. And do not write it down on any website, in any third-party app, or for a friend who is helping you set something up. The seed is only used at the moment of restoring your wallet, in a place you control. Afterwards it goes back to the paper copy and the metal one.

cenas.visual: Ruben talking to camera, holding a sheet of test words. Text on screen: “Test, do not copy.”
cenas.narracao: How do you know the copy works? You do not open it to check, because every time you expose it there is a small exposure. What you do is a restore test, in a new, empty wallet, with none of your main value, following the procedure you already know from module four. If the test works, the copy is good. If it does not, you find out now, and not on the day you need it. Do this test once a year, or whenever you change wallets. And never put the copies together in one photo, one folder or one envelope.

cenas.visual: Checklist on screen with four squares: “no digital”, “two copies”, “two places”, “test done”. Ruben ticking each one.
cenas.narracao: Mission for this lesson, to do this week: check your seed against four questions. Is it free of any digital format? Do you have two copies? Are they in two different places? And have you done the restore test in a new wallet? If the answer to any of these is no, that is where the work is. It is not glamorous, but it is what separates someone who loses a phone from someone who loses access to their coins. In the last lesson of this module we talk about what happens to your seed and your coins when you are no longer around to look after them.

aulas.titulo: Aula 10.4 — Crypto inheritance and the level 2 mission
aulas.gancho: Nobody likes to think about this. But if your coins exist only in your head, when you are gone, they are missing for the people you love too. This has a solution, and it is simpler than it sounds.

cenas.visual: Ruben in a medium shot, with a folded document on the table in front of him. Text on screen: “Crypto inheritance plan”.
cenas.narracao: Let us go to inheritance. This is the last security point of level two, and it is the one most people put off. The idea is simple: someone you trust needs to be able to understand what exists, where it is and how to access it, when you can no longer do so. You do not need to give them the seed, neither now nor ever. What you give them is a map. A map says that you have crypto, in which types of wallet and on which authorised platforms, what the copies are, where they are kept and whom to ask for help finding them. Written this way, the map protects your family and does not expose your coins.

cenas.visual: Animation: three envelopes lined up, labelled “map”, “copies” and “contacts”. Text on screen: “the map without the key”.
cenas.narracao: Separate the information into three parts. The map: what you have and where it is, with no access words. The seed copies, which are the key, stay in the safe places from the previous lesson, and never in the same envelope as the map. And the contacts: who is the trusted lawyer or notary to ask how this works in your case, and who is the person who will read the map when it is needed. The golden rule is that no single part, on its own, gives access to your coins. Whoever reads the map does not have the key. Whoever has the key does not know what it opens. The two have to come together.

cenas.visual: Ruben speaking, with the notebook open on a page titled “Legal point”. Text on screen: “Talk to a professional”.
cenas.narracao: An honest note about the legal side. Inheritance rules vary from country to country, and they vary even more when the assets are digital. I am not going to tell you here what the law provides for your case, because that depends on your situation and on who will inherit. What I ask is that, before you consider your plan finished, you talk to a lawyer or a trusted notary. Take the map, without the access words, and ask how it should be drafted to be valid. And if you live or have assets in another country, ask about that one too. This is not legal advice. It is a warning not to leave the subject for later.

cenas.visual: Notebook page with the level 2 DCA plan sheet: base amount, monthly ceiling, pot, assets, top-up day, alerts. Text on screen: “level 2 mission”.
cenas.narracao: Now the level two mission, which brings together everything you did in modules seven to ten. First, your written DCA plan, with the fixed monthly ceiling and the reserve pot, on a single sheet. It has the base amount, the assets, the top-up day, the size rules with the MTM Smart DCA table and what happens to the money you do not spend. Second, the DCA alerts switched on in the MTM System app, in the settings. Third, the Friday ritual carried out four weeks in a row, with a record of each one in the notebook. If on a Friday you do not buy, you still do the ritual and record what you would have done. Four lines, one per week.

cenas.visual: Calendar with four Fridays marked with a gold tick. Ruben shows the notebook with the four lines. Text on screen: “4 Fridays · 4 records”.
cenas.narracao: Why four weeks and not one? Because one week is a coincidence. Four weeks in a row are a habit beginning. And it is in habit that DCA works, not on the day it went well or badly. Notice also what I am not asking of you: I am not asking you to have got it right, or to have made a profit. I am asking that the process has happened four times, at the same time and on the same sheet. If one Friday is missed for a real reason, such as a trip or an illness, it is not a failure. You restart the count and carry on. What you cannot do is pretend the record exists when it does not.

cenas.visual: Ruben closing the notebook. Final text on screen: “Level 2 mission: plan, alerts, four recorded Fridays.” Underneath, the educational warning.
cenas.narracao: Level two mission, in short: a written DCA plan with ceiling and pot, DCA alerts switched on, and four consecutive Fridays of recorded ritual. It is not measured by what the market did. It is measured by whether you did it. And inheritance comes in here too, in the form of a map, with the key kept separate. Remember the essentials: this is educational content, not financial advice. The risk of loss is real, and the MTM tools help you decide with information. They do not decide for you. Level three brings in perpetuals, which are a different game. Before we get there, the plan for this level has to be done.

aulas.titulo: Aula 11.1 — What a perpetual is, and funding
aulas.gancho: A perpetual is a contract that never expires. It sounds simple, and the part that does not expire is exactly the part that will cost you attention.

cenas.visual: Ruben in a medium shot, almost black background, details in gold. Text on screen: “Educational content. The risk of loss is real.”
cenas.narracao: Before any numbers, the warning that will be on screen throughout this module: educational content. The risk of loss is real. With perpetuals you can lose everything you put up as margin, and that happens faster than most people think. This module is for understanding, not for starting. Level three is optional. And before any real euro, what counts is the simulated account, as you have known since the start of the bootcamp. With that said, let us look at what a perpetual is. I want you to leave here with one clear sentence.

cenas.visual: Animation: a contract with an endless arrow and the words “no expiry date”. Text on screen: “perpetual = no date”.
cenas.narracao: A normal futures contract has an expiry date. At the end of that date it is settled, and that is the end of it. A perpetual has no such date. It stays open for as long as you want it to, and as long as you have margin to keep it open. To stay close to the spot price, the perpetual uses a mechanism called funding. It is not a brokerage fee. It is a payment that happens from time to time, between those who are long and those who are short. When the perpetual trades above the spot price, those who are long pay those who are short. When it trades below, the opposite happens. It is the part most people ignore, and it weighs more than it seems on positions that stay open for days.

cenas.visual: Table on screen: “Illustrative example · long position of €1,000 notional · funding of 0.05% per period”. Ruben points at the table.
cenas.narracao: Let us look at an illustrative example. You have a long position with one thousand euros of notional value, which is the total size of the position, not the money you put in. The funding is zero point zero five per cent per payment period. Per period, you pay fifty cents. If the funding is positive, those who are long pay. If it is negative, those who are long receive. The number is only there to make the sum, and funding changes over time. What matters is the mechanism: someone who stays in a position for a long time with the funding working against them pays a small amount every day, and that does not show up on the candlestick chart.

cenas.visual: Split screen: on the left the perpetual's chart, on the right the spot price chart, with the gap between the two flashing. Text on screen: “perpetual vs spot price”.
cenas.narracao: Why does the perpetual stay close to the spot price? Because funding pushes. When there are many people long and the perpetual trades above the real price, funding turns positive, and those who are long pay to keep their position. That tends to cool demand on the long side. The reverse happens when many people are short: funding turns negative, and the shorts are the ones who pay. It is not magic, it is an incentive. In practice, funding is a cost or an income that runs while the position is open, and its sign changes with the market's conditions.

cenas.visual: Exercise sheet with a three-day timeline and fields “funding paid” for each day. Ruben with the pen in his hand.
cenas.narracao: Two-minute exercise, on paper. A long position of one thousand euros of notional, with funding of zero point zero five per cent per period, and three periods a day, which is one of the common formats. How much do you pay in twenty-four hours? Three periods of fifty cents make one euro and fifty cents. One euro and fifty cents a day, on a notional of one thousand. An illustrative example, of course. Now repeat the sum with the position open for a whole week. If the funding works against you every day, how much do you pay in total? Do the sum without a calculator, and only then check it. Next lesson we look at what happens to your margin when things go wrong.

aulas.titulo: Aula 11.2 — Isolated margin and cross margin
aulas.gancho: Two accounts with the same balance can react in completely different ways to the same fall. The difference lies in a choice that almost nobody reads.

cenas.visual: Screen of a simulated margin panel, with two options, “isolated” and “cross”. Text on screen: “margin: what protects you and what puts you at risk”.
cenas.narracao: Margin is the money you put up to hold the position. It is not the cost of the whole position, it is the collateral. When you open a leveraged perpetual, the platform requires an initial margin, and it is that margin which rises and falls with the market. There are two ways to organise it: isolated and cross. The difference is not in the leverage. It is in who pays when the position goes wrong. This choice sounds technical, but it is one of the most important risk decisions in this module, and it is often the one people make without thinking.

cenas.visual: Animation with two boxes. In isolated, a small box with a wall around it, holding only one position. In cross, a large box with several positions and one shared balance.
cenas.narracao: Isolated margin means each position has its own collateral. If you put one hundred euros into a position, only those one hundred euros are at risk. If the position is liquidated, you lose those hundred, and the rest of the account stays intact. Cross margin means all positions share the available balance. A position in trouble can use the money from the others to hold on. It sounds like an advantage, and sometimes it is, but it has a cost: a single bad position can drag the entire account down. For someone learning, that is a big problem.

cenas.visual: Comparison table on screen: “isolated: limit per position · cross: shares the balance”. Ruben points at the risk row.
cenas.narracao: Let us put the two side by side, with an illustrative example. You have a simulated account of one thousand euros and open two positions. With isolated margin, you give one hundred euros to each. If the first goes wrong and is liquidated, you lose those hundred, and the second carries on with its hundred. With cross margin, both use the full balance of one thousand. If the first goes wrong, the second can use what is left, and liquidation only happens when the whole account reaches the limit. In other words, cross holds out for longer, but when it fails, it fails all together. The numbers are for the account, not for any real position.

cenas.visual: Ruben talking to camera, holding a card. Text on screen: “Cross does not protect you. It only delays.”
cenas.narracao: This is my view, which you can argue with: for someone starting out, isolated margin is the choice I recommend. Someone starting has not yet tested a risk plan, and isolated forces you to decide how much each position gets. That limit is a lesson in itself. With cross, the account works like one single pot, and it is easy to give more margin to a position that is losing, in the hope that it recovers. That is called putting more money into something that is already going wrong. Cross has its place for those who already have written and tested rules, but it is not where you start.

cenas.visual: Exercise sheet with two columns, “isolated” and “cross”, and one field: “what happens to the other position if the first goes wrong?”.
cenas.narracao: Three-minute exercise. If the platform you use allows it, do it in a simulated account: open two small positions with the same leverage, one in isolated margin and one in cross. If it does not allow it, do it on paper. Fill in the sheet: how much money is inside each position, what happens to the other one if the first goes wrong, and which of the two leaves you more at ease. There is no right answer to the last question, only yours. Next lesson we see what liquidation is and how it is calculated, in simplified form, with an illustrative sum.

aulas.titulo: Aula 11.3 — Liquidation, with an illustrative sum
aulas.gancho: Liquidation is the moment when the platform closes your position because there is no longer enough collateral. Nobody asks you. It just happens.

cenas.visual: Ruben with a notebook open to a page with a sum in pencil. Text on screen: “Illustrative example”.
cenas.narracao: Let us work through the liquidation sum step by step, with an illustrative sum. It is not anyone's actual account. These are round numbers, so you can see the mechanics. Imagine a simulated account with five hundred euros of margin on a long position, with ten times leverage. Ten times means the position has a notional value of five thousand euros. The five hundred is your collateral, the five thousand is the size of the bet. This difference is the centre of this lesson. And notice: the example is illustrative, and the platform you use may have different numbers and different rules.

cenas.visual: Animation: a margin bar filling with gold, with a red line that slowly drops as the price falls. Text on screen: “margin being consumed”.
cenas.narracao: When the price moves against your position, the loss comes out of the margin. With five thousand of notional, every one per cent move against you is worth fifty euros. If the price falls ten per cent, you lose five hundred, and the margin drops to zero. In a simplified account, that is where liquidation happens: when the loss consumes the margin. But this is a simplification, and the difference matters. In practice, the platform requires a minimum maintenance margin, and it liquidates before the margin reaches zero. So the real liquidation price sits a little closer to the entry than the simple sum says.

cenas.visual: Table on screen: “entry 100 · simplified liquidation ≈ 90 · illustrative example”. Ruben points at the numbers.
cenas.narracao: Now the price. Imagine the position is long with an entry at one hundred. With this simplified sum, the liquidation sits near ninety, because a ten per cent fall is what the five hundred of margin can absorb against the five thousand of notional. Notice the logic behind it: roughly one divided by the leverage. Ten times gives ten per cent. Twenty times gives five per cent. The higher the leverage, the shorter the distance to liquidation. In other words, leverage does not buy you more time. It shortens your margin for error. This figure is an illustrative example, and it is not a rule for any position.

cenas.visual: Ruben talking to camera, with the line on screen: “Liquidation is not a number. It is a date that arrives without warning.”
cenas.narracao: And now the point I want you to keep. Liquidation does not warn you. There is no moment when the platform tells you it is about to close, and there is no guarantee that the price stops exactly at the value you calculated. In a fast market, with one long candle and suddenly, the price can pass the liquidation level in seconds, and the close happens at whatever price there is at that moment, which can be worse than the number you wrote down. So the liquidation price you see on screen is a reference limit, not a protection. Protection, if it exists, is somewhere else: it is the stop, which we will look at later in this level.

cenas.visual: Ruben closing the notebook. Card on screen: “Recalculate before you open.”
cenas.narracao: Mission for this lesson: take an illustrative account, in a simulation, and calculate the simplified liquidation for three leverage levels, five, ten and twenty. Write down the percentage distance to the liquidation price in each case. Then check it on the panel of the platform you use, if it has one. If the numbers do not match, look for the difference, which is usually in the maintenance margin and the fees. Do not open any real position to do this calculation, not even out of curiosity. Next lesson we talk about costs, which is where the sum usually turns out to be more expensive than it looks.

aulas.titulo: Aula 11.4 — Fees and the real cost
aulas.gancho: A trade can look as though it went well, and once you do the sum on the fees, nothing is left. This lesson is about the sums nobody does in front of the screen.

cenas.visual: Ruben with an invoice sheet, title “illustrative invoice”. Text on screen: “costs you do not see”.
cenas.narracao: Let us talk about money that leaves without being seen. With perpetuals there are at least three kinds of cost. The opening fee, the closing fee and the funding we have already seen. There is also a hidden cost, which is the spread, the difference between the buy price and the sell price at that moment. Each one is small, but added up and multiplied by the leverage and by how often you trade, they can eat a large part of what you thought you had. This invoice is illustrative, with no values from any particular platform. Your authorised platform has its own fee tables, and you have to read them before you open anything.

cenas.visual: Animation: an entry arrow and an exit arrow, each with a small slice cut off. Text on screen: “maker · taker”.
cenas.narracao: The fee depends on how you enter. When you place an order that waits in the order book, and is not executed straight away, you usually pay a lower fee, called maker. When the order executes immediately and takes liquidity from the market, you pay a higher fee, the taker fee. Platforms vary, so check the fee menu of your authorised platform before you open, for each type of order. Also ask yourself whether the order type you are using is the one you want, and not simply the fastest one to click.

cenas.visual: Table on screen: “notional €5,000 · fee of 0.05% per side · illustrative example”. Ruben points at the numbers.
cenas.narracao: Illustrative example, with round numbers. A notional of five thousand euros, and a fee of zero point zero five per cent on each side of the trade, opening and closing. Opening costs two euros and fifty cents. Closing costs another two euros and fifty cents. Total, five euros, on a trade of five thousand. That seems little. Now look at the margin: five hundred euros. Five euros on five hundred is one per cent of the collateral, in fees alone, before the market has moved. If you repeat this trade ten times with the same margin, that is fifty euros, ten per cent of the collateral, going to the platform. None of those fifty euros appears on the chart.

cenas.visual: Ruben talking to camera, with the simulated account panel appearing beside him. Text on screen: “fee cost for the size of the account”.
cenas.narracao: This is where the account panel of Aurum Flow Cripto helps. It shows the notional, the useful leverage and the fee cost for the size of your account, before you open anything. The question you should always ask is this: if the trade does exactly what the plan says, how much is left after the fees? If the answer is almost nothing, the trade may not be worth the effort, however good it looks on the chart. This is not a guarantee of anything. It is a sum done in your head, and it protects you from an illusion.

cenas.visual: Exercise sheet with fields: “notional”, “opening fee”, “closing fee”, “total cost”, “as % of margin”. Ruben pointing at the first field.
cenas.narracao: Five-minute exercise, on paper. A margin of one thousand euros, leverage of five times, and a fee of zero point zero five per cent per side. What is the notional? Five thousand. How much does opening cost? Two euros and fifty cents. How much does closing cost? Another two euros and fifty cents. What is the total cost, as a percentage of the margin? Half a per cent. Now repeat it with leverage of twenty times, keeping the same margin. You do not need to get your platform's fee exactly right. You need to understand that the cost rises with the notional, not with the margin you put in. Next lesson we look at the most important part of this module: why leverage does not change the right risk.

aulas.titulo: Aula 11.5 — Leverage does not change the right risk
aulas.gancho: Leverage sounds like an accelerator. But if it were only an accelerator, what would stop the car? The answer is the stop and the size of the position, not the number on the screen.

cenas.visual: Ruben in a medium shot, almost black background. Text on screen: “Risk is defined by the stop and the size”.
cenas.narracao: We have reached the lesson that sums up level three, and perhaps the most important one in the module. When someone tells you they will use five times, or twenty times, the right question is not what the leverage is. The right question is: how much do I lose if the stop is hit? That question has an answer that does not depend on the leverage. It depends on two things: the distance to the stop and the size of the position. Leverage only tells you how much margin you need to hold that position. We will see why, with sums and with illustrative examples, of course.

cenas.visual: Animation with a formula on screen: “loss = notional × stop distance”. Text on screen: “risk = notional × stop”.
cenas.narracao: The formula fits on a napkin: the loss, if the stop is hit, equals the notional multiplied by the stop distance as a percentage. That is all. Leverage does not enter into it. What enters is the size of the position, which is the notional, and the point where you are willing to get out. With this, the risk per trade is defined before you open. If you want to lose at most one per cent of your account, you choose the notional and the stop distance so that the loss, in that case, is one per cent. Leverage then becomes a consequence of that choice, not the starting point.

cenas.visual: Three columns on screen with the same sum: “account: €1,000 · risk: €10 (1%)”. Illustrative example.
cenas.narracao: Let us take the same account of one thousand euros, with a risk of ten euros per trade, which is one per cent. First case: a stop at two per cent from the entry price. Notional: ten divided by two per cent gives five hundred euros. Leverage, against the account, half a time. Second case: a stop at one per cent. Notional of one thousand euros, leverage of one time. Third case: a stop at half a per cent. Notional of two thousand, leverage of two times. In all three, if the stop is hit, you lose exactly ten euros. What changed was the notional and the leverage, not the risk. This is the point I want you to keep.

cenas.visual: Ruben with the notebook open. Card on screen: “A stop is not a guarantee.”
cenas.narracao: An important caveat: the stop is an order, and an order can be executed at a worse price than the one you wrote, if the market makes a sudden jump. In a sharp move, the close can come out further away than the level you marked. So the stop reduces the risk, but does not eliminate it. And liquidation still exists, because if the margin is too small for the stop distance, the platform closes the position before the stop is reached. The rule is not “I set a stop and I can relax”. The rule is: the stop sits far enough away for normal noise, and the position is small enough that a jump does not wipe out your account.

cenas.visual: Ruben closing the notebook. Text on screen: “Level 3: simulated account only, up to 30 trades with a journal.”
cenas.narracao: Now the level three rule, which is not negotiable. This level is done only in a simulated account, MTM Funded or WebTrader, until you have completed thirty trades with a full journal. Thirty, not three. The journal records the date, the plan, the stop, the notional, the risk in euros, the fee, the reason for entry, the reason for exit and what you learned. Only after thirty trades can you think about a real account, and that decision is yours, never made with rent money. Mission for this lesson: open your simulated account, do the risk calculation with the model from this lesson, record the first lines of the journal, and write at the top of the sheet: zero of thirty.

modulos.titulo: Módulo 12 — The Aurum Flow Cripto strategy (≈17 min)

aulas.titulo: Aula 12.1 — The philosophy: only with the trend
aulas.gancho: Two traders look at the same one-hour chart. One buys every dip, because it's cheap. The other waits to see which way the market is going. Guess which of the two I teach.

cenas.visual: Ruben in a medium shot, almost black background. On-screen text: "Educational content. The risk of loss is real."
cenas.narracao: Welcome to level three. This level is optional and it is the most demanding. We are going to study the Aurum Flow Cripto strategy, a crypto perpetuals scanner optimized for the one-hour chart. It is not a money machine, nor a promise. It is a set of rules that you can read, test and, above all, refuse. Every line of this lesson is a rule. Before you go on, notice the warning on screen: the risk of loss is real, and it can be total. This is not a formality. It is the premise of everything that follows.

cenas.visual: One-hour chart of a crypto pair, in charcoal and gold, with a long arrow pointing up.
cenas.narracao: The first house rule: Aurum Flow only trades with the trend. If the market is clearly rising, it looks for buys. If it is clearly falling, it looks for sells. It sounds obvious, but many of a beginner's losses come from doing the opposite: buying a fall because it's already cheap, or selling a rise because it's already expensive. Being cheap or expensive says nothing about direction. It can get even cheaper tomorrow. The trend is the only thing that tells you which way the market is pushing.

cenas.visual: Two charts side by side. On the left, an entry against the trend, with a red box. On the right, an entry with the trend, with a green box. Label: illustrative example.
cenas.narracao: Look at these two illustrative examples. On the left, someone buys into a strong drop, convinced the price will bounce back. The market keeps falling and the stop is hit. On the right, the entry happens after the price makes a new high and turns back up. Neither case comes with guarantees, and one nice example proves nothing. But the second is the kind of entry the method looks for, because the wind is blowing in the same direction as the boat. That is the difference we want you to train. Look at this carefully, because it is the basis of everything that follows.

cenas.visual: Ruben with an open notebook. On the page, handwritten: "1H · with the trend · no trend, no entry".
cenas.narracao: Why the one-hour chart? Because it is a balance. The five-minute chart changes every moment and picks up noise. The daily shows the big picture, but gives few signals. The one-hour keeps the trend reading clean and gives signals at a reasonable frequency. That is why Aurum Flow was optimized for it. And you should know one thing: if you change the chart, you are using a different strategy, even if the name is the same. Don't treat the 1H as a technical detail. It is the foundation of everything.

cenas.visual: Ruben in a close-up, speaking to the camera.
cenas.narracao: An honest note before we move on. This strategy does not tell you how many trades you will win, nor how much you make on each one. I don't have that rate to give you, and no material in this course has it. If anyone sells you a signal with a win rate, be suspicious straight away. What the method gives you is discipline and a written plan. The rest you learn yourself, with your own markings, and that is exactly what we train in this module's mission, in a simulated account. There is no shortcut here, and that is why it is worth practising.

cenas.visual: List on screen, charcoal background: "1. Clear trend on the 1H · 2. Direction with the trend · 3. Written plan before you click".
cenas.narracao: Summary. First, the trend decides. Second, you only enter with it. Third, you never enter without a written plan before touching any button. In the next lesson we see how the trend is measured, with the three DEMA averages and the momentum confirmation. Until then, do one simple thing: open a one-hour chart and say out loud which way the market is going. Don't draw any more conclusions than that. Just that, for now. Pay close attention to this, because it is the basis of everything that follows. Write this in your notebook before you move on.

aulas.titulo: Aula 12.2 — The three-DEMA filter and the momentum confirmation
aulas.gancho: Saying 'there is a trend' is easy. Proving it with numbers is another story. Three averages and a strength indicator are there for that.

cenas.visual: One-hour chart with three lines: DEMA 15 in light gold, DEMA 50 in gold, DEMA 238 in grey.
cenas.narracao: To measure the trend, Aurum Flow uses three DEMA averages, of 15, 50 and 238 periods. A DEMA lags less than a simple average and reacts faster. The 15 shows the recent move, the 50 the medium term, the 238 the background. When all three are ordered in the same direction and the price is on the same side, the filter says there is a trend. When they are tangled together, the filter says there isn't. And a filter that says no is as useful as one that says yes, because it saves you a bad entry.

cenas.visual: Two charts: on the left, the three lines ordered and the price above them; on the right, the lines crossed. Captions: "aligned" · "tangled".
cenas.narracao: Notice the difference. On the left, the three averages are ordered, with the fastest on top and the slowest at the bottom, and the price is trading above them. That is an uptrend. On the right, the lines cross each other and the price keeps crossing them from one side to the other. That is sideways. Both are illustrative examples. If you look at ten charts like these, you will see that sideways shows up more often than you would like. With the filter, it is a no without drama, not a signal you have to force.

cenas.visual: Ruben with a finger on the screen, pointing at the RSI indicator in the lower panel. Text: "RSI · momentum confirmation".
cenas.narracao: The trend filter tells you which way to look, but not when. That is where the momentum confirmation comes in, done with the RSI. The RSI measures the recent strength of moves on a scale from zero to one hundred. On a buy entry, we want the RSI to confirm strength in the same direction as the signal, not turn against it. On a sell entry, it is the opposite. There is no magic number here for you to memorize. The rule is the direction: momentum has to be on the side of the trend.

cenas.visual: Golden checklist on screen with two boxes: "trend: three DEMA aligned" and "momentum: RSI confirming". Both ticked.
cenas.narracao: Put the two parts together and you have the entry gate. First, the three DEMA say there is a trend and say which way it goes. Second, the RSI confirms that the strength is going in the same direction. Only with both, the signal is eligible. If one fails, there is no signal. That is not a preference, it is a closed door. And notice that this does not oblige you to pick the top or the bottom. It obliges you to wait for the market to show its hand before you show yours. Don't jump to conclusions from what you have just heard.

cenas.visual: Ruben writing three questions in his notebook: "DEMA aligned? · RSI confirming? · same direction?"
cenas.narracao: Do the exercise you will repeat in every lesson of this module. Choose a one-hour chart. First question: are the three averages ordered? Second: does the RSI confirm the same direction? Third: do both answers point to the same side? If the answer to any of them is no, write no signal and move on to the next chart. It is not a failure. It is the filter doing its job, and doing it without asking you for an opinion. There is no shortcut here, and that is why it is worth practising. Write this in your notebook before you move on.

cenas.visual: Ruben in a medium shot, charcoal background. Line on screen: "The filter doesn't predict. Ask the same question every time."
cenas.narracao: Summary. The three DEMA answer the trend question. The RSI answers the momentum question. The signal only exists when both answers point the same way. There is no prediction here. There is a question asked the same way every time, so that you don't decide based on your mood of the day. In the next lesson we read a complete signal, from entry to the last target, and see the percentage distances that make it comparable. Pay close attention to this, because it is the basis of everything that follows. Write this in your notebook before you move on.

aulas.titulo: Aula 12.3 — Reading a signal: entry, stop and % distances
aulas.gancho: A signal is a card with four numbers. If you can read all four, you know what you are accepting before you accept it.

cenas.visual: Aurum Flow signal screen, zoomed in on the card. Captions: "entry" · "stop" · "targets". Label: illustrative example.
cenas.narracao: This is a signal. It is an illustrative example, put together for the lesson. At first glance four things matter: the entry price, the stop, the three targets, and the distance of each level in points and in percentage. The signal is a static plan. It was fixed on the candle that generated it and it does not rewrite itself when the price moves. If the price has already moved away from the entry, the plan stays exactly the same. This distinction will matter in the mission, because you will compare the written plan with what the market did afterwards.

cenas.visual: Animation: a vertical line with the entry, the stop below it and a bracket marked "1.5 × ATR". Text: "stop = 1.5 × ATR".
cenas.narracao: The stop sits at a distance of one and a half ATR. ATR is the average range of recent candles. It tells you how much the asset usually moves in one hourly candle. By multiplying by one and a half, the stop is far enough that normal noise does not hit it, and close enough that a loss is the expected one. The idea is for the stop to follow the asset's real behavior, not a fixed number you chose on impulse. A stop chosen on impulse is a bet in disguise.

cenas.visual: Ruben with a calculator. On screen: "entry 100 · stop −2%". Label: illustrative example.
cenas.narracao: Let's do the maths, with an illustrative example. The entry is one hundred, and the stop sits two per cent below, that is, at ninety-eight. That is your risk distance: two per cent. Now the targets. The first, at one and a half to one, is three per cent above the entry. The second, at three to one, six per cent. The third, at six to one, twelve per cent. Notice that every number is measured against the risk, never against the absolute price. That is what lets you compare signals on assets with completely different prices.

cenas.visual: Table on screen: "Entry 100 · Stop 98 (−2%) · Target 1: 103 (+3%) · Target 2: 106 (+6%) · Target 3: 112 (+12%)". Label: illustrative example.
cenas.narracao: Here is the same example in a table. Entry one hundred, stop ninety-eight, and the targets at one hundred and three, one hundred and six and one hundred and twelve. Again: illustrative example, because a number without context invites fantasy. I am not telling you the price will get there. I am telling you that, if you enter, this is what the plan asks for. Each level costs the two per cent risk and returns one and a half, three or six times that risk, if it is reached. Nothing more, and nothing less. Write this in your notebook before you move on.

cenas.visual: Ruben at the notebook, with a form: "entry · stop · stop distance in % · target 1 · target 2 · target 3".
cenas.narracao: To practise, copy this form into your notebook and always fill it in the same order. Entry, stop, the stop distance in percentage, and the three targets with their respective distances. If a signal does not let you fill in these fields without guessing, it is not complete enough for you yet. Don't use it. Read the card until you can fill it in from memory, without help, and only then move on to the decision. The order matters: first you read, then you decide. Pay close attention to this, because it is the basis of everything that follows. There is no shortcut here, and that is why it is worth practising.

cenas.visual: Ruben in a medium shot. Line on screen: "Read before you act."
cenas.narracao: Summary. A signal is a fixed plan with four parts. The entry is where the plan starts. The stop is where the plan admits it was wrong, measured in ATR. The targets are where the plan collects, measured in multiples of the risk. The percentage distances let you compare signals and understand the weight of each one on your balance. In the next lesson we talk about the targets in more detail, and about a rule you have to write down before you need it: what you do when the first target is hit. Write this in your notebook before you move on.

aulas.titulo: Aula 12.4 — The three targets, partial exits and break-even
aulas.gancho: When the price goes your way, the problem changes. It is no longer what you do if you are wrong. It is what you do when you are right.

cenas.visual: Chart with the entry and the three targets as horizontal gold lines, of increasing intensity. Text: "1:1.5 · 1:3 · 1:6".
cenas.narracao: The three targets sit at one and a half, three and six times the risk. They are not three predictions. They are three decision points. The first is the nearest, so it is the one reached first. The last is the most ambitious, and it may never be reached. A signal that reaches the second target did not fail at the first. Each target is a different moment, with its own decision, and that is why the plan separates them instead of lumping them into a single number. Don't jump to conclusions from what you have just heard.

cenas.visual: Ruben showing his notebook, on the page of exit rules. Text: "partial exit · written before entry".
cenas.narracao: Now the part that changes how you trade: partial exits. The idea is simple. You don't have to close the whole position in the same place. You can close one part at the first target, another at the second, and leave a part running for the third. What you have already collected stays collected, and what remains has room to run. But the percentage of each part is not a number you pick on top of the chart. It is a rule you write before entering. Decided during the trade, it is already emotion, and emotion tends to choose the wrong exit.

cenas.visual: Screen with the stop moving up to the entry after the first target. Caption: "break-even: stop at entry". Text: "personal rule · written beforehand".
cenas.narracao: Break-even is the step most people skip and later regret. When the price hits the first target, you can move the stop to the entry. If the market comes back, the part still open closes near zero, instead of giving back the full risk. Careful: this is your rule. Don't count on any button doing it for you, and the decision to apply it is entirely yours. Write it in the words you will use. For example: when the first target is hit, I close one part and move the stop to the entry.

cenas.visual: Example chart: the price rises to target 1, then returns to the entry. Label: illustrative example · no guarantees.
cenas.narracao: Let's look at this with an illustrative example, with the entry at one hundred and the stop at ninety-eight. The price rises to one hundred and three. Say you close one part and move the stop to one hundred. Then the market turns back and reaches one hundred. The part still open closes at break-even, and the part you collected at the first target stays as profit. If the price had dropped right after the entry, the loss would be the original stop, and nothing more. What the rule changes is what happens after the plan has proven it was right.

cenas.visual: Ruben in a close-up, speaking to the camera. Text: "Don't copy anyone's percentages."
cenas.narracao: Now the notebook exercise. Write four lines: the percentage you close at the first target, the one you close at the second, the part you leave running for the third, and the stop rule. You don't need to copy anyone's percentages, not even the ones that appear in this course. You need to have your own. And also write down what you will do if the price reaches the second target and turns back. Whoever doesn't have that line written always decides at the last minute, and at the last minute nobody decides well. Write this in your notebook before you move on.

cenas.visual: Ruben in a medium shot. On-screen text: "1:1.5 · 1:3 · 1:6 · exits written · break-even is your rule".
cenas.narracao: Summary. Three targets, three decisions. Partial exits that you define before entering. Break-even as a written rule, which protects the trade once the plan has been right. None of this guarantees a profit. It is a way of not letting emotion decide what you do with an open trade. In the next lesson, the part that protects the most: when not to enter. Most of a beginner's mistakes do not happen inside the trade. They happen before it, when they enter without a reason. Pay close attention to this, because it is the basis of everything that follows. There is no shortcut here, and that is why it is worth practising.

aulas.titulo: Aula 12.5 — When not to enter, and the mission
aulas.gancho: The lesson fewest people want to see is the one that protects the most. In this method, the best decision is often not to enter.

cenas.visual: Ruben in a medium shot, almost black background. On-screen text: "Not entering is also a decision."
cenas.narracao: There are three situations in which the rule is not to enter, even when a signal is on the screen. The first: the signal goes against the trend. We have already seen why. If the three DEMA say one thing and the signal says another, there is no signal for you, however good it looks. The second: there is a high-impact news event scheduled for the next few hours. The third: you have already reached your daily loss limit. That is the most important one, and we will look at it calmly in module thirteen, because that is where many accounts are lost.

cenas.visual: Chart with a sell signal marked in red. Beside it, the three DEMA aligned upwards. Text: "against the trend → don't enter". Label: illustrative example.
cenas.narracao: Look at this illustrative example. A sell signal appears, but the three averages are aligned upwards. There is a pullback candle, and instinct says now. It isn't. The trend is on the other side, and the signal is just a reaction to a pause. When in doubt, ask yourself just one thing: am I entering with the trend? If the answer is no, the answer to the entry is also no. You don't need more arguments than that. Don't jump to conclusions from what you have just heard. Write this in your notebook before you move on.

cenas.visual: Economic calendar with a day marked in gold. Text: "high-impact news · no new entries in that window".
cenas.narracao: The second situation is the calendar. Before each session, check whether there is a high-impact news event scheduled for the next few hours. If there is, the rule is simple: you do not open new positions in that window. In those hours, the price can jump for reasons no one-hour chart can read. You can keep studying, marking and recording. What you don't do is enter on top of news you cannot control, just because the chart looked clean five minutes earlier. Pay close attention to this, because it is the basis of everything that follows.

cenas.visual: Ruben with his notebook. Three boxes below the exit rules: "against the trend", "strong news", "daily limit reached".
cenas.narracao: Write these three no-entry rules below your exit rules. Against the trend: I don't enter. Strong news in the window: I don't open a new position. Daily limit reached: I don't enter any more that day, even if the signal looks perfect on paper. Notice that these rules do not depend on how you feel. They depend on facts that either hold or don't. That is what makes them useful, and what makes them easy to follow when you need them most. There is no shortcut here, and that is why it is worth practising. Write this in your notebook before you move on.

cenas.visual: Screen with the text: "Module 12 mission: mark 10 past signals on the 1H chart, in a simulated account."
cenas.narracao: Now the mission. You will mark ten past Aurum Flow signals on the one-hour chart, in a simulated account, on the MTM WebTrader or in an MTM Funded account. It is not real money and it is not about being right. It is about training your reading. For each signal, note the entry, the stop, the three targets with their percentage distances, whether the signal passed the trend and momentum filters, and whether the first target was hit, yes or no. Don't draw conclusions from ten signals. Ten signals give you practice, nothing more, and practice is what we are after.

cenas.visual: Ruben in a close-up, with the warning on screen: "Educational content, not financial advice. The risk of loss is real."
cenas.narracao: One last word. None of these ten signals tells you what the next one will do. The simulated account exists for that: to make mistakes at no real cost. And before a single real euro, the programme asks for thirty simulated trades with a complete journal. This module is only the first step, and it is not a shortcut. Educational content, not financial advice. The risk of loss is real, and it can be total. In module thirteen we talk about the part that protects your account: position size. Don't jump to conclusions from what you have just heard.

modulos.titulo: Módulo 13 — Risk and position size (≈15 min)

aulas.titulo: Aula 13.1 — 1% risk per trade
aulas.gancho: You can have the best strategy in the world and still end up with no account. A run of big, bad trades is all it takes. The defence is not to be right more often. It is to lose a little at a time.

cenas.visual: Ruben in a medium shot, almost black background. On-screen text: "Educational content. The risk of loss is real."
cenas.narracao: This is the most tedious module of level three and, for many people, the most important. Before we talk numbers, the usual warning. Educational content. The risk of loss is real, and it can be total. This lesson does not promise you will win. It promises you something more modest and more useful: that one bad trade will not take away what it took you years to build. That is the only promise a course on risk can honestly make. And even that depends on you, on following the rule every day, with no exceptions that seem reasonable at the time.

cenas.visual: Animation: a balance bar divided into a hundred equal slices, with one gold slice lit. Text: "1% of the balance per trade".
cenas.narracao: The rule we are going to use is this: you risk at most one per cent of the balance on each trade. One per cent, not whatever you think the signal deserves. If you have €1,000 in your simulated account, the maximum risk of a trade is €10. And be careful: risk is not the amount invested. It is how much you lose if the stop is hit. They are different things, and confusing the two is the origin of many accounts that disappear. Notice that the gold slice is small on purpose. A small slice does not bring you down. Illustrative example, with a simulated account, as always.

cenas.visual: Two blocks side by side. Left: "invested €500 · stop −2% · risk €10". Right: "invested €200 · stop −15% · risk €30". Label: illustrative example.
cenas.narracao: Look at these two cases, illustrative examples. In the first, you invest five hundred euros, but the stop is at two per cent. If it is hit, you lose ten euros. In the second, you invest only two hundred, but the stop is at fifteen per cent, and you lose thirty. Anyone who only looks at the amount invested thinks the first is the big risk. They are wrong. The number that controls the account is the loss at the stop. So the right question is not how much do I invest?, it is how much do I lose if the stop is hit?. That question protects the balance, and it is the one we will train throughout the module.

cenas.visual: Ruben with an open notebook. On the page, the formula: "maximum risk = balance × 1%". Below: "€1,000 × 1% = €10".
cenas.narracao: Write the formula at the top of your notebook: balance times one per cent. With a thousand simulated euros, the loss ceiling of each trade is ten euros. That ceiling does not change because the signal looks good to you. An exciting signal does not entitle you to risk more. A weak signal may lead you to risk less, and that is also fine. What changes from trade to trade is the size of the position, and that is next lesson. The risk stays fixed. If you ever write another number in your notebook, stop and go back to this page. The mistake is in the calculation, never in the market.

cenas.visual: Ruben in a close-up, speaking to the camera. Text: "ten losses in a row of 1% ≈ 10% of the account".
cenas.narracao: Let's be realistic. You will lose trades. That is part of the method and not a sign that the method is broken. With one per cent, a loss is a scratch. Ten losses in a row of one per cent each take roughly ten per cent off the account. It is a bad stretch, and it recovers with patience and rules. What destroys accounts is the opposite: risking ten or twenty per cent on one trade because this time is different. If you ever hear that sentence in your head, remember the formula. It does not argue. It calculates. And that is why it works.

cenas.visual: Ruben in a medium shot, charcoal background. List on screen: "1% of the balance · risk is the loss at the stop · €1,000 → €10".
cenas.narracao: Summary. The risk of each trade is one per cent of the balance. It is not what you invest, it is what you lose if the stop is hit. This rule protects you from streaks, because no single loss can take you out of the game. It also forces you to do something DCA has already taught you: decide the size before you feel the pressure of the market. In the next lesson we take this rule and calculate the exact size of the position, from the stop distance you learned in module twelve. It is not magic. It is a division.

aulas.titulo: Aula 13.2 — Calculating the size from the stop distance
aulas.gancho: You already know how much you can lose: ten euros. The question almost nobody asks is still missing: how much can I buy so that, if the stop is hit, I lose exactly those ten?

cenas.visual: Screen with the module 12 example: entry at 100, stop at 98. Label: illustrative example.
cenas.narracao: Let's use the module twelve example, with the entry at one hundred and the stop two per cent below, at ninety-eight. Illustrative example, as always. The simulated account has a thousand euros and the maximum risk is ten. The question is: how much should I have invested in this position so that the stop, if hit, costs exactly ten euros? It is not a number you guess. It has a formula, and the formula fits on a card. I will show it to you slowly, with the calculator in hand, so that you can redo the calculation yourself without looking at me.

cenas.visual: Diagram with the formula highlighted: "Size = risk in € ÷ stop distance in %".
cenas.narracao: The formula is this: the size of the position equals the risk in euros divided by the stop distance in percentage. The risk is ten euros. The stop distance is two per cent. Ten divided by two per cent, or by zero point zero two in the calculator, gives five hundred. Five hundred euros of position. If the price falls two per cent, you lose two per cent of five hundred, which is ten euros. Exactly your risk, not a cent more. Each piece has a role: the risk sets the ceiling, the stop sets the distance, and the size is what fits between the two.

cenas.visual: Table on screen: "stop 2% → position €500 · stop 4% → €250 · stop 5% → €200". Text: "same risk, different sizes".
cenas.narracao: Notice what happens when you change only the stop distance, keeping the risk at ten euros. With the stop at two per cent, the position is five hundred euros. With the stop at four per cent, it drops to two hundred and fifty. With the stop at five per cent, it is two hundred. The risk is always ten. A wider stop forces a smaller position. A tighter stop lets you buy more. Illustrative example, but the lesson is firm: never choose the size before you know where the stop is. The stop decides the position, not the other way round.

cenas.visual: Ruben at the notebook, with four numbered steps: "1 balance · 2 risk of 1% · 3 stop distance in % · 4 size = 2 ÷ 3".
cenas.narracao: Write the procedure in four steps, always in the same order. One: the account balance. Two: the risk, one per cent of that balance. Three: the stop distance in percentage, taken from the signal plan. Four: you divide two by three. That result is the size. If you don't have the stop distance, you don't have a signal, and no size can be calculated. Don't guess the distance or round it to whatever suits you. It comes from the plan written before you entered, and that is where it should stay.

cenas.visual: Ruben with a second example in the notebook: "€10 ÷ 3% = €333 → rounded down to €330". Label: illustrative example.
cenas.narracao: Second example, also illustrative. The stop is now at three per cent. Ten divided by zero point zero three gives three hundred and thirty-three. You don't round up. Rounding up is increasing the risk without meaning to, and an account that grows without you noticing is exactly what we want to avoid. You round down, to three hundred and thirty, without hesitating. Notice that the wider stop gave a smaller position, as we saw a moment ago. The rule always adds up, and that is what makes it reliable. When it doesn't, the mistake is in the calculation.

cenas.visual: Ruben in a medium shot. On-screen line: "Stop first, size after."
cenas.narracao: Summary. Stop first, size after. The formula is the risk in euros divided by the stop distance in percentage, and you always round down. There is no opinion in this calculation. There is a distance, a risk and a result. If one day you feel the size should be bigger because the signal is good, remember this lesson: conviction is not part of the formula. In the next lesson we look at leverage, which many people confuse with size, and at the Aurum Flow account panel, which shows several of these calculations already done.

aulas.titulo: Aula 13.3 — Useful leverage and the account panel
aulas.gancho: Leverage is the button most people confuse with position size. And confusing the two is the shortest route to losing more than you wanted.

cenas.visual: Screen with a leverage control being moved. Text: "leverage ≠ size ≠ risk".
cenas.narracao: Let's separate three things that look like one. Leverage is the multiplier the platform gives you to open a position bigger than the money you have deposited. Size, or notional, is the total value of the position. And risk is how much you lose if the stop is hit. Leverage does not create risk out of nothing. It changes how much money you have to set aside as margin, and it makes it easy to open large positions without noticing. If the size and the stop have not changed, the risk has not changed either, whatever leverage you chose.

cenas.visual: Aurum Flow account panel, with today's values blurred. Text: "useful leverage · notional · fees · risk % per trade".
cenas.narracao: The Aurum Flow account panel shows four things for the size you chose. The useful leverage: the leverage the position needs for the size you chose, not the maximum the platform offers. The notional, which is the total value of the position. The cost in fees, on entry and exit, which eats part of the result. And the risk as a percentage per trade. The values on screen are blurred, because they do not matter for the lesson. What matters is learning to read all four, not memorizing numbers.

cenas.visual: Ruben with the example on screen: "account €1,000 · position €500 · useful leverage ≈ 1×". Label: illustrative example.
cenas.narracao: Apply this to the example from a moment ago: a thousand-euro account, a five-hundred-euro position. The useful leverage is low, about one times. That means the position fits in the account without stretching anything. Now imagine the panel showed you ten times for the same position. What would change? The size would still be five hundred, and the stop would still be at two per cent. The only thing that would change is the margin the platform asks to hold the position. Whoever chooses the leverage is not choosing the risk. The risk was already written into the stop and the formula.

cenas.visual: Ruben at the notebook, with the rule written in bold: "use the leverage the size requires, never the maximum".
cenas.narracao: The rule you write in your notebook is this, without exceptions: the leverage I use is the one the calculated size requires, never the maximum offered, even if the platform presents it as the normal option. If the account fits without leverage, I don't use leverage. If the position needs some leverage, the panel shows it to you. And you always check the notional before you press confirm. It is not a rule of fear, it is a rule of precision. The platform shows the maximum because that is what it shows.
