Your interest is different: it is the size you calculated in the previous lesson, and nothing else.

cenas.visual: Ruben with the fee calculation on screen: "illustrative example: 0.1% fee per side · position €500 → €0.50 on entry + €0.50 on exit".
cenas.narracao: Finally, fees. In an illustrative example, with a fee of zero point one per cent per side, a five-hundred-euro position pays fifty cents on entry and fifty cents on exit. It seems little. But with a two per cent stop and a risk of ten euros, one euro of fees is ten per cent of the risk you defined. It is not a detail. That is why the panel shows the cost, and why you look at it before you confirm, not after. The real fee is your platform's, and it is in its terms. Check it. Don't use mine as if it were yours.

cenas.visual: Ruben in a medium shot. On-screen text: "leverage ≠ size ≠ risk · 4 numbers on the panel · fees count".
cenas.narracao: Summary. Leverage is how the platform asks for margin. Size is the value of the position. Risk is the loss at the stop. Don't confuse the three. The Aurum Flow panel shows the useful leverage, the notional, the fees and the risk per trade, and your rule is to look at all four before pressing any button. In the last lesson of the module we talk about what happens after a loss, after a bad day, and how to stop in time, before a bad day turns into a bad week.

aulas.titulo: Aula 13.4 — Daily limit, losing streaks and stopping rules
aulas.gancho: The worst decision in an account is rarely the first loss. It is the fourth, after a bad morning, when you decide that 'now is the time'.

cenas.visual: Ruben in a medium shot. On-screen text: "a bad day can also be planned for".
cenas.narracao: Last lesson of the module, and perhaps the one that saves you the most. Everything we have seen so far is about single trades. But whoever loses money almost always loses in sequence. One loss, then another, then a third, and the head starts asking for an immediate recovery. That urge has a name: chasing losses. And the antidote is not willpower, which runs out quickly. It is a rule written before the day starts. Whoever decides what to do after three losses at ten in the morning is already deciding with a head in revenge mode. That is why the decision has to be made beforehand.

cenas.visual: Bar chart with three red bars, each marked "−1%". Label: illustrative example.
cenas.narracao: Look at this series, illustrative example. Three losses of one per cent each. On the thousand-euro account, that is around thirty euros. It hurts, but it is not the end. The problem starts when the fourth trade comes out bigger, because the person wants to recover quickly. At that moment, the risk stops being the one per cent of the rule and becomes a desperate bet. Nobody decides that on purpose. It happens gradually, with the justification that this time it pays off. The stopping rule exists to prevent that shift, and so you don't have to argue about it with yourself in the worst moment.

cenas.visual: Ruben with the notebook, writing three stopping rules. Text: "daily limit · losing streak · stop is stop".
cenas.narracao: Write three stopping rules, with your own numbers. The first is the daily loss limit. For example, and it is only an illustrative example, two per cent of the balance in one day: once you hit it, you close the platform. The second is the losing streak: three losses in a row on the same day, and you stop. The third is the most important: after a stop, you don't come back to the screen that day, not even to see if the signal has improved. This is the rule that saves the most accounts, because the market owes you nothing and it will always be back tomorrow. The numbers you write are yours. The ones I use here are small on purpose.

cenas.visual: Two-minute checklist on screen: "limit written? · streak written? · maximum trades? · news in the window checked?".
cenas.narracao: Before each session, run a two-minute routine. Is the daily limit written down? Is the losing streak written down? Do you know the maximum number of trades you will take? Have you checked the news in the window? If the answer to any of these is no, you don't start. Notice that this routine says nothing about the market. It says everything about you. It is the part of trading that most resembles the Friday ritual of the DCA: rules before the money, not during it. Someone who has this routine done does not need to be smarter than the market. They need to be more predictable than their own emotions.

cenas.visual: Screen with the text: "Module 13 mission: size calculator for 5 signals, in a €1,000 simulated account".
cenas.narracao: Module mission. Choose five past Aurum Flow signals and do the calculations in a simulated account of one thousand euros. For each signal, fill in the size calculator: the risk in euros, the stop distance in percentage, the calculated size rounded down, the useful leverage the panel shows, and the cost of fees. Don't open any real position for this. You need to do the calculation five times, without skipping any. If one of them leaves you in doubt, go back to the formula and not to instinct. The calculator has no opinion. Your intuition does, and that is why the calculator comes first.

cenas.visual: Ruben in a close-up, with the warning on screen: "Educational content, not financial advice. The risk of loss is real, and it can be total."
cenas.narracao: End of module thirteen, and of the risk block. One per cent per trade. Size from the stop. Leverage that the size requires, never the maximum. Daily limit and losing streak written down before the first signal. None of these rules guarantees a profit. What they do is limit what a bad streak can take from you, and that is already a lot. Educational content, not financial advice. The risk of loss is real, and it can be total. In module fourteen we see how to execute without emotion, with the WebTrader, the simulated accounts and MTM Auto.

aulas.titulo: Aula 14.1 — MTM WebTrader and the MTM Funded simulated account
aulas.gancho: If there is one thing the market teaches quickly, it is this: emotion does not wait until you are ready. So before any money, we train in a place where a mistake costs no real money.

cenas.visual: Dark screen, with the phrase in gold: "Educational content. The risk of loss is real." Then Ruben in a medium shot, at a desk, with a closed notebook in front of him.
cenas.narracao: Before we start, a warning that applies to this whole module. Educational content. The risk of loss is real. In this lesson you get to know the tools you will practise with, and the first rule is the most important of all: practice is done in a simulated account, never with rent money, never with money you need for the month's bills. I know it is tempting to skip this part and go straight to the real account. Don't skip it. Those who train calmly learn what haste hides. We will look at the three pieces of this module: the MTM WebTrader, the MTM Funded simulated account and, further on, MTM Auto. None of this is a shortcut to making money. It is a place to learn to do things well, with written rules, before any real risk.

cenas.visual: MTM WebTrader screen open in the browser, with the chart in the centre and the trading panel beside it. Small caption: "illustrative screen".
cenas.narracao: First piece: the MTM WebTrader. It is the browser version of the MoreThanMoney execution tool. You open it on the computer, you see the asset's chart and the panel where orders are placed. You don't need to know everything at once. At this stage, what matters is one thing only: understanding where each element of the screen is before you touch any button. Whoever clicks without knowing where they are is not training, they are improvising. And improvising with emotion, on a screen with buy and sell buttons, is the simplest recipe for a decision you will regret.

cenas.visual: Screen with the label "MTM Funded simulated account" and, beside it, a large tag: "SIMULATED".
cenas.narracao: Second piece: the MTM Funded simulated accounts. Notice the word on the screen: simulated. These are simulation accounts, with money that does not exist. There is no real deposit, no withdrawal, no real balance to lose. What you train here is the method: the entry, the stop, the size, the record. When emotion appears, and it will, the difference is this: the money is simulated, but the discipline you practise is real. Be careful, though. A simulated account does not reproduce the nerves of losing real money. So the test of the simulation is not winning. It is following the rules, trade by trade, even when the account looks small and the temptation looks big.

cenas.visual: Animated list on screen: "1 · open the simulated account · 2 · choose one asset from your plan · 3 · write the rule before clicking".
cenas.narracao: How you train, in practice. First, you open the simulated account in the WebTrader. Second, you choose a single asset, one you already know from the earlier modules. Third, and this is the step people skip: you write the rule before clicking. Why you enter, where the stop goes, what the size is, and what you will do if the price moves against you. Only then do you place the order. If you can't write the rule in two sentences, you don't enter. This sounds like bureaucracy, and it is. Bureaucracy is what protects you from emotion at the moment it appears with the most force, which is almost always when the price moves fast.

cenas.visual: Ruben with the notebook open. On screen, the phrase: "Simulation trains the method. It proves nothing."
cenas.narracao: One last note, because it is easy to fool yourself. A simulated account that goes up does not prove the strategy works. A simulated account that goes down does not prove you are bad. What the simulation shows is whether you followed your own process, and that is the only indicator that matters to you at this stage. Don't look at the balance as a trophy. And if someone shows you a screenshot of a simulated account with a high balance, as proof that they make money, be suspicious. A screenshot is not a statistic, and a training account is not a real track record. When you need a number, ask for the full series of trades, not the pretty picture. Illustrative example, of course: a screenshot with a high balance can hide a hundred trades without a single written rule.

aulas.titulo: Aula 14.2 — MTM Auto: copying with rules and limits
aulas.gancho: Copying looks like the solution for those who don't have time. But there is one question almost nobody asks before switching it on: who answers for what happens afterwards?

cenas.visual: MTM Auto screen with the list of available strategies. Highlighted: the expression "rules and limits".
cenas.narracao: Third piece of this module: MTM Auto. It is MoreThanMoney's tool for copying strategies, and the keyword is this: with rules and limits. In other words, it is not a button that copies everything blindly. Before you switch on a strategy, you have to see which rules it follows and which limits the tool applies. This is very different from copying someone who turned up in a message group, without knowing anything about what that person does. Here there are rules in plain view, and that is already half the way to an informed decision. But only half. The other half is yours.

cenas.visual: Screen split in two: on the left, "strategy rules"; on the right, "tool limits". Arrows connecting the two columns.
cenas.narracao: Before you switch on any strategy, read three things. First, what it does: which markets it works in, with what kind of entries and how often. Second, the limits that apply on your side of the copy. Third, what happens when things go wrong. If you cannot say, in your own words, what the strategy does and what happens in the worst case, don't switch it on. And notice something that seems counterintuitive: a strategy that has been rising for a long time does not, for that reason, carry less risk. It may even carry more, because confidence grows just before a fall.

cenas.visual: Ruben in a close-up, with the phrase on screen: "Copying is not delegating responsibility."
cenas.narracao: Now the part that matters most. Copying does not take away your responsibility. When you switch on a copy, you remain the owner of the decision to have switched it on. The tool executes, but whoever chose the strategy, whoever decided how much they are willing to risk, and whoever decides to stop, is you. This holds even when the strategy belongs to someone you trust, and even when the tool is the house's own. The tool executes what is written. It does not know how much of your money is rent money, it does not know you have a bill to pay on Friday, and it does not know that you are tired and eager to win back a loss. Only you know those things, and only you can take them into account.

cenas.visual: Calendar with three weeks, an arrow going down. Caption: "illustrative case".
cenas.narracao: Illustrative case. Inês, thirty-five, switched on a copy because she did not have time to follow the markets. For a few weeks it seemed perfect. Then a drop came, and she had not defined how much she was willing to lose. She put in more money to recover and, before she knew it, she was no longer copying a strategy. She was trying to win back a loss. The tool did exactly what was written. The mistake was not writing down her own limit. If Inês had defined, before switching it on, how much she could lose and what she would do when she reached that amount, the story would have been different. Illustrative example, of course.

cenas.visual: Checklist on screen: "1 · I know what the strategy does · 2 · I know the limits · 3 · I know how much I can lose · 4 · I know when I stop".
cenas.narracao: Before copying, four questions, written in your notebook. Do I know what the strategy does? Do I know the limits that apply? Do I know how much I can lose, in euros, without it affecting my life? And do I know when I stop, and what I do that day? If any answer is no, the copy stays off. The practical exercise of this lesson is done in the simulated account: you switch on MTM Auto in a simulated account, observe for a week and write down, each day, what you felt. Copying is not the end of the process. It is just one more piece of it.

aulas.titulo: Aula 14.3 — The trading journal
aulas.gancho: If it isn't written down, it didn't happen. That sounds exaggerated, until we notice how many decisions we make from memory, and how often we recount them wrongly.

cenas.visual: Notebook open at the journal page, with the fields appearing one by one. Caption: "template in the course notebook".
cenas.narracao: This lesson is about the trading journal. It is not a pretty dossier. It is a page where you write each trade before, during and after. The full template comes in the student notebook, but the idea is simple: a trade that is not in the journal, for learning purposes, did not exist. Because memory is generous with wins and cruel with mistakes. A week later, you remember having been right. You don't remember having entered outside the rule, or having moved the stop in a hurry. The journal exists to end that automatic selection our brain makes without asking permission.

cenas.visual: Two animated columns: on the left, "before": date · asset · reason · rule · size · stop · targets. On the right, "after": result · rule followed? · what I felt.
cenas.narracao: Let's go through the fields. Before entering, you record the date, the asset and the reason for the entry, written in one sentence, and which rule you are applying. You record the size of the position and how much you lose if the stop is hit, always in euros, never only in percentage. And you record the stop and the targets. Before you touch the button, the journal already has everything. After closing, you add the result, whether the rule was followed, and one line about what you felt. Illustrative example: I entered because the price returned to the average; I lose twenty euros if the stop is hit; I followed the rule; I felt rushed at ten in the morning.

cenas.visual: Ruben pointing at the column "rule followed? yes or no", highlighted in gold.
cenas.narracao: The most important column is the one almost nobody fills in: was the rule followed, yes or no. Because the goal at this stage is not to win. It is to execute the process you wrote. A losing trade with the rule followed is a good training trade. A winning trade outside the rule is a warning, not a compliment. If you mark no and the trade made a profit, write exactly that, without excuses. That no will be the most useful piece of information you get in a whole week, because it shows you where emotion got involved, even when it went well. Always write it, even when the answer bothers you.

cenas.visual: Journal sheet with three filled-in lines. Caption: "illustrative case".
cenas.narracao: Illustrative case: Rui, twenty-nine, made three trades in one week. On the first, he followed the rule and lost the expected amount, without drama. On the second, he moved the stop halfway through, because he didn't want to watch the loss grow. On the third, he entered with no written reason, just because the chart seemed to be moving fast. When he did the review, the last two lines had no in the rule column. That was when he understood the problem. It was not the market. It was him stepping out of the process, twice, in silence. The journal showed that in two minutes. Memory would have hidden it all.

cenas.visual: Ruben with the notebook closed. On-screen text: "Write before. Close after. Never rewrite."
cenas.narracao: Two rules so you don't spoil the journal. First: write before you enter. A journal written afterwards is a story, and stories adjust themselves. Second: never rewrite an old line. If you get a word wrong, you cross it out and write over it, with the date of the correction. If you erase what you did badly, you are erasing the only thing that can teach you. The journal is not there to judge you. It is there to show yourself what you really did, dated today and without makeup. Take this out of the notebook and keep it in view, so you can reread it before each session.

aulas.titulo: Aula 14.4 — Weekly audit and the 30-minute routine
aulas.gancho: Thirty minutes a week, with the journal open in front of you. Without this routine, the journal is just a notebook full of lines.

cenas.visual: Animated clock with thirty minutes split into four blocks: "prepare 5 · review trades 10 · audit rules 10 · decide 5".
cenas.narracao: This is the routine. Thirty minutes, once a week, always on the same day and at the same time. It breaks down like this: five minutes to prepare, ten to review the week's trades, ten to audit the rules, and five to decide on one single thing to change. Notice the time. Thirty minutes is short on purpose. A review that lasts three hours turns into anxiety, and a five-minute review turns into an excuse. Thirty minutes is enough to be honest, and not so long that you want to change everything at once. Choose the day and time in your calendar, as if it were a booked meeting.

cenas.visual: Journal screen with the week filled in. Arrows pointing at the column "rule followed".
cenas.narracao: First, review the trades. You open the week's journal and read each line from top to bottom, without editing anything. You look for three things: how many trades you made, how many followed the rule, and at what moments you stepped out of the process. Don't look at the result in euros as a judge. The result is a data point, and a single data point deceives. A week of profit with three rules broken is a bad week. A week of loss with all rules followed is a well-trained week. Read with a pencil in hand and mark the lines that make you uncomfortable, without correcting them.

cenas.visual: List on screen: "audit · size within the plan? · stop moved? · entry with no written reason? · rule by rule, with proof from the journal".
cenas.narracao: Then, the audit. For each rule written in your plan, you answer yes or no, with evidence taken from the journal. Was the size within what you defined? Was the stop moved? Was there any entry with no written reason? Any no is a point of attention, and every point of attention has a cause. The most frequent cause is almost never technical. It is emotional: boredom, haste, the urge to recover, fear of missing the rise. Give it a name, write it beside the line, and see whether it repeats the following week. It is not a punishment. It is a cool-headed reading, done with the same calm you would bring to reviewing any other process.

cenas.visual: Ruben writing on a sheet, with the phrase on screen: "One thing to change this week."
cenas.narracao: Now, the hardest step: deciding one thing. Only one. Ask yourself which mistake repeated the most, and write a concrete rule to avoid it. For example: from now on, no order goes in without a written reason. And here is the golden rule of this lesson: don't change the rules halfway through the week. Change them on review day, after you have seen them written down. Changing everything on the back of the last trade is the quickest way to never know what works and what doesn't. If the change is too big, shrink it until it fits in a single sentence.

cenas.visual: Final screen with the routine in five lines: "fixed day and time · journal open · audit · one change · review log".
cenas.narracao: Last step, and this one is not to be skipped: log the review itself. Date, number of trades, number of rules followed, and the change you chose. That way, three months from now, you can see whether your discipline went up or down, and not just what you feel about it. Thirty minutes a week, without fail, is worth more than a study marathon that never repeats. And if one week you can't, do the short version: ten minutes, just the audit. Something small and done beats something big and postponed. Without a log, the review did not happen.

aulas.titulo: Aula 14.5 — Stopping rules, psychology and the level 3 mission
aulas.gancho: The worst decision of a market day is almost never the first. It is the fourth, made to win back the third.

cenas.visual: Screen with "stopping rules" in large letters and, below, three items: "consecutive losses · maximum daily loss · cut-off time".
cenas.narracao: We have reached the last lesson of the module, and the part that decides whether the others are worth anything. Stopping rules. These are the rules that say when you stop, before you start arguing with yourself. There can be three: a maximum number of consecutive losses, a maximum loss amount for the day, and a time after which you do not enter. Write them with the numbers you choose. There is no magic number, not even mine. There is your number, written beforehand and kept. And if the number is hit, the day ends there, even if the chart is doing exactly what you wanted.

cenas.visual: Three spiral arrows on screen: "I lose" → "I increase the size" → "I lose more".
cenas.narracao: Now psychology, without beating around the bush. There is a classic spiral. You lose a trade and feel the urge to win it back. You increase the size of the next one, to recover faster. You lose again, because the bigger position amplifies the loss, and you enter a third to plug the hole. Each step seems reasonable at the time. Together they are a disaster. Break this spiral with a simple rule: never increase the size after a loss. The size is the one in the plan, always, the one you wrote before any emotion showed up. Notice that the spiral does not need greed. The urge to plug a hole is enough.

cenas.visual: Ruben taking a deep breath, in silence. On screen, in large letters: "24-hour pause".
cenas.narracao: And when you feel emotion taking over, use the pause. If you have hit a stopping rule, or if you feel you can't think clearly, close the WebTrader and don't come back that day. If you really want to look at a market again, wait twenty-four hours and come back with the journal in front of you. The pause is not weakness. It is the cheapest rule there is, and the one that saves the most money for whoever uses it. If someone tells you that you have to decide now, because the opportunity won't come back, you already know what that is. Close the conversation, breathe, and go back to your plan.

cenas.visual: Notebook with a crossed-out page and an underlined sentence: "I want to win it back". Caption: "illustrative case".
cenas.narracao: Illustrative case: Tiago, forty, had no stopping rule. One morning, he lost two trades in a row and decided he would recover before lunch. It was not the first time he had thought that way, but it was the first time the journal was in front of him. He wrote, without meaning to: I want to win it back. That sentence gave everything away. He closed the screen. At the Friday review, he realised the losses that morning had the same origin: haste. Illustrative example, of course, because what matters is the pattern, not the value of each trade. Think about this during your next week, before you need it.

cenas.visual: Mission screen, with a box to tick and the title "Level 3 mission". Checklist: "stopping rules written · 30 simulated trades · complete journal · weekly review done".
cenas.narracao: The level three mission, which is optional, and which is the most demanding in this course: thirty trades in a simulated account, with a complete journal, before you think about a real account. Thirty. Not thirty days of luck. Thirty trades with the rules written beforehand, with the size from the plan, and with the weekly review done. Each trade with its journal line filled in, including the rule column. If at the end you have not followed the rules consistently, the mission is not complete, and you start again more calmly. Nobody needs level three to be an investor with DCA. And think about a real account only after this, and only with money you are prepared to lose completely.

modulos.titulo: Módulo 15 — Taxes, the 90-day plan and the certificate (≈15 min)

aulas.titulo: Aula 15.1 — Taxes in Portugal: the 365-day rule
aulas.gancho: With crypto, tax is not paid on the day you buy. It can show up, however, on the day you sell, if you are not prepared.

cenas.visual: Animated calendar with 365 days filling up, and a marker flagging day 365.
cenas.narracao: Let's get to taxes, with a preliminary note: I speak in general terms, because the rules change, and whoever decides your situation is a certified accountant. That said, there is a basic principle you should know. In Portugal, crypto capital gains on assets held for less than 365 days are taxed at 28 per cent. If you hold them for 365 days or more, they are, as a rule, exempt. A capital gain is the positive difference between the sale value and the purchase value. If you sell for less than you paid, there is no gain to tax. The principle is simple. The details are what change the sum, and they are what catch those who are not prepared. The purchase date and the sale date count days, and a single day's difference can change everything.

cenas.visual: Figures on screen: "€1,000 purchase · €1,300 sale · €300 gain · €84 tax at 28%". Caption: "illustrative example · round figures, no fees".
cenas.narracao: Let's look at an illustrative example, with round figures and no fees. You buy one thousand euros of crypto and, three months later, you sell for one thousand three hundred. The gain is three hundred euros. On those three hundred you apply the twenty-eight per cent, which gives eighty-four euros. Notice this carefully: the tax does not fall on the total of one thousand three hundred, it falls only on the gain. If the same investment had been held for 365 days or more, the general rule would be different, and the sum would, as a rule, be exempt. All of this can change, so always confirm the current version before drawing conclusions.

cenas.visual: Screen with a record sheet: columns "Date", "Asset", "Quantity", "Value in euros", "Fees", "Type of operation".
cenas.narracao: So, record everything. Every purchase, every sale and every swap, with the date, the asset, the quantity, the value in euros at the time and the fees paid. Add a column for the type of operation. Don't rely on memory or on loose screenshots, because in a year you won't remember everything. A simple spreadsheet is enough to start. If you swap one coin for another, record both ends of the operation, because both can count. And keep this sheet alongside the trading journal you learned about in module 14. They are two different records, and both pay you back for the time they take.

cenas.visual: Large warning on screen: "Confirm with a certified accountant". Below, in a list: "crypto-to-crypto swaps · staking · airdrops · aggregation".
cenas.narracao: Now the most important warning of the lesson. Crypto-to-crypto swaps, staking income, airdrops and other cases may be treated differently, and I don't want to guess that in a video. There is also the option of aggregation, in which the gain goes into your annual income. It may be more or less advantageous, depending on your tax bracket, and that comparison needs someone who sees your complete figures. Don't make tax decisions based on a video, nor on what someone said in a message group. Take your record sheet and the questions you wrote beforehand to the meeting with the accountant.

cenas.visual: Large text on screen: "Do you live in France or another country? The rules are different. Confirm with the local tax authority and an accountant." Ruben in a close-up.
cenas.narracao: An important note for anyone who does not live in Portugal, for example in France or another country. This lesson explains the Portuguese rules, and the rules of other countries are different. They can differ in the rate, the deadline, the way you declare and the way they treat crypto. Don't apply anything I have said to your situation without confirming it. What you should do is contact the tax authority of your country of residence and an accountant qualified in that country. Ask for the answer in writing and bring your records. If you live in France, for example, the conversation is with the French authorities and a French professional, not with this video.

cenas.visual: Illustrative case: Pedro, thirty-one, a designer in Lisbon, leafing through old statements on a laptop. Caption: "illustrative case".
cenas.narracao: Illustrative case: Pedro made several purchases and sales over the year, without recording anything. When the time came to declare, he did not know the exact dates or the amount he had paid in each operation. He spent weeks searching through statements and old conversations. The tax itself was not the worst part. The worst was the stress of rebuilding a whole year from memory. A ten-minute record each month would have avoided all of that. In short: under 365 days can mean 28 per cent on the gain, 365 days or more is, as a rule, exemption, and the record is your best ally.

aulas.titulo: Aula 15.2 — Your 90-day plan
aulas.gancho: Ninety days sounds like a long time. But what you are going to see is a calendar with three phases and one rule: don't skip any.

cenas.visual: Ninety-day calendar in three coloured blocks: "days 1–30 · fundamentals and first purchase", "days 31–60 · the DCA ritual", "days 61–90 · level 3, optional, in a simulated account".
cenas.narracao: The ninety-day plan has three phases, and each one has its mission. Days one to thirty: fundamentals and first purchase. Days thirty-one to sixty: the DCA ritual, the Friday one, done every week and recorded. Days sixty-one to ninety: level three, which is optional, and which only happens in a simulated account. Notice the order. First you understand your key and your money, then you buy with rules, and only then do you practise whatever you want to practise, with no real risk. There are no shortcuts between the phases. If one goes wrong, repeat it before you move on.

cenas.visual: Phase one screen with four blocks: "week 1 · security", "week 2 · choose and verify", "week 3 · first purchase", "week 4 · review".
cenas.narracao: Phase one, days one to thirty. Week one: security. Authenticator app, password manager, and the seed phrase written by hand, kept in two separate places. Week two: you choose an authorised platform, complete identity verification, and understand the fees and the difference between a market order and a limit order. Week three: the first purchase, with a small amount, for example ten euros, followed by a test transfer to your wallet. Illustrative example, of course. Week four: you review the anti-scam checklist and sign the level one mission. Without the signed checklist, level one is not closed.

cenas.visual: Ruben with the notebook open. On screen: "Friday ritual · 15 minutes · four weeks in a row · record kept".
cenas.narracao: Phase two, days thirty-one to sixty. This is where the Friday ritual comes in, which you learned in module 7 with the MTM Smart DCA, and everything you put together in modules 8, 9 and 10: your Portfolio with the reserve pot, the reading of the market, and the rules for taking profits. The level two mission is simple to state and hard to fulfil: a written DCA plan, with the monthly cap and the pot, the DCA alerts switched on in the app, and the ritual done four weeks in a row, recorded in the notebook. If one Friday is missed, you don't start over. You record what happened and come back the following Friday. What counts is consistency, not perfection.

cenas.visual: Phase three screen with three boxes: "complete journal", "stopping rules written", "30 simulated trades". Caption: "optional".
cenas.narracao: Phase three, days sixty-one to ninety, and here it is optional. If you want to move on to level three, with the Aurum Flow Cripto and the perpetuals, the rule is the same one we saw in module 14: simulated account, written stopping rules, and thirty trades with a complete journal before you think about a real account. If you don't want to, that's fine. An investor who does DCA with discipline and reviews their plan does not need derivatives to be doing good work. Derivatives are a choice, never an obligation, and never with money you need.

cenas.visual: Notebook with the ninety-day plan, with the dates filled in by hand. Caption: "illustrative case".
cenas.narracao: Illustrative case: Sara made the plan with the notebook beside her. In phase one, she reached week three without buying anything, because she didn't trust the platform. Instead of jumping to phase two, she repeated week two, did the verification and only then bought. In phase two, she missed a Friday because of a trip. She noted the gap in the notebook and carried on the following week. When she reached ninety days, she had not done everything perfectly. She had done everything in the right order. And that is what the plan asks for.

cenas.visual: Ruben closing the notebook. On screen: "One phase at a time."
cenas.narracao: One last rule for the plan. Write it on a sheet, with the real start and end dates of each phase, and sign it. Put the review of each phase in the calendar, as if it were a booked appointment. And don't move on to the next phase just because you feel bored. Boredom is normal in DCA, and that is exactly where most people give up. If the phase is closed, you move on. If it isn't, you go back to the missing week. This is not a race. It is a calendar, and the calendar is yours. Keep a copy of the plan in the course notebook, so you always have it to hand.

aulas.titulo: Aula 15.3 — Review of the whole course
aulas.gancho: Fourteen modules later, the honest question is this: what do you really take with you?

cenas.visual: Map with three levels side by side: "level 1 · modules 1 to 5", "level 2 · modules 6 to 10", "level 3 · modules 11 to 14, optional".
cenas.narracao: Let's review the whole course in a few minutes, by level. Level one, fundamentals, modules one to five: money and blockchain, the map of coins, the first safe purchase, your key and the anti-scam shield. Level two, investor with the MTM Smart DCA, modules six to ten: the cycles and the halving, your DCA with the house tools, the Portfolio with the reserve pot, the reading of the market and taking profits with written rules. Level three, optional, modules eleven to fourteen: perpetuals, the Aurum Flow Cripto strategy, risk and position size, and executing without emotion. Three levels, one idea: each one depends on the one before.

cenas.visual: Checklist on screen: "level 1 mission · first purchase · test transfer · anti-scam checklist signed".
cenas.narracao: Level one review. The mission was a first purchase, small, on an authorised platform, a test transfer to your wallet, and the anti-scam checklist signed. If the three boxes are ticked, level one is closed. If they are not, don't move on. A purchase made without the key safely stored and without the checklist is a risk you don't need to take. Notice that I did not ask you for a result. I asked you for a process: verify, store, confirm and record. That is what you can control, and it is what the course has taught you to do.

cenas.visual: Screen with the level two and three missions, side by side, with the word "written" highlighted.
cenas.narracao: Level two review: a written DCA plan, with monthly cap and reserve pot, DCA alerts switched on, and four weeks in a row of the Friday ritual, recorded. And level three, if you did it: thirty simulated trades with a complete journal and written stopping rules. Ask yourself, for each mission: what is written down? If the answer is only I think so, the mission is not closed. The course asks you for paper, not memory. That paper is the proof that you are learning, and it is also the only honest way to assess your own progress.

cenas.visual: List of concepts on screen: "key and seed · DCA · reserve pot · settlement · journal · stopping rules · capital gain".
cenas.narracao: Now the concepts that cannot be missing, and that you should be able to explain without looking at your notes. Why the key is yours. What DCA is, and why it does not stop. What the reserve pot is. What settlement is, and why leverage does not create money. What the journal is for. And why a stopping rule exists before emotion shows up. If you cannot explain one of these concepts in your own words, go back to the corresponding module. You don't have to memorize. You have to understand. If you want, write each one in a sentence and compare it with the version in the corresponding module when you're done.

cenas.visual: Ruben, close-up, with the phrase on screen: "Choose what you apply first. Not everything."
cenas.narracao: A typical temptation at the end of a course is to apply everything in the same week. Don't do that. Choose one thing you have learned and apply it for a month. It can be the security checklist, it can be the Friday ritual, it can be the journal. A small, constant practice is worth more than ten big intentions. And if you realise you are missing a module, go back to it before you move on. There is no prize for finishing first, and what matters is that you understand what you are doing. If you feel that urge, write it in the notebook and wait a week before acting.

cenas.visual: Screen with five numbered questions: "1 · what stayed? · 2 · what am I still not following? · 3 · which rule will I change? · 4 · which mission is missing? · 5 · what do I ask the accountant?"
cenas.narracao: Before the exam, five questions, written in the notebook. What has stayed with me? What am I still not following? Which rule will I change this week? Which mission still needs closing? And what do I want to ask the accountant, if I have tax doubts? Write the answers down, with the date. These five questions are your personal summary of the course, and they are worth more than any summary I could give you. The final exam is next. You don't have to answer them out loud, but you do have to write them down, with today's date, and keep them alongside the ninety-day plan. They are your starting point for what comes after the course, and it is worth doing them with time and without rushing.

aulas.titulo: Aula 15.4 — Final exam, certificate and follow-up
aulas.gancho: We have reached the exam. Before it, one question only you can answer: what are you going to do with all of this, next week?

cenas.visual: Screen with the title "Final exam" and, below it, "questions about the fourteen modules". Ruben in a medium shot.
cenas.narracao: The final exam covers the fourteen modules. It asks about what you have learned, not about what the market will do, because nobody knows that. You will find questions about the key and security, about DCA and the pot, about the journal, about the 365-day rule and about reading risk. If you did the missions with paper, the exam is a calm review. If you skipped modules, this is the moment to go back to them. There is no trick. There is process, and the exam only asks for what the course has already asked of you along the way.

cenas.visual: Certificate model on screen, with the name field blank and the caption "MTM completion certificate".
cenas.narracao: When you pass the exam, you receive the MTM certificate. It is worth being clear about what it is. It is a certificate of completion of this course. It is not a licence, it is not a regulated professional qualification, and it does not authorise you to provide financial advice to anyone. It shows that you completed the programme and did the missions. Use it with that honesty. If someone tells you that a certificate like this gives access to guaranteed returns, you are looking at the warning sign you already know from other modules. Notice that the certificate is the end of a study path, not the start of a career.

cenas.visual: Screen with two boxes: "monthly group sessions" and "course room in the app's chat".
cenas.narracao: After the course, there is follow-up. One group session a month, for you to bring the questions that have come up in the ritual, the journal and the plan. And the course room, in the app's chat, where you can ask other students and clear up doubts about each module. One thing to watch: it is a space for learning, not for deciding for anyone. It is not a buy or sell recommendation, and nobody in the room knows your situation. If anyone asks you for money, data or your key, leave the conversation and report it.

cenas.visual: Checklist on screen: "1 · missions closed · 2 · exam taken · 3 · 90-day plan signed and stored".
cenas.narracao: Before you close the course, three things. First, the missions for the levels you decided to do, with the paper filled in. Second, the final exam, taken calmly and without rushing to finish. Third, the ninety-day plan signed and stored somewhere separate from your seed phrase. Don't mix the two, because whoever keeps the plan and the key in the same place has a security problem. This checklist is your proof that you reached the end with method. If any of these is not done, it is not the end of the world: go back to the corresponding module, do what is missing, and only then consider the course finished.

cenas.visual: Ruben, close-up, with three sentences on screen: "The key is yours." · "The numbers are illustrative." · "Wait twenty-four hours."
cenas.narracao: Now, the final warning, which is not optional. This course is educational content. It is not financial advice, it is not a recommendation to buy or sell any asset, and it knows nothing about your situation, your income, your debts or your goals. Crypto is a high-risk market. The risk of loss is real, and you can lose part or all of what you put in. Three rules to take with you. The key is yours, and no legitimate party will ask you for it: not support, not a technician, not someone friendly in a conversation. The example numbers are always illustrative, and be suspicious of anyone who promises you gains and of anyone who rushes you. And a written plan, with twenty-four hours of waiting, is worth more than any hunch.

cenas.visual: Final screen with the MoreThanMoney logo and the phrase: "Look after your key".
cenas.narracao: Before closing, the final mission of the course: write your ninety-day plan on a sheet, with today's date, sign it, and store it somewhere safe, separate from your seed phrase. Then, answer the five review questions. Thank you for giving this course the time it asks for. Not everyone sits down to study this calmly, and that already says a lot about you. Remember: educational content, not financial advice, and the risk of loss is real. Look after your key. Until next time. Also reread the module 14 review about the spiral, because that is where temptation usually comes back.
